full_text_sections.discussion: DISCUSSIONThis study investigated the etiologies of AFI cases reported in Amapa State from 2018 to 2022. Of 727 evaluated individuals, definitive diagnoses established 185 cases (25.4%), including 23 cases of co-infection.Our findings are in line with previous regional studies. Dengue remains the predominant AFI etiological agent in Latin America, with chikungunya and zika showing an increased prevalence. Leptospirosis, though often overlooked, represents a prevalent bacterial contributor1,16.Notably, this study found one case of mayaro virus infection, consistent with its rare occurrence in Amapa State (six confirmed cases nationwide in 2015-2025) 17 . Following systematic PCR testing, no individual in our cohort was positive for Oropouche virus disease, despite epidemiological data (2015-2025) reporting 16,571 cases nationwide, including 218 in Amapa State. A recent increase in its detection (2023-2024) likely reflects greater diagnostic capacity and active case-finding 17 . These results suggest Amapa State may represent a zone of “silent expansion” for Oropouche virus disease, in which overlapping arbovirus transmission obscures true disease burden. Strengthening surveillance, expanding laboratory capacity, and prioritizing differential diagnostics are essential to capture epidemiological dynamics and guide interventions. While multiplex syndromic panels are ideal, widespread molecular testing faces strict budget and logistical constraints within the public health system in Amapa State. A more sustainable solution could be a tiered “reflex testing” cascade at LACEN-AP. Under this protocol, a negative molecular result for primary arboviruses (dengue/zika/chikungunya) would automatically trigger reflex testing for leptospirosis and parvovirus B19 using the original biological sample. This flow could optimize laboratory resources, cut costs, and bypass initial clinical triage blind spots without requiring secondary patient appointments. Lessons from the Amazon highlight the global importance of integrated arbovirus surveillance in regions with overlapping transmission.The fact that 80.5% of initial hypotheses were generically classified as suspected arboviruses exposes a profound “dengue-centric” bias. Because the early symptoms of dengue, parvovirus B19, and leptospirosis overlap almost entirely, physical triage alone is insufficient. To address this, the regional health system must implement targeted continuing medical education focusing on broad syndromic classifications—such as “acute exanthematous febrile syndrome”—rather than single-pathogen guessing. Furthermore, standard patient intake forms should mandate structured epidemiological risk questions regarding recent floodwater exposure (leptospirosis), mining or forest exposure (malaria/arboviruses), and artisanal acai consumption (acute Chagas disease) to guide clinical suspicion before laboratory results are available.Leptospirosis remains a critical public health challenge in Amapa State linked to seasonal flooding, precarious sanitation, and transmission in wetland and stilt-house communities 18 , 19 . Despite its prevalence, underreporting persists due to symptomatic overlap with malaria and dengue 20 . Our finding that Leptospira spp. was the second most prevalent confirmed pathogen underscores its critical standing in the regional etiology of AFI. Unlike arboviral infections, which only require supportive care, leptospirosis demands timely antibiotic therapy to prevent severe, potentially fatal complications such as Weil’s disease or pulmonary hemorrhage syndrome. Relying entirely on early clinical differentiation or waiting days for laboratory confirmation in highly endemic zones often results in catastrophic therapeutic delays. Therefore, in areas with high dengue and leptospirosis co-endemicity, clinical protocols must explicitly support the initiation of empirical antibiotic treatment (such as doxycycline or amoxicillin) for patients presenting with severe febrile syndromes and clear epidemiological risk factors, prioritizing clinical survival over definitive laboratory timelines.Parvovirus B19 occurred in 16 cases (7.6%), representing a notable proportion of AFI diagnoses. Its clinical recognition remains challenging as its early symptoms closely mimic arboviruses such as dengue, Zika, and chikungunya. In tropical regions, B19V is often misdiagnosed as dengue due to overlapping presentations of fever, headache, and rash 21 , 22 . The post-pandemic resurgence of B19V in 2024-2025 marked a significant epidemiological shift driven by an “immunity gap” in pediatric populations. IgM positivity peaked at ~40% in children aged 5-9 years and ~10% in adults, complicating AFI differential diagnosis 23 .Of the 727 investigated individuals, viral hepatitis was suspected in 10 cases (1.4%), with three confirmed cases of hepatitis A and B (1.4%). No HEV cases were identified despite evidence that HEV genotype 3 is a zoonotic pathogen of concern in Brazil 24 , 25 .Meta-analyses estimate anti-HEV IgG seroprevalence at ~6% nationally, with regional variations: ~3% in the Amazon and up to 14.2% in rural Rondônia 26 - 28 . Diagnostic invisibility remains a major challenge as public health screening routinely ignores HEV testing, particularly in vulnerable Amazonian populations. Overlapping clinical presentations with hepatitis b and d further obscure HEV detection, suggesting that some acute hepatitis cases of “unknown etiology” may represent undiagnosed HEV.Measles occurred in 15 cases (7.1%). Despite mass vaccination programs, Brazil lost its measles-free status in 2018 following outbreaks linked to Venezuelan migration and low vaccination coverage 29 , 30 . Although elimination status was regained in 2023-2024, new cases in Tocantins in 2025 highlight ongoing vulnerability. The porous border of Amapa State with French Guiana and high mobility of illegal gold miners create a unique epidemiological corridor sustaining measles and other infectious diseases.Malaria transmission remains a major concern in Oiapoque, one of the highest transmission zones in the Americas. Despite persistent “silent” transmission by asymptomatic carriers in mobile populations, our cohort only included two malaria cases (0.95%), reflecting the predominance of samples collected in Macapa. Epidemiological data shows a downward trend in Amapa State, with a 16.8% reduction in cases from 2024 to 2025 and an 82% decline in Macapa. Nonetheless, the Oiapoque border remains the main epidemiological challenge in the state 31 - 34 . The cohort included a case of acute Chagas disease, reflecting the specific epidemiological profile of Amapa State. From 2018 to 2022, the state remained a high-endemicity region for acute Chagas disease in the Brazilian Amazon, with oral transmission—primarily by consumption of artisanal acai and bacaba juice—emerging as the dominant route of infection 35 , 36 .A notable finding in this study was the elevated detection of multiple infectious agents. Across 727 patients, this study found 209 reactive results, with co-detection of distinct pathogens in 23 cases. Similar patterns have been reported in regions endemic for malaria and arboviruses, in which simultaneous infections are confirmed by multiple molecular assays 37 , 38 . In such contexts, potential cross-reactivity further compounds diagnostic complexity. The cross-reactivity between zika, dengue, and yellow fever serological assays, for example, is primarily attributed to the high degree of structural homology within the envelope protein in members of the Orthoflavivirus genus 39 .The seasonal transmission pattern in this study likely reflects the equatorial climate of the region, in which persistently high precipitation and elevated temperatures sustain vector breeding sites throughout the year. Thus, the continuous circulation of febrile illnesses in Amapa State may obscure the more distinct seasonal peaks and lag patterns in other climatic se…
full_text_sections.conclusion: CONCLUSIONSThe causes of AFI in Amapa are multiple and may involve infection by more than one etiological agent. This underscores the complexity of diagnostic accuracy in regions with overlapping multiple arbovirus and bacterial transmission. The detection of rare pathogens such as Mayaro virus and acute Chagas disease reflects the unique ecological and epidemiological profile of the region. These findings reinforce the role of Amapa State as a sentinel for infectious disease surveillance as its porous borders, ecological connectivity, and high human mobility sustain transmission corridors. Strengthening laboratory capacity, integrating differential diagnostics, and expanding surveillance systems are essential to capture the true burden of AFI and to guide targeted interventions. While acknowledging the limitations inherent to retrospective designs and diagnostic constraints, this study emphasizes the global relevance of integrated surveillance in ecologically dynamic regions. Crucially, addressing these challenges requires improving data completeness, such as by the meticulous entry and digital optimization of GAL forms, to ensure accurate epidemiological tracking in complex equatorial settings.

A comprehensive understanding of their etiologies is essential for advancing clinical practice, guiding public health strategies, and informing policy development.The ecology of the Amazon basin—characterized by deforestation, flooding, and high vector diversity—creates favorable conditions for arboviruses and bacterial pathogens, amplifying the risk of febrile outbreaks 2 . Thus, the region experiences a wide spectrum of febrile illnesses caused by viral, bacterial, and parasitic agents, reflecting diverse ecological and climatic conditions 3 .The overlapping clinical manifestations of diseases such as dengue, malaria, leptospirosis, and rickettsial infections complicate accurate diagnosis. This diagnostic uncertainty often results in delayed or inappropriate treatment. Misdiagnosis may postpone life-saving antibiotic therapy, whereas indiscriminate prescribing contributes to antimicrobial resistance. The Pan American Health Organization 4 has emphasized antimicrobial resistance as a regional priority, highlighting its impact on healthcare costs and mortality.Community-acquired AFI contributes substantially to regional morbidity and mortality, considerably straining healthcare systems and requiring significant resource allocation for surveillance and management. Socioeconomic factors, including poverty and limited access to healthcare, exacerbate transmission dynamics and hinder effective disease control 5 .Surveillance represents a critical component of disease control. The Brazilian Amazon is recognized as a global hotspot for emerging viruses 2 . Integrated screening systems may serve as sentinel mechanisms for early detection. As deforestation and mining activities intensify, human populations increasingly encounter novel vectors such as mosquitoes and midges, underscoring the importance of screening febrile patients for malaria and arboviruses6. While dengue remains a major concern, the unique geography of the state—bordering French Guiana and the Atlantic Ocean, and dominated by dense rainforest and wetlands—heightens the risk of diverse infectious diseases. High rainfall and humidity render leptospirosis endemic, particularly in peri-urban areas such as Macapa and Santana 5 . Recent land-use transformations, including illegal mining and the expansion of acai production, have had measurable epidemiological consequences. papers.title_original: Sentinel surveillance of acute febrile illness in a Brazilian Amazon region: laboratory findings and epidemiological implications

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to identify the potential etiologies of viral and other infections in acute febrile illness (AFI) cases reported from 2018 to 2022 in the Amazon region of Amapa State, Brazil, to better understand the epidemiological landscape of these infections.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study was a sentinel surveillance conducted in public health laboratories in the Amazon region of Amapa State, Brazil, from 2018 to 2022, analyzing samples from 727 individuals. Definitive diagnoses were obtained in 185 individuals (25.4%), yielding 209 positive results and including 23 cases of co-infection.
analysis.methods: Diagnostic tests included serology, polymerase chain reaction (PCR), and sequencing, with results recorded on GAL. Confirmatory methods at the Virology Laboratory of the Institute of Tropical Medicine of Sao Paulo (LV-IMT-FMUSP) involved enzyme linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), electrochemiluminescence, reverse transcription PCR (RT-PCR), and sequencing for viral agents, while bacterial and fungal infections were confirmed using cultures and other specific tests.
analysis.main_results: Measles was identified as one of the pathogens with 15 positive results out of 53 tests (28.3%). Other notable findings included dengue (109/650, 16.8%), leptospirosis (20/98, 20.4%), chikungunya (16/86, 18.6%), and parvovirus B19 (16/21, 76.2%). There were 23 cases of co-infection, with measles being involved in 7 cases.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted these findings as highlighting the significant role of measles virus in the etiology of acute febrile illness in the region, contributing to the understanding of the disease burden and the need for targeted surveillance and control measures.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform public health strategies for measles surveillance and control in the Amazon region, emphasizing the importance of integrating laboratory data with clinical and demographic information to better manage and prevent outbreaks.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's descriptive analysis may limit the depth of interpretation, and the statistical significance of some findings was affected by the Benjamini-Hochberg correction, suggesting moderate evidence strength for the observed associations.

analysis.summary_en: This study conducted sentinel surveillance of acute febrile illness (AFI) in the Amazon region of Amapa State, Brazil, from 2018 to 2022, identifying measles virus as a significant etiological agent. Measles was detected in 15 out of 53 tests (28.3%), with 7 cases of co-infection involving dengue. The study combined clinical and demographic data with laboratory results from GAL and LV-IMT-FMUSP, using methods such as ELISA, RT-PCR, and sequencing. While the findings highlight the role of measles in the region's AFI cases, the descriptive nature of the analysis and the impact of statistical corrections on some results suggest moderate evidence strength. These results can inform public health strategies for measles surveillance and control in the area.

papers.title: Determinants of childhood vaccination differ between conflict-affected and non-conflict regions in Cameroon

source_records.title: Determinants of childhood vaccination differ between conflict-affected and non-conflict regions in Cameroon

papers.full_text: AbstractIntroductionChildhood vaccination remains one of the most effective public health interventions, yet coverage is often lowest in settings affected by conflict and structural disadvantage. Cameroon has faced overlapping humanitarian crises in its Far North, North-West, and South-West regions, but evidence comparing determinants of full vaccination between conflict-affected and non-conflict regions remains limited. This study explores determinants of full vaccination status in 12–23 months children in Cameroon, stratified by conflict regions.MethodsWe conducted a secondary analysis of the 2018 Cameroon Demographic and Health Survey, including 1,824 living children aged 12–23 months. Full basic vaccination was defined as receipt of one dose of BCG, three doses of pentavalent vaccine, three doses of polio vaccine, and one dose of measles vaccine. Survey-weighted logistic regression was used to identify factors associated with full vaccination overall and by conflict status.ResultsOverall, 53.08% of children were fully vaccinated. Coverage was lower in conflict-affected than in non-conflict regions (45.29% versus 55.97%). In unadjusted analysis, conflict status was associated with lower odds of full vaccination, but this association was no longer significant in the adjusted model. At the national level, higher odds of full vaccination were associated with richer household wealth, maternal secondary or higher education, antenatal care attendance, and postnatal care. In conflict-affected regions, maternal secondary or higher education, postnatal care, and facility delivery remained significant predictors of full vaccination.DiscussionFull vaccination coverage in Cameroon remains below desirable levels, with lower crude coverage in conflict-affected regions. However, after adjustment, conflict status was not independently associated with full vaccination, suggesting that socioeconomic conditions and contact with maternal health services are more important determinants. DHS.01. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to data collection. This study used the Children’s Recode (KR) dataset. The analysis was restricted to living children, one per household, aged 12–23 months at the time of the survey, which is the standard age group used to assess completion of basic childhood vaccination. A child was considered fully vaccinated if they had received one dose of Bacille Calmette–Guérin (BCG), three doses of pentavalent vaccine, three doses of polio vaccine (excluding the birth dose), and one dose of measles vaccine. Vaccination was considered received if the vaccination date was recorded on the card, the vaccination was marked on the card without a date, or the mother reported that the child had received the vaccine.The main exposure of interest was residence in a conflict-affected region. The Far North, North-West, and South-West regions were classified as conflict-affected because they have experienced sustained armed conflict during the study period, whereas the remaining seven regions were classified as non-conflict regions. This classification was based on the regional level available in the DHS dataset, which represents the finest geographic resolution accessible for public-use data. All other regions were classified as non-conflict regions. Figure 1 shows the geographical classification of conflict-affected and non-conflict regions of Cameroon. Weighted percentages were reported together with unweighted frequencies. Differences between conflict-affected and non-conflict regions were assessed using design-adjusted Pearson chi-square tests. Associations between explanatory variables and full vaccination were examined using survey-weighted logistic regression models, and statistical significance was evaluated using Wald tests. All analyses accounted for the complex sampling design of the DHS by applying sampling weights and adjusting for clustering at the primary sampling unit level and stratification. Potential interaction effects between selected covariates, including conflict status with maternal education, household wealth, and antenatal care visits, were explored by including multiplicative interaction terms in the survey-weighted logistic regression models. Interaction terms with p < 0.05 were considered statistically significant and retained in the final model. As none of the interaction terms reached statistical significance, they were not retained in the final models. Model discrimination was assessed using Tjur’s coefficient of discrimination (Tjur’s R2), calculated as the difference between the mean predicted probabilities among fully vaccinated and non-fully vaccinated children. Observations with missing values in variables included in the regression analyses were excluded using complete-case analysis. Missing data were minimal for all study variables, with the exception of antenatal care visits, for which 119 observations (6.5%) had missing information. Bivariate logistic regression analyses were performed to examine the association between each independent variable and full vaccination status. Candidate explanatory variables were selected a priori based on previous literature and their potential relevance to childhood vaccination. Among these candidate variables, those associated with the outcome at p < 0.20 in bivariable analyses were entered into the multivariable logistic regression models. The p < 0.20 threshold was chosen to avoid excluding potentially important confounders during model building (26, 27). Separate multivariable models were estimated for the entire country, for conflict-affected regions, and for non-conflict regions. Multicollinearity among the explanatory variables was assessed using variance inflation factors (VIFs). No evidence of problematic multicollinearity was observed for the three models. Adjusted odds ratios (AORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were reported. Statistical significance in the final models was defined as a two-sided p-value <0.05.All statistical analyses were performed using Stata (version 16; StataCorp, College Station, TX, USA). full_text_sections.abstract: AbstractIntroductionChildhood vaccination remains one of the most effective public health interventions, yet coverage is often lowest in settings affected by conflict and structural disadvantage. Cameroon has faced overlapping humanitarian crises in its Far North, North-West, and South-West regions, but evidence comparing determinants of full vaccination between conflict-affected and non-conflict regions remains limited. This study explores determinants of full vaccination status in 12–23 months children in Cameroon, stratified by conflict regions.MethodsWe conducted a secondary analysis of the 2018 Cameroon Demographic and Health Survey, including 1,824 living children aged 12–23 months. Full basic vaccination was defined as receipt of one dose of BCG, three doses of pentavalent vaccine, three doses of polio vaccine, and one dose of measles vaccine. Survey-weighted logistic regression was used to identify factors associated with full vaccination overall and by conflict status.ResultsOverall, 53.08% of children were fully vaccinated. Coverage was lower in conflict-affected than in non-conflict regions (45.29% versus 55.97%). In unadjusted analysis, conflict status was associated with lower odds of full vaccination, but this association was no longer significant in the adjusted model. At the national level, higher odds of full vaccination were associated with richer household wealth, maternal secondary or higher education, antenatal care attendance, and postnatal care. In conflict-affected regions, maternal secondary or higher education, postnatal care, and facility delivery remained significant predictors of full vaccination.DiscussionFull vaccination coverage in Cameroon remains below desirable levels, with lower crude coverage in conflict-affected regions. However, after adjustment, conflict status was not independently associated with full vaccination, suggesting that socioeconomic conditions and contact with maternal health services are more important determinants. Strengthening antenatal and postnatal care and reducing socioeconomic barriers may improve vaccination coverage, especially in fragile settings.Keywords: Cameroon, conflict-affected settings, Demographic and Health Survey, health inequalities, immunization, vaccination coverage

full_text_sections.discussion: DiscussionSummary of main findingsThis study examined the determinants of full basic childhood vaccination among children aged 12–23 months in Cameroon using nationally representative data from the 2018 Demographic and Health Survey. Overall, just over half of children were fully vaccinated, and vaccination coverage was consistently lower in conflict-affected regions compared with non-conflict regions. In the national model, full vaccination was significantly associated with household wealth, maternal education, antenatal care attendance, and postnatal care for the newborn. An important finding of this study is that, although children living in conflict-affected regions had lower crude vaccination coverage than those living in non-conflict regions, conflict status itself was not independently associated with full vaccination after adjustment. This suggests that the observed disparity in vaccination coverage may be largely explained by differences in socioeconomic conditions and access to maternal and child health services rather than conflict exposure alone. These findings highlight the importance of addressing the underlying structural barriers to immunization in conflict-affected settings, while recognizing that conflict may still indirectly influence vaccination through its effects on healthcare delivery and household vulnerability.Differences between conflict and non-conflict regionsThis study also provides important insights into how determinants of vaccination differ between conflict-affected and non-conflict regions. Children living in conflict-affected regions had lower vaccination coverage overall, which is consistent with previous evidence showing that armed conflict can disrupt health systems, reduce access to services, and undermine routine immunization programs (9, 12). In addition, attacks against healthcare workers, vaccinators and health facilities, as well as insecurity limiting the movement of healthcare personnel, may further disrupt routine immunization activities and reduce access to vaccination services in conflict-affected settings (28, 29). Our findings are also consistent with reports from Cameroon documenting reductions in routine immunization coverage during periods of insecurity, particularly in the South-West region, where armed conflict has challenged the delivery of vaccination services and supplementary immunization activities (20–22, 30). Conflict status was no longer independently associated with full vaccination after adjustment for socioeconomic and healthcare-related factors. However, this finding should not be interpreted as evidence that conflict has no influence on childhood immunization. Rather, it suggests that the crude association was largely explained by differences in socioeconomic characteristics and access to maternal healthcare services, which may themselves represent pathways through which conflict influences childhood vaccination. This interpretation is consistent with the broader literature showing that armed conflict affects immunization primarily through disruption of health services, displacement, reduced access to care, and deterioration of socioeconomic conditions (9, 12). One possible explanation is that the extensive humanitarian response implemented in conflict-affected regions, in collaboration with local health authorities, may have mitigated some of the adverse effects of conflict on routine immunization services (30–32). However, this hypothesis could not be directly evaluated using the available DHS data and should therefore be interpreted with caution.In conflict settings, maternal education and healthcare contact points such as postnatal care and facility delivery appeared particularly important for vaccination uptake. These factors may serve as critical entry points for maintaining vaccination coverage in contexts where health systems are weakened and access to routine services is limited. In contrast, in non-conflict regions socioeconomic inequalities and maternal health service utilization remained the dominant determinants of vaccination. This suggests that while the structural determinants of vaccination remain broadly similar across settings, the relative importance of specific factors may differ depending on the context. This pattern is also consistent with observations from other conflict-affected African settings, including Northeast Nigeria, where caregivers identified disruption of health services, insecurity, and continued engagement with healthcare providers as key factors influencing childhood vaccination uptake (11, 12).Socioeconomic inequalities in vaccination coverageOur findings highlight the important role of socioeconomic factors in determining childhood vaccination coverage. Children from wealthier households had significantly higher odds of being fully vaccinated compared with those from poorer households, particularly in non-conflict regions. These findings are also in agreement with a recent DHS-based analysis from Cameroon, which identified maternal education and healthcare utilization as major determinants of childhood vaccination, although that study focused on pentavalent vaccine uptake rather than complete basic vaccination and did not specifically examine differences between conflict-affected and non-conflict regions (23). Similar socioeconomic gradients in vaccination coverage have been documented in many low- and middle-income countries, where economic resources influence access to health services, transportation, and information about preventive care (33, 34).Maternal education also emerged as an important determinant of vaccination. Children whose mothers had secondary or higher education were significantly more likely to be fully vaccinated, especially in conflict-affected regions. Educated mothers may have greater awareness of the benefits of immunization, better understanding of vaccination schedules, and increased ability to navigate health systems. Previous studies using DHS data from sub-Saharan Africa have consistently reported positive associations between maternal education and childhood vaccination uptake (33–35).Importance of health service utilizationUtilization of maternal health services was strongly associated with vaccination completion. Antenatal care attendance was one of the strongest predictors of full vaccination in both the national and non-conflict models. Mothers who attended antenatal care visits were substantially more likely to have children who completed the basic vaccination schedule. Antenatal care provides important opportunities for health education and counseling, including information about the importance of childhood immunization and the recommended vaccination schedule. Antenatal care attendance has also been proved to increase the likelihood of other mother–child health outcomes, such as delivery in health facility and start breastfeeding of the baby (36, 37).Postnatal care for the newborn was also significantly associated with vaccination completion in all models. Postnatal visits represent critical contact points between families and the health system, during which healthcare providers can reinforce immunization messages, verify vaccination status, and facilitate timely follow-up vaccinations. The lower availability of vaccination cards observed in conflict-affected regions may also reflect broader disruptions in continuity of healthcare. Insecurity, population displacement, and interruptions in routine health services may compromise the retention of personal health records, making it more difficult for caregivers and healthcare providers to verify previous vaccinations and ensure timely completion of the recommended immunization schedule.In conflict-affected regions, facility-based delivery was an additional determinant of full vaccination. Health facility delivery may facilitate early contact with vaccination services, including administration of birth-dose vaccines and registration into routine immunization…
full_text_sections.conclusion: ConclusionIn conclusion, full basic childhood vaccination coverage in Cameroon remains suboptimal and is lower in conflict-affected regions. Socioeconomic factors and utilization of maternal health services are key determinants of vaccination completion. Strengthening antenatal and postnatal care services and addressing socioeconomic barriers may improve vaccination coverage, particularly in conflict-affected areas.
full_text_sections.other: IntroductionDisease prevention through childhood vaccination has been proved to be one of the most effective interventions that saved, and continue to save, million lives worldwide: it is estimated that every year vaccination can avert approximately two million deaths; moreover, vaccination reduces childhood morbidity and disability. Since 1974, when the Expanded Programme of Immunization was launched, it is estimated that vaccination has prevented 146 million deaths among children under 5 years of age (1–3).Sustained high immunization coverage is essential to maximize the impact of vaccination programs and to protect individuals who cannot be vaccinated. This protection relies on herd immunity, which occurs when a sufficiently large proportion of the population is immune to interrupt pathogen transmission. For highly transmissible diseases such as measles, vaccination coverage of around 95% is generally required to prevent outbreaks. Failure to achieve and maintain such coverage increases the risk of outbreaks, particularly in settings where immunization services are disrupted (4–7).Maintaining sufficient vaccination coverage to achieve herd immunity thresholds faces multiple challenges. Concurrent pandemics, public health emergencies, population movements, vaccine hesitancy, and misinformation can all disrupt immunization efforts (8–11). Countries affected by armed conflict typically exhibit lower vaccination coverage, higher incidence and mortality from vaccine-preventable diseases, and elevated risk of epidemics (12). These patterns underscore the compounded risks in settings like Cameroon, where ongoing crises in the Far North, North-West, and South-West regions further constrain immunization programmes. In this context, understanding the current level of vaccination coverage is essential. Vaccination coverage among children in Cameroon is still lower than the target set globally: in 2018, national coverage with the first dose of measles-containing vaccine in Cameroon was approximately 61%, well below the ≥95% coverage generally required to prevent measles outbreaks and below the Immunization Agenda 2030 target of at least 90% national coverage (13, 14).Cameroon is a lower-middle-income country in Central Africa with a population of approximately 28 million people. It is characterized by considerable linguistic, ethnic, and religious diversity, with French and English as its official languages. Despite its natural resources, poverty remains widespread, with approximately 40% of the population living below the national poverty line, and persistent socioeconomic inequalities and ongoing armed conflicts continue to challenge equitable access to healthcare, including childhood immunization (15). Cameroon has experienced overlapping humanitarian crises in its Far North, North-West, and South-West regions over the past decade. In the Far North, armed violence linked to Boko Haram and affiliated groups emerged around 2014, causing recurrent attacks on civilians, population displacement, and a sustained security response by national and regional forces. In the predominantly Anglophone North-West and South-West regions—where approximately 20% of the population resides—protests by lawyers, teachers, and other professional groups began in late 2016 over concerns including language use in courts and schools, perceived marginalization, and central governance structures; these escalated from 2017 into armed confrontation between state security forces and non-state armed groups. These situations have led to substantial internal displacement, restricted access to services, and humanitarian needs across affected areas, with hundreds of thousands of people reported as internally displaced persons and millions requiring assistance (16–19).Very few studies have been conducted to assess the vaccination coverage and its predictors in Cameroon. Although these studies are methodologically robust and valid, they focused on limited factors, such as the dropout in coverage due to the COVID19 pandemic (20, 21), are limited in terms of geographical areas and sample size (22) or focused on the coverage of a specific antigen (23). However, these studies agree on the fact that childhood vaccination coverage in the Cameroon is low and subjected to decline in case of other emergencies. On the other hand, these studies do not systematically assess various levels of factors associated with childhood vaccination in the country, nor compare regions affected by armed conflict with more stable areas.The aim of this study is to explore factors associated with childhood vaccination coverage in Cameroon using the most recent countrywide vaccination coverage survey (DHS 2018); to compare such factors between regions affected by armed conflict with regions more stable; to propose strategies to increase vaccination coverage overall and for specific subgroups of populations. Ethics statementThe Demographic and Health Survey (DHS) of Cameroon conducted between June 2018 and January 2019 (EDSC-V) by the National Institute of Statistics, in close collaboration with the Ministry of Public Health (24). The DHS protocol was reviewed and approved by the ICF Institutional Review Board - ICF IRB FWA00000845 - and by the Cameroon National Ethics Committee for Human Health (CNERSH) -132989.0.000. CM. DHS.01. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to data collection. The datasets used in this study are publicly available and anonymized, and therefore no additional ethical approval was required for this secondary analysis (ICRC Ethics Process exemption reference GVA_CORE_1925). The DHS and ICF granted access to the dataset on the 14 August 2025. Statistical analysisDescriptive statistics were calculated to summarize the characteristics of the study population. Weighted percentages were reported together with unweighted frequencies. Differences between conflict-affected and non-conflict regions were assessed using design-adjusted Pearson chi-square tests. Associations between explanatory variables and full vaccination were examined using survey-weighted logistic regression models, and statistical significance was evaluated using Wald tests. All analyses accounted for the complex sampling design of the DHS by applying sampling weights and adjusting for clustering at the primary sampling unit level and stratification. Potential interaction effects between selected covariates, including conflict status with maternal education, household wealth, and antenatal care visits, were explored by including multiplicative interaction terms in the survey-weighted logistic regression models. Interaction terms with p < 0.05 were considered statistically significant and retained in the final model. As none of the interaction terms reached statistical significance, they were not retained in the final models. Model discrimination was assessed using Tjur’s coefficient of discrimination (Tjur’s R2), calculated as the difference between the mean predicted probabilities among fully vaccinated and non-fully vaccinated children. Observations with missing values in variables included in the regression analyses were excluded using complete-case analysis. Missing data were minimal for all study variables, with the exception of antenatal care visits, for which 119 observations (6.5%) had missing information. Bivariate logistic regression analyses were performed to examine the association between each independent variable and full vaccination status. Candidate explanatory variables were selected a priori based on previous literature and their potential relevance to childhood vaccination. Among these candidate variables, those associated with the outcome at p < 0.20 in bivariable analyses were entered into the multivariable logistic regression models. papers.title_original: Determinants of childhood vaccination differ between conflict-affected and non-conflict regions in Cameroon

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate how determinants of childhood vaccination differ between conflict-affected and non-conflict regions in Cameroon, addressing a public health problem related to vaccine coverage in unstable settings.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A cross-sectional analysis using data from the 2018 Cameroon Demographic and Health Survey was conducted on 1,824 children aged 12–23 months, with the study restricted to those who had all vaccines included in the definition of full vaccination by 12 months of age.
analysis.methods: Survey-weighted logistic regression models were used to assess associations between explanatory variables and full vaccination status, with statistical significance evaluated using Wald tests. Design-adjusted Pearson chi-square tests were used to compare differences between conflict-affected and non-conflict regions. Interaction effects were explored by including multiplicative terms in the regression models.
analysis.main_results: Overall, 53.08% of children were fully vaccinated. In unadjusted analysis, conflict status was associated with lower odds of full vaccination, but this association was no longer significant in the adjusted model. Rural residence was more common in conflict-affected regions (74.55%) than in non-conflict regions (50.17%).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted that conflict status alone was not a significant determinant of vaccination completion after adjusting for other factors, highlighting the importance of socioeconomic and healthcare access variables in influencing vaccination rates.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings inform public health strategies by emphasizing the need to address socioeconomic disparities and improve healthcare access in conflict-affected regions to enhance vaccination coverage.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study was limited by potential under-representation of conflict-affected areas due to insecurity, and missing data on antenatal care visits. Despite these limitations, the evidence is moderate due to the use of survey-weighted methods and adjustment for complex sampling design.

analysis.summary_en: This study examines the determinants of childhood vaccination in Cameroon, comparing conflict-affected and non-conflict regions. It highlights that while conflict status initially appeared to be associated with lower vaccination rates, this association disappeared after adjusting for socioeconomic and healthcare access factors. The research underscores the importance of addressing disparities in wealth, education, and healthcare utilization to improve vaccination coverage. The study used data from the 2018 Cameroon Demographic and Health Survey, applying survey-weighted logistic regression and chi-square tests to account for sampling complexities. Limitations include potential under-representation of conflict-affected areas and missing data, which may affect the generalizability of the findings. The results suggest that targeted interventions should focus on improving access to healthcare services and addressing socioeconomic barriers in conflict-affected regions to enhance vaccination rates.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究旨在调查喀麦隆受冲突影响地区和非冲突地区儿童 疫苗接种 的决定因素有何不同,解决不稳定环境中与 疫苗 覆盖相关的公共卫生问题。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 使用 2018 年喀麦隆人口统计和健康调查的数据对 1,824 名 12-23 个月大的儿童进行了横断面分析,该研究仅限于 12 个月大时所有 疫苗 均包含在完整 疫苗接种 定义中的儿童。
elements_zh.methods: 使用调查加权逻辑回归模型来评估解释变量与完整 疫苗接种 状态之间的关联,并使用 Wald 检验评估统计显着性。使用设计调整的皮尔逊卡方检验来比较受冲突影响地区和非冲突地区之间的差异。通过在回归模型中包含乘法项来探索交互效应。
elements_zh.main_results: 总体而言,53.08%的儿童充分接种了疫苗。在未经调整的分析中,冲突状态与完整 疫苗接种 的较低几率相关,但这种关联在调整后的模型中不再显着。农村居住在受冲突影响地区(74.55%)比非冲突地区(50.17%)更常见。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者解释说,在调整其他因素后,冲突状态本身并不是 疫苗接种 完成的重要决定因素,强调了社会经济和医疗保健获取变量在影响 疫苗接种 率方面的重要性。

analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 使用 2018 年喀麦隆人口统计和健康调查的数据对 1,824 名 12-23 个月大的儿童进行了横断面分析,该研究仅限于 12 个月大时所有 疫苗 均包含在完整 疫苗接种 定义中的儿童。
analysis_zh.methods: 使用调查加权逻辑回归模型来评估解释变量与完整 疫苗接种 状态之间的关联,并使用 Wald 检验评估统计显着性。使用设计调整的皮尔逊卡方检验来比较受冲突影响地区和非冲突地区之间的差异。通过在回归模型中包含乘法项来探索交互效应。
analysis_zh.main_results: 总体而言,53.08%的儿童充分接种了疫苗。在未经调整的分析中,冲突状态与完整 疫苗接种 的较低几率相关,但这种关联在调整后的模型中不再显着。农村居住在受冲突影响地区(74.55%)比非冲突地区(50.17%)更常见。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者解释说,在调整其他因素后,冲突状态本身并不是 疫苗接种 完成的重要决定因素,强调了社会经济和医疗保健获取变量在影响 疫苗接种 率方面的重要性。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果强调需要解决社会经济差异并改善受冲突影响地区的医疗保健服务,以提高 疫苗接种 的覆盖范围,从而为公共卫生战略提供信息。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究的局限性在于,由于不安全因素,受冲突影响地区的代表性可能不足,而且产前保健就诊数据缺失。尽管存在这些局限性,但由于使用了调查加权方法和对复杂抽样设计进行了调整,证据仍然有限。

papers.title: Reproduction number estimation using smoothing methods
papers.abstract: The reproduction number is estimated to understand the potential spread of an infectious disease within a population. Current estimation methods can be broadly categorized into mathematical and statistical methodological frameworks. Within the latter, renewal process, exponential growth and smoothing methods infer reproduction numbers from generation time distributions, growth rates, or smoothed epidemic trajectories. Our evaluation was based on three epidemic scenarios with distinct transmissibility levels (R0= 11.52, 2.88, and 1.06), simulated using stochastic SEIR models, and on the Hagelloch measles outbreak data. We compared five statistical methodsthe exponential growth method (EG), the renewal process method (RP), the Bayesian P-spline smoothing method (BPS), the filtering-based Bayesian inference method (FBI), and a smoothing method that integrates spline smoothing, derivative estimation, and exponential growth analysis within a generalized additive model (DSS). The performance criteria comprised the estimated bias, mean squared error (MSE), coverage rate (CR), significance rate (SR), and false negative rate (FNR). Across the three scenarios, no method was uniformly superior; the ranking depended on the criterion prioritized. RP and DSS produced the most accurate and stable point estimates (bias between − 0.45 and 1.69; MSE ≤ 7.31) together with the best-calibrated and narrowest 95% uncertainty intervals (coverage up to 97%). BPS was particularly unstable: its inflated mean drove MSE, bias, and coverage to 13.51%. FBI reached the highest significance rate at R0 = 1.06 (65.49%), although this sensitivity partly reflected their upward bias; EG showed the only substantial FNR (15.11%). The Hagelloch measles data corroborated these patterns. Under the significance constraint (SR), RP maximized risk control (CR/FNR) and DSS maximized accuracy (Bias/MSE).

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to evaluate different statistical methods for estimating the reproduction number of an infectious disease to better understand its potential spread within a population.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The research compared five statistical methods—exponential growth, renewal process, Bayesian P-spline smoothing, filtering-based Bayesian inference, and a smoothing method integrating spline smoothing, derivative estimation, and exponential growth analysis—across three epidemic scenarios with distinct transmissibility levels and the Hagelloch measles outbreak data.
analysis.methods: The evaluation used three epidemic scenarios simulated with stochastic SEIR models and the Hagelloch measles outbreak data. Performance was assessed using criteria such as estimated bias, mean squared error, coverage rate, significance rate, and false negative rate.
analysis.main_results: Across the three scenarios, no method was uniformly superior; the ranking depended on the criterion prioritized. RP and DSS produced the most accurate and stable point estimates with the best-calibrated and narrowest 95% uncertainty intervals, while BPS was particularly unstable with inflated mean, MSE, bias, and coverage.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted that the performance of the methods varied depending on the evaluation criteria, highlighting the importance of selecting appropriate methods based on the specific goals of the study.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform the choice of statistical methods for estimating reproduction numbers in measles outbreaks, aiding in surveillance and public health decision-making.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its reliance on simulated scenarios and outbreak data, which may not fully represent real-world complexities. The evidence is moderate as it is based on abstract-level reporting.

analysis.summary_en: This study evaluates five statistical methods for estimating the reproduction number of an infectious disease, focusing on measles. The methods include exponential growth, renewal process, Bayesian P-spline smoothing, filtering-based Bayesian inference, and a smoothing method integrating spline smoothing, derivative estimation, and exponential growth analysis. The evaluation was conducted across three epidemic scenarios with varying transmissibility levels and the Hagelloch measles outbreak data. Results showed that no method was uniformly superior, with performance depending on the prioritized criterion. RP and DSS provided the most accurate and stable estimates, while BPS was unstable. The study highlights the importance of selecting appropriate methods based on the specific goals of the analysis. The findings have implications for improving surveillance and public health strategies for measles outbreaks. However, the study is limited by its reliance on simulated and outbreak data, and the evidence is moderate.

elements_zh.methods: 该评估使用了随机 SEIR 模型和 Hagelloch 麻疹 暴发 数据模拟的三种流行病场景。使用估计偏差、均方误差、覆盖率、显着性率和假阴性率等标准评估性能。

elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者解释说,这些方法的性能因评估标准而异,强调了根据研究的具体目标选择适当方法的重要性。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果可以为估计 麻疹 暴发 中繁殖数的统计方法的选择提供信息,从而帮助 麻疹 和公共卫生决策。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究因其对模拟场景和 暴发 数据的依赖而受到限制,这些数据可能无法完全代表现实世界的复杂性。证据是中等的,因为它基于抽象级别的报告。

papers.abstract_zh: 估计再生数可以了解传染病在人群中的潜在传播情况。当前的估计方法可大致分为数学和统计方法框架。在后者中,更新过程、指数增长和平滑方法根据世代时间分布、增长率或平滑的流行轨迹推断繁殖数量。我们的评估基于具有不同传播水平的三种流行病情景(R0= 11.52、2.88 和 1.06),使用随机 SEIR 模型以及 Hagelloch 麻疹 暴发 数据进行模拟。我们比较了五种统计方法:指数增长法 (EG)、更新过程法 (RP)、贝叶斯 P 样条平滑法 (BPS)、基于过滤的贝叶斯推理法 (FBI) 以及在广义加性模型 (DSS) 中集成样条平滑、导数估计和指数增长分析的平滑方法。绩效标准包括估计偏差、均方误差 (MSE)、覆盖率 (CR)、显着性率 (SR) 和假阴性率 (FNR)。在这三种情况下,没有一种方法是一致优越的。排名取决于优先考虑的标准。RP 和 DSS 产生了最准确和稳定的点估计(偏差在 − 0.45 和 1.69 之间;MSE ≤ 7.31)以及最佳校准和最窄的 95% 不确定性区间(覆盖率高达 97%)。BPS 特别不稳定:其夸大的均值导致 MSE、偏差和覆盖率达到 13.51%。FBI 在 R0 = 1.06 (65.49%) 时达到最高显着率,尽管这种敏感性部分反映了其向上偏差;EG 显示出唯一显着的 FNR (15.11%)。Hagelloch 麻疹 数据证实了这些模式。在显着性约束(SR)下,RP最大化风险控制(CR/FNR)和DSS最大化准确性(Bias/MSE)。

analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究旨在评估估计传染病繁殖数量的不同统计方法,以更好地了解其在人群中的潜在传播。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究比较了五种统计方法——指数增长、更新过程、贝叶斯 P 样条平滑、基于过滤的贝叶斯推理以及集成样条平滑、导数估计和指数增长分析的平滑方法——跨越三种具有不同传播水平的流行病场景和 Hagelloch 麻疹 暴发 数据。
analysis_zh.methods: 该评估使用了随机 SEIR 模型和 Hagelloch 麻疹 暴发 数据模拟的三种流行病场景。使用估计偏差、均方误差、覆盖率、显着性率和假阴性率等标准评估性能。
analysis_zh.main_results: 在这三种情况下,没有一种方法是一致优越的。排名取决于优先考虑的标准。RP 和 DSS 产生了最准确和稳定的点估计,具有最佳校准和最窄的 95% 不确定性区间,而 BPS 特别不稳定,具有夸大的平均值、MSE、偏差和覆盖范围。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者解释说,这些方法的性能因评估标准而异,强调了根据研究的具体目标选择适当方法的重要性。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果可以为估计 麻疹 暴发 中繁殖数的统计方法的选择提供信息,从而帮助 麻疹 和公共卫生决策。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究因其对模拟场景和 暴发 数据的依赖而受到限制,这些数据可能无法完全代表现实世界的复杂性。证据是中等的,因为它基于抽象级别的报告。

papers.title: COVID-19 vaccine compliance among pregnant women in Poland during the pandemic

source_records.title: COVID-19 vaccine compliance among pregnant women in Poland during the pandemic
COVID-19 vaccine compliance among pregnant women in Poland during the pandemic

papers.priority_tier_reason: 补充性记录、预印本或证据完整度有限
papers.full_text: IntroductionThis study aimed to assess COVID-19 vaccination adherence and identify the factors associated with vaccine uptake among pregnant women in Poland during the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic. Given the high risk of severe COVID-19 complications, including acute respiratory failure, multiple organ failure, and maternal and neonatal mortality, understanding the factors that influence adherence to immunization guidelines is critical for optimizing maternal–fetal public health strategies.MethodsThis cross-sectional study analyzed 675 questionnaires collected from women hospitalized in the Department of Neonatology at the University Clinical Center in Gdańsk between November 2021 and February 2022. The analysis evaluated associations between vaccination status and vaccine type and demographic characteristics, place of residence, and obstetric history, including fertility disorders and prior miscarriages.ResultsData revealed that more than 50% of respondents received the COVID-19 vaccine during pregnancy. Multivariable analyses showed that lower educational attainment was the most consistent factor associated with lower odds of vaccination. Older age and residence in a large city were associated with higher odds of receving the vaccine in selected models, whereas obstetric history was not significantly associated with vaccination status.ConclusionWhile vaccine uptake was moderate, the findings highlight a significant demographic divide. These findings suggest that tailored, evidence-based vaccine communication during antenatal care is particularly relevant for women with lower educational attainment. Materials and methodsThis cross-sectional study was conducted among postpartum women hospitalized between 18 November 2021 and 28 February 2022, at the Department of Neonatology, University Clinical Center (UCC), Gdańsk, Poland.Data were collected using a structured questionnaire covering past SARS-CoV-2 infections, COVID-19 vaccination status, demographic characteristics, and obstetric history (subfertility and prior miscarriage). The study included deliveries at both premature and term gestational ages, primiparous and multiparous women, and women with and without a history of pregnancy loss. The inclusion criteria encompassed all hospitalized postpartum women, regardless of age, place of residence, and education level.The questionnaire was anonymous and voluntary and was administered in a paper-based format; it comprised 12 closed-ended questions (both single- and multiple-choice).We excluded 14 women due to language barriers with the Polish-language questionnaire, and 2 forms were excluded due to incomplete data.Ultimately, the study included 675 women hospitalized during the study period who provided informed consent to participate.Statistical analyses were performed using Statistica version 9.1. Categorical variables were presented as frequencies and percentages, and associations were examined using the chi-square test of independence. A two-sided p-value of <0.05 was considered statistically significant. Multivariable logistic regression analysis was performed to evaluate the associations between vaccination status and demographic and clinical variables. The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and reported according to the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) guidelines.The Ethical Committee at the Medical University of Gdańsk approved the study (NKBBN/367/2021) on 8 April 2021. ResultsWe stratified respondents into subgroups and performed comparative analyses to determine which groups exhibited higher adherence to national vaccination recommendations. Participants’ characteristics are presented in Table 1.Table 1Patients’ characteristics.Group characteristicn (%)FertilityPrimiparous mothers344 (51%)Multiparous mothers331 (49%)DomicileLarge city (>500,000 inhabitants)358 (53%)Smaller cities171 (25.4%)Countryside146 (21.6%)Age<19 years9 (1.3%)20–25 years67 (10%)26–35 years464 (68.7%)36–40 years118 (17.5%)>40 years17 (2.5%)Educational levelUniversity (>12 years)468 (69.3%)Secondary (12 years)186 (27.6%)Primary (9 years)21 (3.1%)Vaccination against Covid-19 (overall)Not vaccinated287 (42.5%)Vaccinated before or during pregnancy388 (57.5%)Vaccinated against Covid-19 subgroup (n = 388)Only during pregnancy238 (61.3%)Only before pregnancy57 (14.7%)Before and during pregnancy93 (24.0%)The largest vaccinated group consists of women who were vaccinated only during pregnancy (n = 238/675, 35.3%); followed by women vaccinated both before and during pregnancy (n = 93/675, 13.8%); only 8.4% (n = 57/675) of respondents were vaccinated only before pregnancy, whereas 42.5% (n = 287/675) had never received a COVID-19 vaccine.Among the 150 women vaccinated before pregnancy, 38% did not complete the vaccination course during pregnancy.Figure 1 illustrates the overall distribution of vaccinated and unvaccinated participants across the groups.Figure 1Vaccination status of the respondents.Pie chart titled Vaccination status depicting four categories: non-vaccinated at 42.5 percent (287), vaccinated only before pregnancy at 8.4 percent (57), vaccinated only during pregnancy at 35.3 percent (238), and vaccinated before and during pregnancy at 13.8 percent (93).Among women who received a vaccine dose both before and during pregnancy, the dose administered during pregnancy occurred in the third trimester in 57% of cases (n = 53/93), the second trimester in 30.1% (n = 28/93), and the first trimester in 19.4% (n = 18/93)—the latter contrary to PTGiP recommendations. In six women (6.5%), vaccination during pregnancy was recorded in more than one trimester; the available data do not indicate how many doses this represents. In the group vaccinated only during pregnancy, the majority received vaccination confined to a single trimester: the second trimester in 41.6% of women (n = 99/238) and the third trimester in 31.9% (n = 76/238). Smaller subgroups had vaccination recorded across two trimesters—second and third in 4.6% (n = 11/238), first and second in 6.3% (n = 15/238), and first and third in 2.5% (n = 6/238)—while 1.7% (n = 4/238) had vaccination recorded in all three trimesters. Vaccination confined to the first trimester alone occurred in 11.3% of patients (n = 27/238). Overall, 21.8% of women in this group (n = 52/238) had at least one vaccination administered during the first trimester, contrary to PTGiP guidelines.The vast majority of respondents were vaccinated in accordance with the PTGiP recommendations, with the Pfizer vaccine (91.8, 95% CI 88.4–94.3%), while the remaining group received AstraZeneca (4.8, 95% CI 3.0–7.7%), Moderna (2.1, 95% CI 1.0–4.3%), and Johnson & Johnson’s (1.8, 95% CI 0.8–3.9%) vaccines.Before pregnancy, vaccination distribution differed: 72.7% Pfizer (95% CI 65.0–79.2%); 17.3% AstraZeneca (95% CI 12.1–24.2%); 7.3% Moderna (95% CI 4.1–12.7%); and 3.3% Johnson & Johnson’s (95% CI 1.4–7.6%).Furthermore, all women vaccinated with Pfizer’s vaccine before pregnancy (n = 67) continued with the same vaccine during pregnancy. Among the 93 women vaccinated both before and during pregnancy, 19 (20.4, 95% CI 13.5–29.7%) switched from another vaccine to Pfizer, in accordance with PTGiP recommendations.During the study, data on COVID-19 infection rates among participants were also collected. Across the entire cohort, 25% (95% CI 21.9–28.4%) of respondents reported being infected before pregnancy, and 12.4% (95% CI 10.2–15.2%) were infected during pregnancy.The distribution of COVID-19 infections in the “vaccinated during pregnancy” group is slightly different—25.7% (95% CI 21.3–30.7%) were infected before pregnancy, and 8.8% (95% CI 6.2–12.3%) during pregnancy. In the “vaccinated before pregnancy” group, 28.7% (95% CI 22.0–36.4%) were infected before pregnancy, and 14.7% (95% CI 9.9–21.2%) were infected during pregnancy.We also assessed whether educational attainment influenced willingness to vaccinate. Among respondents vaccinated during pregnancy, 82.5% (95% CI 78.0–86.2%) were university educated, 16.3% (95% CI 12.7–20.7%) had secondary education, and 1.2% (95% CI 0.5–3.1%) had primary education. By contrast, in the unvaccinated group, 56.7% (95% CI 51.4–61.8%) had university education, 38.4% (95% CI 33.4–43.6%) had secondary education, and 4.9% (95% CI 3.1–7.8%) had primary education. These differences were statistically significant (χ2(2, N = 675) = 53.53, p < 0.001, Cramér’s V = 0.28, indicating a small-to-medium effect size).Furthermore, we found significant differences in pre-pregnancy vaccination status by educational attainment: among women who were not vaccinated before pregnancy, 64.8% (95% CI 60.6–68.7%) had university education, 31.8% (95% CI 28.0–35.9%) had secondary education, and 3.4% (95% CI 2.2–5.4%) had primary education—compared with the vaccinated group (85.3, 95% CI 78.8–90.1% university; 12.7, 95% CI 8.3–18.9% secondary; 2.0, 95% CI 0.7–5.7% primary), χ2(2, N = 675) = 23.40, p < 0.001, Cramér’s V = 0.19 (indicating a small effect size). Among women already vaccinated before pregnancy, we observed no significant differences in educational attainment between those who completed their vaccination course during pregnancy and those who did not (χ2(2, N = 150) = 0.82, p = 0.662, Cramér’s V = 0.07, negligible effect).We found similar disparities across maternal age categories. Vaccination uptake during pregnancy increased with age: 58.5% (95% CI 50.1–66.5%) for women aged ≥ 36 years, 53.0% (95% CI 46.6–59.4%) for those aged 31–35 years, 44.4% (95% CI 38.2–50.9%) for ages 26–30 years, and 34.2% (95% CI 24.5–45.4%) for women aged <25 years χ2(3, N = 675) = 14.99, p = 0.002, Cramér’s V = 0.15 (small effect size).Significant differences were also observed when evaluating age in relation to pre-pregnancy vaccination uptake: 34.8% (95% CI 27.3–43.2%) in the ≥36 age group, 20.9% (95% CI 16.2–26.6%) in the 26–30 group, 19.1% (95% CI 14.6–24.7%) in the 31–35 group, and 13.2% (95% CI 7.3–22.6%) in the <25 age group χ2(3, N = 675) = 17.49, p < 0.001, Cramér’s V = 0.16 (small effect size).To account for the joint effects of place of residence, age, and education on vaccination decisions, we conducted multivariable logistic regression analyses for five definitions of vaccination status.Forest plots of adjusted odds ratios (aOR) with 95% confidence intervals (95% CI) for sociodemographic predictors of COVID-19 vaccination status in pregnancy, corresponding to the five logistic regression models, are presented in Figure 2.Figure 2Adjusted odds ratios for the association between socio-demographic characteristics and COVID-19 vaccination status during pregnancy. Forest plots showing adjusted odds ratios (ORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for the association between socio-demographic characteristics and vaccination status. (A) Vaccinated before or during pregnancy versus non-vaccinated. (B) Vaccinated before and during pregnancy versus vaccinated only before pregnancy. (C) Vaccinated before pregnancy versus non-vaccinated before pregnancy. (D) Vaccinated during pregnancy versus non-vaccinated or vaccinated only before pregnancy. Odds ratios are presented on a logarithmic scale. Red markers indicate statistically significant associations (p < 0.05), whereas blue markers indicate non-significant associations (p < 0.05).Four-panel forest plot comparing odds ratios for vaccination timing related to pregnancy with factors including city size, age groups, and education, highlighting statistically significant results in red for p less than 0.05 and non-significant in blue for p greater than or equal to 0.05, with panels labeled A through D, each specifying the Nagelkerke R-squared, chi-square, and p-values for model fit.Ever vaccinated before or during pregnancy (n = 388) vs. never vaccinated (n = 287). This model showed the strongest goodness-of-fit (Nagelkerke R2 = 0.174, χ2(7) = 93.38, p < 0.001). Residence in a large city was associated with higher odds of vaccination than in the countryside (OR = 1.529, 95% CI 1.007–2.322, p = 0.046). Maternal age ≥36 years was associated with higher odds than <25 years (OR = 2.685, 95% CI 1.388–5.194, p = 0.003). Both primary (OR = 0.192, 95% CI 0.066–0.561, p = 0.003) and secondary education (OR = 0.266, 95% CI 0.182–0.387, p < 0.001) were associated with significantly lower odds than university education.Vaccinated before and during pregnancy (n = 93) vs. vaccinated only before pregnancy (n = 57), excluding never-vaccinated women (total n = 150). The model was not statistically significant overall (Nagelkerke R2 = 0.031, χ2(7) = 3.47, p = 0.838), and none of the individual predictors reached statistical significance—i.e., among women vaccinated before pregnancy, place of residence, age, and educational attainment did not distinguish those who continued vaccination during pregnancy from those who did not.Vaccinated before pregnancy (n = 150) vs. not vaccinated before pregnancy (n = 525), irrespective of subsequent vaccination during pregnancy. The model was statistically significant (Nagelkerke R2 = 0.086, χ2(7) = 39.26, p < 0.001). Place of residence was not statistically significant. Maternal age ≥36 years was associated with higher odds of pre-pregnancy vaccination (OR = 2.480, 95% CI 1.101–5.587, p = 0.028). Secondary education was associated with lower odds (OR = 0.322, 95% CI 0.189–0.549, p < 0.001), whereas primary education was not a significant predictor (OR = 0.610, p = 0.460).Vaccinated during pregnancy (n = 331) vs. not vaccinated during pregnancy (n = 344), irrespective of vaccination before pregnancy. The model was statistically significant (Nagelkerke R2 = 0.122, χ2(7) = 64.89, p < 0.001). Residence in a large city was associated with higher odds of vaccination during pregnancy (OR = 1.581, 95% CI 1.050–2.378, p = 0.028). Maternal age was not statistically significant. Both primary (OR = 0.190, 95% CI 0.060–0.601, p = 0.005) and secondary education (OR = 0.322, 95% CI 0.220–0.472, p < 0.001) were associated with significantly lower odds of vaccination relative to university education.Across all four statistically significant models, lower educational attainment was consistently and independently associated with lower odds of vaccination, even after adjusting for place of residence and maternal age—indicating that educational attainment was the strongest and most robust predictor among those tested.We also evaluated parity (primiparous vs. multiparous) and history of miscarriage; we found no statistically significant differences in vaccination uptake by these obstetric factors. DiscussionHistorically, the emergence of new pathogens has driven rapid advances in preventive interventions, which have consistently prompted waves of public skepticism and debate regarding vaccine safety and potential adverse effects. This has been accompanied by a rise in public concern and misinformation about vaccine safety and efficacy (15). Insufficient vaccination coverage frequently precipitates localized outbreaks of vaccine-preventable diseases, which could be effectively mitigated through the implementation of mandatory immunization programs (16, 17). Steep declines in vaccine confidence represent a concerning trend, most notable in Eastern and Central Europe, the Baltic states, and the Netherlands (9, 18). Furthermore, the WHO classified Poland as an endemic country for measles due to declining immunization coverage (<95%) (19). Our findings highlight suboptimal COVID-19 vaccination uptake among pregnant women in this cohort, indicating incomplete adherence despite national recommendations. Many women did not follow PTGiP recommendations for COVID-19 vaccination during pregnancy. Most unvaccinated women were younger and had lower educational attainment. In Poland, 22% of women have completed only primary or lower-secondary education, compared with 20% across the broader European Union (20). However, the association between educational attainment and vaccination uptake must be interpreted with caution. Educational attainment is likely closely linked to other determinants of vaccine acceptance, including health literacy, socioeconomic status, access to reliable health information and digital resources, and trust in healthcare professionals and public health institutions. Therefore, the observed association should not be interpreted as causal, but rather as reflecting the complex interplay of multiple sociodemographic and psychosocial factors influencing vaccination decisions.Our findings suggest that younger pregnant women and those with lower educational attainment represent critical target demographics for tailored vaccine communication during antenatal care. However, educational attainment should not be viewed in isolation as a determinant of vaccine uptake, as it is closely intertwined with health literacy, access to reliable medical information, socioeconomic status, and trust in healthcare providers. Targeted counseling by obstetricians and midwives, together with clear, evidence-based educational initiatives, may help enhance vaccine confidence and uptake in these populations.More than half of the respondents resided in urban areas. This distribution may reflect higher vaccination uptake among women in urban settings, potentially driven by better access to healthcare services, specialized antenatal care, and reliable health information. However, this observation should be interpreted cautiously, as the study was not specifically powered or designed to investigate the underlying structural drivers of urban–rural disparities (21–23).This study was conducted among women hospitalized at a single university tertiary center in a large Polish city, which may limit the generalizability of the findings to the broader population of pregnant women in Poland. In addition, only 20% of respondents reported living in rural areas, suggesting that the study sample may…

Categorical variables were presented as frequencies and percentages, and associations were examined using the chi-square test of independence. A two-sided p-value of <0.05 was considered statistically significant. Multivariable logistic regression analysis was performed to evaluate the associations between vaccination status and demographic and clinical variables. The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and reported according to the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) guidelines.The Ethical Committee at the Medical University of Gdańsk approved the study (NKBBN/367/2021) on 8 April 2021.
