full_text_sections.discussion: DiscussionHistorically, the emergence of new pathogens has driven rapid advances in preventive interventions, which have consistently prompted waves of public skepticism and debate regarding vaccine safety and potential adverse effects. This has been accompanied by a rise in public concern and misinformation about vaccine safety and efficacy (15). Insufficient vaccination coverage frequently precipitates localized outbreaks of vaccine-preventable diseases, which could be effectively mitigated through the implementation of mandatory immunization programs (16, 17). Steep declines in vaccine confidence represent a concerning trend, most notable in Eastern and Central Europe, the Baltic states, and the Netherlands (9, 18). Furthermore, the WHO classified Poland as an endemic country for measles due to declining immunization coverage (<95%) (19). Our findings highlight suboptimal COVID-19 vaccination uptake among pregnant women in this cohort, indicating incomplete adherence despite national recommendations. Many women did not follow PTGiP recommendations for COVID-19 vaccination during pregnancy. Most unvaccinated women were younger and had lower educational attainment. In Poland, 22% of women have completed only primary or lower-secondary education, compared with 20% across the broader European Union (20). However, the association between educational attainment and vaccination uptake must be interpreted with caution. Educational attainment is likely closely linked to other determinants of vaccine acceptance, including health literacy, socioeconomic status, access to reliable health information and digital resources, and trust in healthcare professionals and public health institutions. Therefore, the observed association should not be interpreted as causal, but rather as reflecting the complex interplay of multiple sociodemographic and psychosocial factors influencing vaccination decisions.Our findings suggest that younger pregnant women and those with lower educational attainment represent critical target demographics for tailored vaccine communication during antenatal care. However, educational attainment should not be viewed in isolation as a determinant of vaccine uptake, as it is closely intertwined with health literacy, access to reliable medical information, socioeconomic status, and trust in healthcare providers. Targeted counseling by obstetricians and midwives, together with clear, evidence-based educational initiatives, may help enhance vaccine confidence and uptake in these populations.More than half of the respondents resided in urban areas. This distribution may reflect higher vaccination uptake among women in urban settings, potentially driven by better access to healthcare services, specialized antenatal care, and reliable health information. However, this observation should be interpreted cautiously, as the study was not specifically powered or designed to investigate the underlying structural drivers of urban–rural disparities (21–23).This study was conducted among women hospitalized at a single university tertiary center in a large Polish city, which may limit the generalizability of the findings to the broader population of pregnant women in Poland. In addition, only 20% of respondents reported living in rural areas, suggesting that the study sample may underrepresent rural populations and not fully capture disparities in their willingness to receive vaccination.Mathieu et al.’s study (24) reported that, as of 8 February 2026, Poland documented 3,152 cumulative confirmed COVID-19 deaths per million people. This rate exceeded mortality figures observed across Europe (2,823 per million) and worldwide (893 per million). Furthermore, as of 12 August 2024, an average of 171,88 vaccine doses had been administered per 100 people globally. Worldwide, more than 70% of the population had received at least one dose, whereas in Poland, as of December 2023, 60% had received at least one dose.In our study, approximately 50% of pregnant women received a COVID-19 vaccine, with the majority (91.8%) receiving the Pfizer vaccine, in line with PTGiP recommendations. Notably, vaccine uptake was higher among older women, with the highest rates in the “≥ 36 years” group. The “State of Vaccine Confidence in the EU (2022)” report also found that younger respondents (aged 18–34) were less likely than those in the older age group (over 65 years) to agree that vaccines are important, safe, and effective. The “vaccine confidence” gap between younger and older respondents is widening, particularly in Belgium, Bulgaria, Croatia, France, Hungary, Latvia, Poland, and the Netherlands (9). Overall, between 2018 and 2022, vaccine confidence in Europe rose more in the ≥65 age group than in the 18–34 age group. These data are highly concerning, as vaccine confidence in the younger group is directly related to the successful delivery of routine childhood immunization programs worldwide.LimitationsThis study has several limitations to consider when interpreting its findings. First, the study was conducted among women hospitalized at a single university tertiary center in a large Polish city, which may limit the generalizability of the results to the broader population of pregnant women in Poland. Furthermore, only 20% of participants reported living in rural areas, suggesting that the sample may not adequately represent the geographical distribution of pregnant women in Poland or potential disparities in attitudes toward vaccination across urban and rural settings.Another limitation concerns the observed association between educational attainment and vaccination uptake. Although women with higher educational attainment were more likely to be vaccinated, this association should not be interpreted as a direct causal effect. Educational attainment may reflect a broader set of sociodemographic and contextual characteristics, including socioeconomic status, access to healthcare services, health literacy (the capacity to obtain and evaluate health-related information), and trust in medical professionals. Furthermore, the exclusion of women unable to complete the Polish-language questionnaire may have introduced selection bias, limiting the generalizability of the findings to non-Polish-speaking populations. Because these potential confounding factors were not comprehensively assessed in the present study, residual confounding cannot be ruled out. Future studies incorporating a wider range of social and behavioral variables are warranted to clarify the mechanisms underlying the relationship between education and vaccination decisions.
full_text_sections.conclusion: ConclusionSince 2025, the Polish Chief Sanitary Inspectorate has expanded vaccination recommendations to include routine COVID-19 vaccination for all pregnant women. The recommended vaccinations currently include influenza, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), diphtheria–pertussis–tetanus (Tdap), and COVID-19 (25). Consequently, perinatal and neonatal infection rates are anticipated to decline over the coming years. Our findings indicate that lower educational attainment was the most consistent sociodemographic factor associated with lower COVID-19 vaccination uptake among pregnant women in this cohort. Older maternal age and residence in a large city were also associated with higher odds of vaccination in selected multivariable analyses. These findings support the need for tailored, evidence-based vaccine communication during antenatal care, particularly for women with lower educational attainment. Further multicenter studies incorporating socioeconomic factors, health literacy, access to healthcare, and attitudes toward vaccination are warranted to better understand the determinants of maternal vaccine uptake. Recent studies demonstrate that higher educational attainment promotes greater trust in medical expertise, leading to improved adherence to medical recommendations and higher vaccination uptake (26, 27).
full_text_sections.other: IntroductionThe World Health Organization (WHO) declared the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic on 11 March 2020 (1). The virus was first identified in Wuhan, China, where clinicians first encountered infections caused by a novel coronavirus in November 2019 (2). The distinction from other coronavirus infections was clear—the novel disease was markedly more transmissible and rapidly led to respiratory failure, multiple organ failure, and death in vulnerable individuals (3). Like other viral infections, COVID-19 spread swiftly and quietly around the world, which caused global anxiety (4). Early in 2020, global efforts accelerated to manufacture a vaccine against severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2). In December 2020, both the Pfizer/BioNTech and Moderna vaccines received approval for general use in Europe and the United States (5). These two manufacturers developed an innovative vaccine composed of nucleoside-modified mRNA that encodes a mutated version of the full-length spike protein of SARS-CoV-2, encapsulated in lipid nanoparticles (5, 6). Concurrently, numerous other pharmaceutical companies worldwide developed alternative vaccine platforms. In Poland, the setting of the present study, only two other adenoviral vector vaccines were approved—Vaxzevria (Oxford/AstraZeneca; authorized by the European Medicines Agency [EMA] in January 2021) and Jcovden (Janssen/Johnson & Johnson; EMA authorization granted in March 2021) (7).Since 2020, studies have shown that Pfizer and Moderna (mRNA-1273) vaccines demonstrate comparable effectiveness against SARS-CoV-2 when administered as a two-dose primary series spaced 3–4 weeks (5). Over time, vaccine efficacy against incident infection waned, driven by viral antigenic evolution and the emergence of variants with escape mutations relative to the ancestral wild-type strain (8).The effectiveness of vector-type vaccines varies between 92% (for AstraZeneca’s vaccine against the Delta variant when administered in two doses) and 71% (for the single-dose Johnson & Johnson vaccine against the Delta variant when administered in a single dose [as recommended in Poland]). (9)However, growing public skepticism toward vaccination since the late 1990s has contributed to reduced vaccine acceptance and uptake globally, particularly among children (10, 11). Immunization uptake during pregnancy is even lower (12, 13). Regarding vaccine safety in Poland, the overall vaccine confidence has declined across Europe (especially in the Netherlands, the United Kingdom, the Baltic States, and Eastern Europe). However, there is no comparison between 2020 and 2022 data on the COVID-19 vaccine. New data show that only 68% of Polish respondents find the COVID-19 vaccine safe, compared to 74% of the EU population (9).ObjectiveOur study aimed to assess adherence to compliance with the COVID-19 vaccination recommendations of the Polish Society of Gynecologists and Obstetricians (Polskie Towarzystwo Ginekologów i Położników-PTGiP), published in April 2021, among pregnant women hospitalized at the University Clinical Center (UCC) in Gdańsk, Poland (14). Second, age, place of residence, education, and obstetric history were analyzed to identify determinants of higher adherence. Moreover, the study evaluated the prevalence of SARS-CoV-2 infection among women before and during pregnancy. Polish medical reports lack data not only regarding COVID-19 vaccine confidence and adherence among pregnant women, but also COVID-19 morbidity in this population. In the context of declining vaccine confidence, a lack of awareness of the health hazards of COVID-19 infection during pregnancy, and rising anti-vaccine hesitancy, studies such as this one are necessary to address this critical knowledge gap. analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to evaluate vaccine compliance among pregnant women in Poland during the pandemic, addressing the need to understand factors influencing vaccination decisions in this population.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study analyzed data from a cohort of pregnant women in Poland, focusing on vaccination status, timing, and demographic characteristics such as age, education, and place of residence.
analysis.methods: The researchers conducted multivariable logistic regression analyses to assess the joint effects of place of residence, age, and education on vaccination decisions, using adjusted odds ratios (aOR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) to quantify associations.
analysis.main_results: More than 50% of respondents received the COVID-19 vaccine during pregnancy. Vaccination timing was most common in the second trimester (41.6%) and third trimester (31.9%). Lower educational attainment was associated with significantly lower odds of vaccination, with primary education showing an OR of 0.192 (95% CI 0.066–0.561, p = 0.003) and secondary education showing an OR of 0.266 (95% CI 0.182–0.387, p < 0.001) compared to university education. Residence in a large city was associated with higher odds of vaccination during pregnancy (OR = 1.581, 95% CI 1.050–2.378, p = 0.028).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings suggest that educational attainment significantly influences vaccination decisions among pregnant women, highlighting the need for tailored communication strategies in antenatal care to improve vaccine uptake.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These results can inform targeted public health interventions to address disparities in vaccine compliance among pregnant women, particularly those with lower educational attainment, and improve vaccination strategies in antenatal settings.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's evidence is moderate, as it relies on self-reported data and observational analysis, which may introduce bias. The sample size and demographic distribution may also limit generalizability.

analysis.summary_en: This study examines COVID-19 vaccine compliance among pregnant women in Poland during the pandemic, focusing on factors such as age, education, and place of residence. It finds that over 50% of respondents received the vaccine during pregnancy, with the majority vaccinated in the second or third trimester. Lower educational attainment is significantly associated with reduced vaccination odds, with primary and secondary education showing ORs of 0.192 and 0.266, respectively, compared to university education. Residence in large cities correlates with higher vaccination rates. The study uses multivariable logistic regression to adjust for confounding variables, revealing that educational level is the strongest predictor of vaccination behavior. These findings suggest the importance of tailored communication strategies in antenatal care to address disparities in vaccine uptake. However, the study's reliance on self-reported data and observational methods limits the strength of its evidence, indicating a moderate confidence level in the conclusions.

analysis_en.main_results: More than 50% of respondents received the COVID-19 vaccine during pregnancy. Vaccination timing was most common in the second trimester (41.6%) and third trimester (31.9%). Lower educational attainment was associated with significantly lower odds of vaccination, with primary education showing an OR of 0.192 (95% CI 0.066–0.561, p = 0.003) and secondary education showing an OR of 0.266 (95% CI 0.182–0.387, p < 0.001) compared to university education. Residence in a large city was associated with higher odds of vaccination during pregnancy (OR = 1.581, 95% CI 1.050–2.378, p = 0.028).
analysis_en.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings suggest that educational attainment significantly influences vaccination decisions among pregnant women, highlighting the need for tailored communication strategies in antenatal care to improve vaccine uptake.
analysis_en.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These results can inform targeted public health interventions to address disparities in vaccine compliance among pregnant women, particularly those with lower educational attainment, and improve vaccination strategies in antenatal settings.
analysis_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's evidence is moderate, as it relies on self-reported data and observational analysis, which may introduce bias. The sample size and demographic distribution may also limit generalizability.

papers.title: Anti-Rubella antibodies seroprevalence among pregnant women in South-Western Romania

source_records.title: Anti-Rubella antibodies seroprevalence among pregnant women in South-Western Romania
Anti-Rubella antibodies seroprevalence among pregnant women in South-Western Romania

papers.full_text: AbstractIntroductionRubella infection during pregnancy poses significant risks, including congenital rubella syndrome (CRS), miscarriage, and fetal death. Vaccination programs have reduced rubella incidence globally, but regional differences in coverage and immunity persist. The objective of the study was to assess the seroprevalence of anti-rubella IgM and IgG antibodies among pregnant women in South-Western Romania, with a focus on temporal trends, demographic factors, and the impact of vaccination eligibility.MethodsThis observational, cross-sectional study included pregnant women screened for TORCH infections at the County Clinical Emergency Hospital of Craiova, Romania, during two periods: 2013–2016 and 2019–2022. Serum samples were tested for anti-rubella IgM and IgG antibodies. Participants were stratified by age, area of residence (rural/urban), and eligibility for rubella vaccination based on birth year.ResultsA total of 3,268 samples were analyzed. The seroprevalence of acute rubella infection (IgM positive) was low and slightly decreased from 0.54% (2013–2016) to 0.50% (2019–2022), with the most notable decrease in rural areas and among women aged 21–25 years. The overall seroprevalence of protective IgG antibodies was stable (88.28% vs. 88.91%), but remained below the WHO target of 95%. IgG seroprevalence increased among the youngest (<20 years) and 31–35 years age groups, particularly in rural areas, suggesting improved vaccination coverage and natural immunity from past outbreaks. Mapping in Dolj County revealed high seroprevalence near major cities.DiscussionDespite improvements, the relatively low IgG seroprevalence in South-Western Romania highlights the need to reinforce vaccination campaigns, especially in rural areas and among family physicians. Enhanced education and access to vaccination are essential to achieve the WHO eradication target and prevent CRS.Keywords: antibodies, congenital infections, pregnant women, rubella, seroprevalence studies 2.Material and methods2.1.Study design and participantsThis observational, cross-sectional study included pregnant women from South-Western Romania who presented for routine TORCH screening at the Gynecology Department of the County Clinical Emergency Hospital of Craiova, Romania. Two study periods were analyzed (2013–2016 and 2019–2022). In the first period, 368 women were tested for IgM and 367 for IgG, compared with 2,779 and 2,669 women, respectively, in the second period. Not all participants were tested for both antibodies: some women were tested only for IgM or only for IgG as part of routine clinical care, which explains the difference between the number of women tested for each antibody; no additional exclusion criteria were applied beyond having at least one valid rubella serology result.2.2.Sample size calculationAccording to the National Institute of Statistics, the South-Western (Oltenia) region of Romania had 974,202 women of childbearing age (15–49 years) in 2019 (9). Using the lowest regional rubella IgG seroprevalence reported in Romania at the time of study design (91.4%) (10), we estimated that a minimum sample of 121 pregnant women would be required to estimate seroprevalence with a two-sided 95% confidence interval and a ± 5% margin of error, using the standard formula n = Z2p(1−p)/d2 (Z = 1.96). The achieved sample sizes for IgG testing (367 in Group 1 and 2,669 in Group 2) exceeded this minimum, corresponding to margins of error of approximately ±2.87% and ±1.06%, respectively; the smaller Group 1 sample therefore yields comparatively less precise estimates, a point considered further in the Limitations.2.3.Data collection and variablesFor each participant, demographic data including age and area of residence (urban or rural) were recorded, together with the results of anti-rubella IgM and IgG serological testing.2.4.Laboratory testingPregnant women were screened during the first trimester of pregnancy as part of routine prenatal care.Between 2013 and 2016, anti-rubella IgM and IgG antibodies were measured using an electrochemiluminescence immunoassay (ECLIA) on the Cobas e601 analyzer (Roche Diagnostics, Basel, Switzerland). Between 2019 and 2022, serological testing was performed using a chemiluminescent microparticle immunoassay on the Architect i1000 system (Abbott Laboratories, Abbott Park, IL, USA) with original reagents. Both platforms report anti-rubella IgG results in international units per milliliter, calibrated against the WHO International Standard for anti-rubella immunoglobulin. However, multicentric evaluations of commercial rubella IgG immunoassays, including these two platforms, have shown that quantitative titers and, to a lesser extent, qualitative classification near the assay cut-off may differ between platforms despite this common calibration (11). This potential source of inter-assay variability should be considered when interpreting between-period comparisons and is discussed further in the Limitations.2.5.Statistical analysisData were exported from the hospital electronic database (HIPOCRATE) and analyzed using STATA version 17 (StataCorp LLC, College Station, Texas, USA). Continuous variables were expressed as mean ± standard deviation, while categorical variables were reported as counts and percentages.Comparisons between the two study periods were performed using the chi-square test for categorical variables. Differences in mean age between groups were assessed using the Student's t-test, as age was normally distributed. A p-value <0.05 was considered statistically significant.Because this is a cross-sectional study, associations between vaccination-eligibility cohorts (or area of residence) and antibody seroprevalence are expressed as prevalence ratios (PR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI), rather than risk ratios, in line with recommended practice for prevalence (rather than incidence or risk) data (12). PR estimates were calculated as the ratio of the crude prevalence in each comparison subgroup to that of the reference subgroup (women born before 1989, not eligible for rubella vaccination), with 95% CIs derived using the standard log-linear approximation and a continuity correction (+0.5) applied to comparisons involving zero-count cells.IgM seropositivity was interpreted descriptively as a possible marker of recent or acute rubella infection and was not used to estimate population-level rubella immunity; a positive IgM result alone does not equate to confirmed acute infection, since definitive confirmation would require IgG avidity testing or reverse-transcription PCR, both of which were outside the scope of this cross-sectional serological survey.2.6.Vaccination eligibility cohortsParticipants were stratified into four subgroups based on year of birth as a proxy for eligibility for rubella vaccination in Romania, in accordance with the national immunization schedule (Table 1).Table 1Correspondence between birth year and eligibility for rubella vaccine in Romania.Birth year<19891989199019911992199319941995199619971998199920002001200220032004200520062007Age group G126–3021–2521–2521–2521–25<20<20<20<20<20<20–––––––––Age group G231–3526–3026–3026–3026–3026–3021–2521–2521–2521–2521–25<20<20<20<20<20<20–––Eligible RCVNOYESD1YESD1YESD1YESD1YESD1YESD1–––––––––––––Eligible MMRNONONONONONONONONOYES D2YES D2YES D2YES D2YES D2YES D2YES D1 + 2YES D1 + 2YES D1 + 2YES D1 + 2YES D1 + 2D1, one dose of RCV vaccine.D2, second dose of MMR vaccine.D1 + 2: both doses of MMR vaccine.Women born before 1989 were considered non-eligible for rubella vaccination, as they were older than 15 years at the time of introduction of the rubella-containing vaccine in 2003. Women born between 1989 and 1994 were eligible for the monovalent rubella-containing vaccine (RCV) administered to adolescent girls between 2003 and 2008. Women born between 1995 and 1996 constituted a vaccination gap cohort, as they were not eligible for either the RCV program or the childhood MMR schedule. Women born in 1997 or later were considered eligible for the MMR vaccine; those born between 1997 and 2002 received only the second MMR dose, while those born from 2003 onward were eligible for both doses.Women born between 1997 and 2002, listed in Table 1 as eligible only for the second MMR dose, received a first dose of monovalent measles vaccine (without a rubella component) in infancy, before the MMR vaccine replaced it in the national immunization schedule in 2004; their first exposure to a rubella-containing vaccine therefore occurred with the second MMR dose, administered at 6–7 years of age, typically as a school-based catch-up dose (7, 10, 13). This is also the only birth cohort in this classification, together with the 1989–1994 RCV-eligible cohort, that received a rubella-containing vaccine as a single dose rather than the two-dose MMR schedule.2.7.Institutional review board statementThe study was conducted according to the ethical principles regarding human experimentation and clinical research, and was approved by the Committee of Ethics and Academic and Scientific Deontology, Craiova, Romania (approval no. 84/16.09.2020). 2.1.Study design and participantsThis observational, cross-sectional study included pregnant women from South-Western Romania who presented for routine TORCH screening at the Gynecology Department of the County Clinical Emergency Hospital of Craiova, Romania. Two study periods were analyzed (2013–2016 and 2019–2022). In the first period, 368 women were tested for IgM and 367 for IgG, compared with 2,779 and 2,669 women, respectively, in the second period. Not all participants were tested for both antibodies: some women were tested only for IgM or only for IgG as part of routine clinical care, which explains the difference between the number of women tested for each antibody; no additional exclusion criteria were applied beyond having at least one valid rubella serology result. Mapping in Dolj County revealed high seroprevalence near major cities.DiscussionDespite improvements, the relatively low IgG seroprevalence in South-Western Romania highlights the need to reinforce vaccination campaigns, especially in rural areas and among family physicians. Enhanced education and access to vaccination are essential to achieve the WHO eradication target and prevent CRS.Keywords: antibodies, congenital infections, pregnant women, rubella, seroprevalence studies
full_text_sections.methods: 2.Material and methods2.1.Study design and participantsThis observational, cross-sectional study included pregnant women from South-Western Romania who presented for routine TORCH screening at the Gynecology Department of the County Clinical Emergency Hospital of Craiova, Romania. Two study periods were analyzed (2013–2016 and 2019–2022). In the first period, 368 women were tested for IgM and 367 for IgG, compared with 2,779 and 2,669 women, respectively, in the second period. Not all participants were tested for both antibodies: some women were tested only for IgM or only for IgG as part of routine clinical care, which explains the difference between the number of women tested for each antibody; no additional exclusion criteria were applied beyond having at least one valid rubella serology result.2.2.Sample size calculationAccording to the National Institute of Statistics, the South-Western (Oltenia) region of Romania had 974,202 women of childbearing age (15–49 years) in 2019 (9). Using the lowest regional rubella IgG seroprevalence reported in Romania at the time of study design (91.4%) (10), we estimated that a minimum sample of 121 pregnant women would be required to estimate seroprevalence with a two-sided 95% confidence interval and a ± 5% margin of error, using the standard formula n = Z2p(1−p)/d2 (Z = 1.96). The achieved sample sizes for IgG testing (367 in Group 1 and 2,669 in Group 2) exceeded this minimum, corresponding to margins of error of approximately ±2.87% and ±1.06%, respectively; the smaller Group 1 sample therefore yields comparatively less precise estimates, a point considered further in the Limitations.2.3.Data collection and variablesFor each participant, demographic data including age and area of residence (urban or rural) were recorded, together with the results of anti-rubella IgM and IgG serological testing.2.4.Laboratory testingPregnant women were screened during the first trimester of pregnancy as part of routine prenatal care.Between 2013 and 2016, anti-rubella IgM and IgG antibodies were measured using an electrochemiluminescence immunoassay (ECLIA) on the Cobas e601 analyzer (Roche Diagnostics, Basel, Switzerland). Between 2019 and 2022, serological testing was performed using a chemiluminescent microparticle immunoassay on the Architect i1000 system (Abbott Laboratories, Abbott Park, IL, USA) with original reagents. Both platforms report anti-rubella IgG results in international units per milliliter, calibrated against the WHO International Standard for anti-rubella immunoglobulin. However, multicentric evaluations of commercial rubella IgG immunoassays, including these two platforms, have shown that quantitative titers and, to a lesser extent, qualitative classification near the assay cut-off may differ between platforms despite this common calibration (11). This potential source of inter-assay variability should be considered when interpreting between-period comparisons and is discussed further in the Limitations.2.5.Statistical analysisData were exported from the hospital electronic database (HIPOCRATE) and analyzed using STATA version 17 (StataCorp LLC, College Station, Texas, USA). Continuous variables were expressed as mean ± standard deviation, while categorical variables were reported as counts and percentages.Comparisons between the two study periods were performed using the chi-square test for categorical variables. Differences in mean age between groups were assessed using the Student's t-test, as age was normally distributed. A p-value <0.05 was considered statistically significant.Because this is a cross-sectional study, associations between vaccination-eligibility cohorts (or area of residence) and antibody seroprevalence are expressed as prevalence ratios (PR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI), rather than risk ratios, in line with recommended practice for prevalence (rather than incidence or risk) data (12). PR estimates were calculated as the ratio of the crude prevalence in each comparison subgroup to that of the reference subgroup (women born before 1989, not eligible for rubella vaccination), with 95% CIs derived using the standard log-linear approximation and a continuity correction (+0.5) applied to comparisons involving zero-count cells.IgM seropositivity was interpreted descriptively as a possible marker of recent or acute rubella infection and was not used to estimate population-level rubella immunity; a positive IgM result alone does not equate to confirmed acute infection, since definitive confirmation would require IgG avidity testing or reverse-transcription PCR, both of which were outside the scope of this cross-sectional serological survey.2.6.Vaccination eligibility cohortsParticipants were stratified into four subgroups based on year of birth as a proxy for eligibility for rubella vaccination in Romania, in accordance with the national immunization schedule (Table 1).Table 1Correspondence between birth year and eligibility for rubella vaccine in Romania.Birth year<19891989199019911992199319941995199619971998199920002001200220032004200520062007Age group G126–3021–2521–2521–2521–25<20<20<20<20<20<20–––––––––Age group G231–3526–3026–3026–3026–3026–3021–2521–2521–2521–2521–25<20<20<20<20<20<20–––Eligible RCVNOYESD1YESD1YESD1YESD1YESD1YESD1–––––––––––––Eligible MMRNONONONONONONONONOYES D2YES D2YES D2YES D2YES D2YES D2YES D1 + 2YES D1 + 2YES D1 + 2YES D1 + 2YES D1 + 2D1, one dose of RCV vaccine.D2, second dose of MMR vaccine.D1 + 2: both doses of MMR vaccine.Women born before 1989 were considered non-eligible for rubella vaccination, as they were older than 15 years at the time of introduction of the rubella-containing vaccine in 2003. full_text_sections.discussion: 4.DiscussionThis is the largest study performed in the South-West Romania regarding the seroprevalence of anti-Rubella antibodies in pregnant women, which came to complete the studies performed in other regions of Romania.We observed a decrease in the mean age of pregnant women that addressed for testing anti-Rubella antibodies, which can reflect a decrease in the mean age of pregnant women in general or better access to healthcare for young pregnant women.The increase of more than 7-fold in the number of pregnant women tested for anti-Rubella antibodies from 2013 to 2016 to 2019–2022 can be explained by the increase in medical information of patients and progress of laboratory technology associated with a reduction of testing costs, which become affordable for the average pregnant women (15, 16).Because the national immunization program for rubella was introduced in Romania in 2003 (8), we expect a higher proportion of tested women under 20 years of age to be IgG-positive.4.1.History of Rubella in RomaniaIn Romania, the first rubella cases were reported even since 1949 (17). In years 2002–2003, in Romania was recorded a large rubella outbreak (17), with over 115,000 reported cases, leading to an incidence rate of 531/100,000 inhabitants and 150 cases of suspected CRS, but only seven were confirmed. The epidemic affected mostly children, with an incidence rate of 2564/100,000 for the 5–9 years age group and 2446/100,000 in the 10–14 years age group.As response measures, in the absence of an RCV, was implemented an outbreak response plan that included surveillance for anti-rubella antibodies in the affected children of pregnant women who either had rubella disease or had a history of contact with a confirmed rubella case.This outbreak contributed to the acceleration of RCVs into the national vaccination programme.Between 2011 and 2012 another rubella outbreak occurred in Romania, with reported incidence rates of 20.6/100,000 inhabitants in 2011 and 97.5/100,000 inhabitants in 2012 (18). During the same period, 137 cases of CRS were reported. Most IgM positive cases were in the 15–19-year-old age group, and 97.7% of cases had no history of vaccination.4.2.Anti-Rubella IgM antibodies seroprevalenceGlobally, according to the CDC, the number of reported rubella cases has declined from 94,277 in 2012 to 10,194 in 2020 (19). The CRS showed an increased incidence from 302 reported cases in 2012 to 603 reported cases in 2020. This apparent increase in incidence was actually a reporting bias, as new countries with large populations (Bangladesh, India, Indonesia, and Pakistan) were included in the WHO surveillance network (19).In February 2020, 27 rubella cases were reported in six countries (Ireland, Germany, Italy, Poland, Portugal, and Norway), of which 18 were reported in Poland (20).In our study, the prevalence of anti-rubella IgM antibodies was 0.54% between 2013 and 2016 (2 cases) and 0.50% (14 cases) between 2019 and 2022 (Table 3). A similar seroprevalence (0.531%) was reported in a rubella outbreak in Romania in 2003 (17). In a study performed during the 2010–2011 rubella outbreak in Romania, 88 (28.02%) of 314 pregnant women tested positive for IgM (a marked difference from the low, inter-epidemic seroprevalence found in the present study, consistent with the much higher pre-test probability of true infection during an active community outbreak, as opposed to the low-prevalence, endemic setting of our cohorts, where a larger relative proportion of IgM-positive results are expected to be false positives; see below) (18). A study performed in the same period reported a peak prevalence of 10.525% among children under 14 years of age from urban areas in Northern Romania (21). Between 2008 and 2010 in the Banat region (Western Romania), a seroprevalence of 0.479% was reported among women of childbearing age, compared with 0.273% between 2015 and 2018 (22). The results of our study confirmed this descending trend in IgM seroprevalence from 0.54% between 2013 and 2016 and 0.50% between 2019 and 2022. The ECDC website reported only four rubella cases in Romania during 2019–2020 and no reported cases since 2021 (20).When interpreting the results of the IgM antibody test, we must consider the possibility of a false-positive result due to laboratory error. Even if modern methods for the detection of antibodies have high specificity, if many women are screened, there is a real possibility that some of the results are false positives (23). A study performed in the United States on pregnant women concluded that up to 11% of cases positive for IgM antibodies were actually negative (24). Also, is demonstrated cross reactivity between IgM anti-rubella antibodies and the rheumatoid factors that is present in blood in many auto-immune diseases (23).A false-positive IgM result was documented in samples collected from women infected with viruses, such as parvovirus B19, or those that were positive for rheumatoid factor (18, 23).4.3.Anti-Rubella IgG antibodies seroprevalenceThe seroprevalence of anti-Rubella IgG antibodies of 88.28% during 2013–2016 and 88.91% during 2019–2022 was rather low compared to the WHO target of 95% seroprevalence rate (19). Globally, seroprevalence rates as low as 53% have been reported (10). In Europe, a meta-analysis found 16 studies reporting a seronegativity rate > 10% (<90% seropositivity) (25). The lowest reported seroprevalence was 81.2% in pregnant women in Greece in 2006, and the highest was 98.6% in women of childbearing age in the Czech Republic (26). The WHO sets a goal of eradication of rubella in Europe by 2030 (27).Comparing the seroprevalences reported in our study with those reported in other regions of Romania, we observed that in Western Romania, higher seroprevalences were reported between 2008 and 2010 (94.1%) and 2015–2018 (91.5%) in women of childbearing age (22).We did not observe a significant change in the overall seroprevalence between the two time periods (88.28% vs. 88.91%; p = 0.721) (Table 4). If we consider the age group, we observed a non-significant increase in seroprevalence in young women aged < 20 years, from 78.57% between 2013 and 2016 to 85.11% between 2019 and 2022 (p = 0.362). This numerically higher (though not statistically significant) seroprevalence can be tentatively explained if we consider the eligibility for vaccination because women that had 15–20 years between 2013 and 2016 were born between 1993 and 2000, which was confirmed by studies in Western Romania (28). Those born between 1993 and 1994 were eligible for the RCV vaccine, those born between 1995 and 1996 were not eligible for either vaccine, and those born between 1997 and 2000 were eligible for the second dose of the MMR vaccine (Table 1). In contrast, pregnant women aged 15–20 years between 2019 and 2022 were born between 1999 and 2004 and were eligible for at least one dose of MMR vaccine (Table 1), which explains the higher seroprevalence. In this age group, the (non-significant) difference was numerically larger in urban areas (66.67% vs. 77.94%, p = 0.529) than in rural areas (81.82% vs. 87.38%, p = 0.462) (Table 4). Another age group in which we saw an increase in seroprevalence (from 82.50% to 92.42%) was 31–35 years. These women were not eligible for an RCV vaccine; thus, the increase in seroprevalence can be attributed to natural immunization. This could be due to two rubella outbreaks that occurred in Romania in 2003 and 2011–2012 (17, 18). A study performed in 1989 (29) showed a seroprevalence of 75.3% in this age group, whereas another study from Western Romania reported a seroprevalence in women aged 26–34–93.6% between 2008 and 2010 and 91.8% between 2015 and 2018. We can conclude that the seroprevalence is on an ascending trend in Romania from 1989 to 2022. full_text_sections.conclusion: 5.ConclusionsThis study provides updated evidence on rubella immunity among pregnant women in South-Western Romania. Acute rubella infection was rare across both study periods, while overall anti-rubella IgG seroprevalence remained stable but consistently below the 95% threshold associated with WHO elimination targets. Although rural–urban differences diminished over time, population-level immunity remains insufficient to prevent congenital rubella syndrome.The identification of lower IgG seroprevalence in specific birth cohorts, particularly women born during the 1995–1996 vaccination gap and those born in the MMR-eligible era, highlights persistent immunity gaps despite long-standing vaccination programs. These findings suggest that vaccination eligibility alone does not guarantee adequate protection in women of reproductive age.Strengthening rubella prevention in South-Western Romania requires targeted catch-up vaccination strategies, enhanced counseling by family physicians, and sustained surveillance of susceptible cohorts. Addressing these immunity gaps is essential for achieving rubella and congenital rubella syndrome elimination goals.

The risk of CRS is strongly dependent on gestational age at infection, being highest during the first trimester and decreasing thereafter (5). For this reason, rubella immunity among women of childbearing age remains a critical public health concern, even in the post-vaccination era.CRS is a preventable condition characterized by permanent disabilities, most commonly sensorineural deafness, cardiac malformations, ocular abnormalities, and neurodevelopmental impairment (2, 5). papers.title_original: Anti-Rubella antibodies seroprevalence among pregnant women in South-Western Romania

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to assess the seroprevalence of anti-rubella antibodies among pregnant women in South-Western Romania to evaluate immunity levels and identify potential gaps in vaccination coverage. This is important due to the risk of congenital rubella syndrome in fetuses if mothers are not immune during pregnancy.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This cross-sectional study was conducted in South-Western Romania between 2013 and 2022, focusing on pregnant women during their first trimester. Participants were stratified into four subgroups based on birth year, reflecting vaccination eligibility according to the national immunization schedule.
analysis.methods: Serological testing for anti-rubella IgM and IgG antibodies was performed using an electrochemiluminescence immunoassay (ECLIA) on the Cobas e601 analyzer. The study used prevalence ratios (PR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) to compare associations between vaccination eligibility cohorts and antibody seroprevalence, applying a continuity correction for zero-count cells.
analysis.main_results: The seroprevalence of acute rubella infection (IgM positive) was low and slightly decreased from 0.54% (2013–2016) to 0.50% (2019–2022). In rural areas, the highest seroprevalence was observed in women born between 1995 and 1996 (vaccination gap subgroup), while the lowest was in those born between 1989 and 1994 (eligible for RCV vaccine). The proportion of women tested in urban areas decreased significantly from Group 1 (223/367, 60.49%) to Group 2 (1,169/2,669, 43.80%; p < 0.001).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the findings as indicating a slight decline in acute rubella infection rates, particularly in rural areas and among younger women, suggesting potential improvements in vaccination coverage. However, they emphasized that the wide confidence intervals for some comparisons indicate the need for further research to confirm these trends.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings provide insights into the current immunity status of pregnant women in South-Western Romania, which is crucial for informing targeted vaccination strategies and preventing congenital rubella syndrome. They also highlight the importance of addressing vaccination gaps in specific demographic subgroups.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's limitations include the use of a cross-sectional design, which precludes causal inferences, and the wide confidence intervals for some comparisons due to small sample sizes. The evidence is moderate in strength, as the results are based on serological data without definitive confirmation of acute infection through additional testing methods.

analysis.summary_en: This study assessed the seroprevalence of anti-rubella antibodies among pregnant women in South-Western Romania between 2013 and 2022. It found a slight decrease in acute rubella infection rates (IgM positive) from 0.54% to 0.50%, with the most notable decline in rural areas and among women aged 21–25 years. The study stratified participants into four subgroups based on birth year to reflect vaccination eligibility. While the overall IgG seroprevalence remained similar between the two periods, the proportion of women tested in urban areas decreased significantly. The authors interpreted these findings as suggesting potential improvements in vaccination coverage, though they cautioned that the wide confidence intervals for some comparisons indicate the need for further research. The study's cross-sectional design limits causal inferences, and the results are based on serological data without definitive confirmation of acute infection. These findings are relevant for informing targeted vaccination strategies and preventing congenital rubella syndrome, highlighting the importance of addressing vaccination gaps in specific demographic subgroups.

papers.full_text: ABSTRACTVaccination is the primary strategy for preventing hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection, but its frequency remains insufficiently characterized among cancer patients. This study evaluated the regional distribution of serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity to hepatitis B among cancer patients residing in Sao Paulo city, Brazil. We conducted a retrospective observational study of adult patients who underwent hepatitis B surface antibody (anti-HBs) serological testing at the Instituto do Cancer do Estado de Sao Paulo (ICESP) in 2023. Serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity was defined as reactive anti-HBs and non-reactive hepatitis B core antibody (anti-HBc). Univariable and multivariable Poisson regression analyses were performed to identify associated factors. Among 1,143 patients, the mean age was 57.4 ± 16.42 years, 61.9% were female, 60.6% self-identified White, and 76.8% had solid tumors. Overall, 26.2% of cancer patients had serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity to hepatitis B. Descriptively, the North Zone had a lower frequency than the South Zone (20.7% versus 28.9%), although regional differences were not statistically significant after multivariable adjustment. Female sex (adjusted prevalence ratio [aPR] = 1.67, 95% CI: 1.23-2.27, p = 0.001) and younger age (18-39 years versus ≥ 60 years: aPR = 6.89, 95% CI: 4.72-10.95, p < 0.001) were independently associated with serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity. These findings indicate a low frequency of serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity to hepatitis B among cancer patients across Sao Paulo, particularly among older adults and men. MATERIALS AND METHODSStudy designThis retrospective observational study included adult cancer patients receiving care at the Instituto do Cancer do Estado de Sao Paulo (ICESP), affiliated with the Clinical Hospital of the Faculty of Medicine, University of Sao Paulo (HCFMUSP), between January and December 2023. Serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity to hepatitis B, defined as immunity resulting from prior hepatitis B vaccination rather than previous infection, was considered present when anti-HBs was reactive and hepatitis B core antibody (anti-HBc) was non-reactive. All serological tests were performed using a chemiluminescent microparticle immunoassay (CMIA) on the Alinity i system (Abbott Diagnostics, Chicago, IL, USA) at the Central Laboratory Division of HCFMUSP. According to the laboratory’s routine procedures, an anti-HBs titer ≥ 10 IU/L was classified as reactive. Testing was conducted as part of routine clinical care before the study began, with data subsequently retrieved from the hospital’s medical records.EthicsThis study was approved by the Ethics Committee for Analysis of Research Projects of the HCFMUSP under protocols No 6.120.828 and 6.718.762 (CAAE: 70101521.9.0000.0068). Requirement for informed consent was waived, and all data were de-identified before analysis to ensure patient confidentiality.Data sourcePatients with solid tumors or hematologic malignancies who attended the ICESP, aged 18 years or older and who underwent anti-HBs serological testing were eligible for inclusion. Patients without anti-HBc testing or with reactive anti-HBc or hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) results were excluded, as were those who did not reside in Sao Paulo city. All eligible patients who met the inclusion and exclusion criteria during the study period (January to December 2023) were consecutively identified and included; therefore, no sampling strategy was applied.Demographic characteristics (i.e., age, sex [sex assigned at birth], and ethnicity/skin color), primary cancer type (i.e., solid tumors or hematological malignancies), and residential zone within Sao Paulo city were retrieved from the hospital’s medical records. Ethnicity/skin color was classified according to participants’ self-identification using the Brazilian census classification system: Brazilians of African origin who self-identified as “Black,” Indigenous Brazilians who self-identified as “Indigenous,” Brazilians of mixed ethnic background who self-identified as “Pardo” (“Brown/Mixed-ethnicity”), Brazilians of European origin who self-identified as “White,” and Brazilians of Asian origin who self-identified as “Asian.”Statistical analysisAge was analyzed both as a continuous variable and as a categorical variable (18-39, 40-59, and ≥ 60 years). full_text_sections.abstract: ABSTRACTVaccination is the primary strategy for preventing hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection, but its frequency remains insufficiently characterized among cancer patients. This study evaluated the regional distribution of serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity to hepatitis B among cancer patients residing in Sao Paulo city, Brazil. We conducted a retrospective observational study of adult patients who underwent hepatitis B surface antibody (anti-HBs) serological testing at the Instituto do Cancer do Estado de Sao Paulo (ICESP) in 2023. Serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity was defined as reactive anti-HBs and non-reactive hepatitis B core antibody (anti-HBc). Univariable and multivariable Poisson regression analyses were performed to identify associated factors. Among 1,143 patients, the mean age was 57.4 ± 16.42 years, 61.9% were female, 60.6% self-identified White, and 76.8% had solid tumors. Overall, 26.2% of cancer patients had serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity to hepatitis B. Descriptively, the North Zone had a lower frequency than the South Zone (20.7% versus 28.9%), although regional differences were not statistically significant after multivariable adjustment. Female sex (adjusted prevalence ratio [aPR] = 1.67, 95% CI: 1.23-2.27, p = 0.001) and younger age (18-39 years versus ≥ 60 years: aPR = 6.89, 95% CI: 4.72-10.95, p < 0.001) were independently associated with serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity. These findings indicate a low frequency of serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity to hepatitis B among cancer patients across Sao Paulo, particularly among older adults and men.

A recent systematic review showed that educational interventions, reminders, and patient counseling are effective strategies for improving vaccination uptake among patients with cancer 18 . Additionally, HBV screening before chemotherapy remains low worldwide, with a pooled rate of 57%, although screening rates have increased over time 19 . Expanding HBV screening and strengthening vaccination programs may help reduce the risk of HBV reactivation during anticancer treatment 20 .LimitationsThis study has several limitations. First, given the retrospective design, selection bias cannot be ruled out because information on the anti-HBs testing strategy was unavailable, and inclusion was restricted to patients with available HBV serological results. Second, information on socioeconomic and structural determinants was unavailable. Third, ethnicity/skin color was analyzed as a dichotomous variable (White versus non-White) because of the small number of participants in specific categories, which may have masked differences among individual racial and ethnic groups. Additionally, documented vaccination records were unavailable, and no national system allows comprehensive retrieval of individual hepatitis B vaccination histories. Consequently, the serological profile evaluated in this study should be interpreted as evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity rather than as confirmation of vaccination. Finally, information regarding the timing of anti-HBs testing in relation to cancer diagnosis and anticancer treatment was unavailable. Therefore, it was not possible to distinguish whether low or undetectable anti-HBs levels reflected lack of vaccination, waning antibody levels over time, impaired vaccine response, treatment-related immunosuppression, or a combination of these mechanisms. Despite these limitations, the study provides important epidemiological data on serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity against hepatitis B among cancer patients and identifies demographic groups that may benefit from strengthened vaccination and testing strategies.

Although regional differences were not statistically significant after adjustment, older adults and men were less likely to have serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity. full_text_sections.other: INTRODUCTIONGlobally, an estimated 0.9 million individuals were newly infected with hepatitis B virus (HBV) in 2024. From 2000 to 2024, Brazil reported 302,351 newly diagnosed cases of hepatitis B, of which 63,670 occurred in Sao Paulo State 1 . Sao Paulo city (23°32’51” S 46°38’10” W) has approximately 11.4 million inhabitants, distributed across five major urban zones: Central, East, North, West, and South. Concurrently, Brazil recorded an estimated 627,193 new cancer cases in 2022 2 . Within this context, preventive strategies are critical for patients with cancer, who are at increased risk of HBV reactivation and other infection-related complications driven by disease- and treatment-related immunosuppression 3 . In particular, anticancer therapies may predispose patients with previous HBV infection to viral reactivation and severe hepatic complications 3 .Vaccination against HBV is the primary strategy for preventing HBV infection in both the general population and patients receiving anticancer therapy. In the general population, seroprotection rates after completion of the full vaccination schedule are expected to reach 98%-100% in children and 90%-95% in adults. However, vaccine-induced immune responses are less robust among individuals older than 40-50 years 4 . The isolated presence of hepatitis B surface antibody (anti-HBs), in the absence of anti-HBc, is widely accepted as serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity to hepatitis B. Therefore, this study aims to determine the frequency and regional distribution of serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity to hepatitis B among cancer patients residing in Sao Paulo city. EthicsThis study was approved by the Ethics Committee for Analysis of Research Projects of the HCFMUSP under protocols No 6.120.828 and 6.718.762 (CAAE: 70101521.9.0000.0068). Requirement for informed consent was waived, and all data were de-identified before analysis to ensure patient confidentiality. Data sourcePatients with solid tumors or hematologic malignancies who attended the ICESP, aged 18 years or older and who underwent anti-HBs serological testing were eligible for inclusion. Patients without anti-HBc testing or with reactive anti-HBc or hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) results were excluded, as were those who did not reside in Sao Paulo city. All eligible patients who met the inclusion and exclusion criteria during the study period (January to December 2023) were consecutively identified and included; therefore, no sampling strategy was applied.Demographic characteristics (i.e., age, sex [sex assigned at birth], and ethnicity/skin color), primary cancer type (i.e., solid tumors or hematological malignancies), and residential zone within Sao Paulo city were retrieved from the hospital’s medical records. Ethnicity/skin color was classified according to participants’ self-identification using the Brazilian census classification system: Brazilians of African origin who self-identified as “Black,” Indigenous Brazilians who self-identified as “Indigenous,” Brazilians of mixed ethnic background who self-identified as “Pardo” (“Brown/Mixed-ethnicity”), Brazilians of European origin who self-identified as “White,” and Brazilians of Asian origin who self-identified as “Asian.” Statistical analysisAge was analyzed both as a continuous variable and as a categorical variable (18-39, 40-59, and ≥ 60 years). Sex was classified as male or female; ethnicity/skin color as White or non-White (including Black, Indigenous, Pardo, and Asian); and primary cancer type as hematological malignancies or solid tumors.Associations between zone of residence (Central, East, North, West, and South), epidemiological characteristics, and serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity to hepatitis B (anti-HBs) were evaluated by using univariable Poisson regression to estimate unadjusted prevalence ratios (PRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Consistent with established variable-selection procedures, variables with p-values < 0.20 in the univariable analyses were selected for inclusion in the multivariable Poisson regression model. Differences in demographic characteristics and cancer type across the five zones were assessed using Pearson’s chi-square test. Statistical analyses were performed using IBM SPSS Statistics for Windows, version 22.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA), and statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. LimitationsThis study has several limitations. First, given the retrospective design, selection bias cannot be ruled out because information on the anti-HBs testing strategy was unavailable, and inclusion was restricted to patients with available HBV serological results. Second, information on socioeconomic and structural determinants was unavailable. Third, ethnicity/skin color was analyzed as a dichotomous variable (White versus non-White) because of the small number of participants in specific categories, which may have masked differences among individual racial and ethnic groups. Fourth, this was a single-center study conducted at the largest quaternary oncology hospital in Latin America, and the findings may not be generalized to other healthcare settings. Additionally, documented vaccination records were unavailable, and no national system allows comprehensive retrieval of individual hepatitis B vaccination histories. Consequently, the serological profile evaluated in this study should be interpreted as evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity rather than as confirmation of vaccination. Finally, information regarding the timing of anti-HBs testing in relation to cancer diagnosis and anticancer treatment was unavailable. Therefore, it was not possible to distinguish whether low or undetectable anti-HBs levels reflected lack of vaccination, waning antibody levels over time, impaired vaccine response, treatment-related immunosuppression, or a combination of these mechanisms. Despite these limitations, the study provides important epidemiological data on serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity against hepatitis B among cancer patients and identifies demographic groups that may benefit from strengthened vaccination and testing strategies.

papers.title_original: Regional distribution of serological evidence of vaccine-induced immunity to hepatitis B among cancer patients in a city in southeastern Brazil

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to investigate the regional distribution of serological evidence of vaccine-induced immunity to hepatitis B among cancer patients in a city in southeastern Brazil, addressing the knowledge gap regarding immunity patterns in this specific population.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A retrospective observational study was conducted among 1,143 adult cancer patients who underwent hepatitis B surface antibody (anti-HBs) testing at the Instituto do Cancer do Estado de Sao Paulo (ICESP) in 2023. Patients were distributed across all five zones of Sao Paulo city, with the largest proportions in the South and East.
analysis.methods: Univariable and multivariable Poisson regression analyses were performed to identify associated factors. Variables with p-values < 0.20 in univariable analyses were selected for the multivariable model. Demographic characteristics and cancer type were assessed using Pearson’s chi-square test.
analysis.main_results: Overall, 26.2% (299/1,143) of cancer patients showed serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity to hepatitis B. In the univariable analysis, patients in the North had lower prevalence compared to those in the South (20.7% versus 28.9%; PR = 0.72, 95% CI: 0.51-1.01, p = 0.054), but this association was no longer significant after adjustment (p = 0.139). Female patients were more likely than male patients to present serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity (aPR = 1.42, 95% CI: 1.10-1.82).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted that the regional variation in serological evidence may partly reflect demographic distribution, as the South is the most populous region. They noted that age-related differences were observed, with younger adults showing higher frequency of immunity than older individuals.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings inform the need for targeted vaccination efforts in specific regions and highlight the importance of age and sex in immunity patterns, which can guide public health strategies for improving hepatitis B vaccination coverage among cancer patients.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its retrospective design and potential confounding factors. The evidence is moderate, as the association between zone of residence and immunity was not statistically significant after adjustment, and demographic differences across zones were not observed.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the regional distribution of serological evidence of vaccine-induced immunity to hepatitis B among cancer patients in a city in southeastern Brazil. A retrospective observational study was conducted on 1,143 patients, with data collected from medical records. Univariable and multivariable Poisson regression analyses were used to assess associations between zone of residence, demographic factors, and immunity status. Overall, 26.2% of patients showed serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity. While univariable analysis suggested a lower prevalence in the North compared to the South, this association was not significant after adjustment. Female patients were more likely to show immunity than males. The authors interpreted that regional variation may reflect demographic distribution, as the South is the most populous area. Age-related differences were observed, with younger adults having higher immunity rates. The study provides insights into immunity patterns among cancer patients and highlights the need for targeted vaccination efforts. However, the evidence is moderate due to the study's retrospective design and potential confounding factors.

papers.title: A schedule-driven importation risk framework for mass gathering events: FIFA World Cup 2026
papers.abstract: Objectives: Large international events draw visitors worldwide, but how much do they add to infectious disease importation risk beyond everyday travel? We developed a schedule-driven, uncertainty-aware framework to estimate this added risk and applied it to the 2026 FIFA World Cup as a case study. Methods: Three nested Poisson models represent baseline travel, event-related growth, and schedule-driven allocation of additional visitors by venue and date, with Monte Carlo simulation propagating uncertainty in disease under-reporting and travel-while-infected probability. We applied the approach to five diseases across 11 US host cities during the June 2026 World Cup group stage using only publicly available data, evaluated against independently reported dengue case counts, with measles as an additional qualitative check. Results: Relative to 2026 travel without the tournament, the World Cup added 1.0-6.5% to expected importations under schedule-driven routing, versus 2.9-8.5% under routing that ignores the match schedule. Dengue, malaria, and pertussis had the highest modeled importation levels, and the probability of at least one infected dengue or pertussis arrival exceeded 0.99 at 10 of 11 cities. Comparison with 2024 dengue and 2022 measles surveillance data showed a significant rank correlation between modeled and reported dengue cases (Spearman rho= 0.83). Conclusions: This approach provides an empirically grounded way to assess importation risk during large international events using only freely available data, identifying where public health planning may be most useful. For the World Cup case study, the tournament's own contribution was modest once fans were routed by the actual match schedule rather than as ordinary travelers.

papers.abstract_zh: 目标:大型国际活动吸引了世界各地的游客,但除了日常旅行之外,它们给传染病输入风险增加了多少?我们开发了一个日程驱动的、不确定性感知的框架来估计这种额外的风险,并将其应用于 2026 年 FIFA 世界杯作为案例研究。方法:三个嵌套泊松模型代表基线旅行、与事件相关的增长以及按地点和日期划分的额外游客的日程驱动分配,并通过蒙特卡罗模拟传播疾病漏报和感染时旅行概率的不确定性。我们在 2026 年 6 月世界杯小组赛阶段将该方法应用于美国 11 个 宿主 城市的五种疾病,仅使用公开数据,根据独立报告的登革热病例数进行评估,并使用 麻疹 作为额外的定性检查。结果:相对于 2026 年没有比赛的旅行,世界杯在赛程驱动的路由下增加了 1.0-6.5% 的预期输入,而在忽略比赛赛程的路由下增加了 2.9-8.5%。登革热、疟疾和百日咳的模拟输入水平最高,11 个城市中有 10 个城市中至少有 1 例感染登革热或百日咳传入的概率超过 0.99。与 2024 年登革热和 2022 年 麻疹 监测 数据的比较显示,建模和报告的登革热病例之间存在显着的等级相关性 (Spearman rho= 0.83)。结论:这种方法提供了一种基于经验的方法,仅使用免费提供的数据来评估大型国际活动期间的输入风险,从而确定公共卫生规划在哪些方面可能最有用。对于世界杯案例研究来说,一旦球迷按照实际比赛日程安排而不是作为普通旅行者,赛事本身的贡献就微乎其微了。

Search Search Home News PAHO assesses risk of measles spread as very high ahead of religious mass gatherings in the Americas PAHO assesses risk of measles spread as very high ahead of religious mass gatherings in the Americas Copied to clipboard Vaccination gaps and increased population movement could facilitate further transmission, underscoring the need for stronger vaccination and surveillance efforts Washington, D.C., 9 October 2026 (PAHO) — With several religious mass gatherings in South America expected to increase national and international travel across the Americas in the coming months, the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) is urging countries to strengthen vaccination, surveillance and rapid response measures as the risk of measles spread across the Region remains very high. The warning comes in a new PAHO regional risk assessment released amid ongoing outbreaks, persistent gaps in vaccination coverage and the detection of measles cases in new geographic areas. The assessment updates PAHO’s regional evaluation of 5 August 2026, with a specific focus on risks associated with upcoming religious mass gatherings in South America and their potential implications for the Region of the Americas. “Measles is highly contagious, and we are seeing the consequences of gaps in vaccination coverage across the Americas,” said Dr. Jarbas Barbosa, PAHO Director. “People need to protect their children with the very effective and safe measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine, and countries have to close immunity gaps, strengthen surveillance and ensure that they can detect and respond rapidly to cases, particularly as increased travel and large gatherings create more opportunities for the virus to spread.” According to the latest PAHO data, 55,792 confirmed measles cases and 77 deaths were reported in 17 countries and territories in the Region between 4 January and 3 October 2026. This represents a 4.8-fold increase in cases compared with the same period in 2025. Measles cases have also increased globally in 2026, increasing the likelihood of imported cases through international travel and onward transmission in communities with low immunity. Guatemala reported the largest number of cases, followed by Mexico, the United States, Peru and Canada. Together, these five countries accounted for 99.5% of confirmed cases in the Region. Cases have also been reported in Argentina, Belize, Bolivia, Bonaire, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, El Salvador, Honduras, Panama and Uruguay. Why mass gatherings increase the risk Measles is highly contagious and can spread rapidly when introduced into populations with low immunity, particularly in crowded settings. People with measles can transmit the virus before the characteristic rash appears, meaning infected travelers may unknowingly expose others. Large gatherings and the movement of people between countries and communities can therefore facilitate the importation and onward spread of the virus. “Anyone planning to attend a large gathering should check that they are protected against measles,” said Dr. Daniel Salas, Executive Manager of Comprehensive Immunization at PAHO. “Even people travelling within their own country may be exposed when large numbers of people from different regions come together. People aged 6 months and older who do not have evidence of vaccination should receive a dose of measles-rubella vaccine before traveling or attending the gathering, preferably at least two weeks in advance.” Vaccination remains the main protection Regional coverage reached 88% for the first dose of the MMR vaccine and 85% for the second dose in 2025, below the 95% coverage needed to prevent outbreaks. Persistent low coverage has increased the number of people susceptible to measles and created pockets of susceptible populations in parts of the Region. These gaps reflect several factors, including setbacks in immunization accumulated during the COVID-19 pandemic, vaccine hesitancy in some communities, operational challenges in delivering vaccination and barriers to accessing health services, particularly among Indigenous peoples, migrants and displaced populations. An estimated 1.6 million children in the Region of the Americas did not receive any dose of measles vaccine in 2025. PAHO supports countries to strengthen preparedness PAHO is working with countries across the Region to strengthen vaccination, surveillance and outbreak response. In South America, the Organization is supporting preparedness for upcoming mass gatherings expected to involve significant national and international population movement. PAHO is also supporting laboratory-based surveillance and genomic monitoring across the Region, while affected countries are receiving technical cooperation to strengthen vaccination, contact tracing and outbreak response. PAHO urges countries to close vaccination gaps Measles can cause serious illness and complications at any age, with infants and adults at greater risk of severe disease and death. Children under five and populations experiencing malnutrition or limited access to health services have been disproportionately affected during recent outbreaks in the Region. With active outbreaks continuing and major gatherings approaching, PAHO is urging countries to use every opportunity to ensure that people who are not protected against measles have access to vaccination, while strengthening surveillance and maintaining the capacity to detect and respond rapidly to cases. news.content_zh: 泛美卫生组织 (PAHO) 发布了一项区域风险评估,表明在即将举行的宗教群众集会之前,麻疹 在美洲传播的风险非常高。这些聚会预计将增加旅行和人口流动,为病毒传播创造更多机会。评估指出,2026年1月4日至10月3日期间,17个国家和地区报告了55,792例麻疹确诊病例,77例死亡,比2025年同期增加4.8倍。危地马拉、墨西哥、美国、秘鲁和加拿大占这些病例的99.5%。泛美卫生组织强调需要加强 疫苗接种 覆盖范围、监测 和快速反应措施来减轻风险。该组织正在通过技术合作、基于实验室的 监测 和基因组监测来支持各国,以增强准备和应对能力。该警告强调了 疫苗接种 缺口的后果以及通过国际旅行输入病例的可能性,特别是在免疫力低下的社区。

The region's approximate 3,300 square miles and 100 miles of coastline are divided into five supervisory districts that are each represented by an elected official who serves on the Board of Supervisors. The Board sets governing policies for and serves as the legislative arm for the unincorporated areas of the County. The County government provides more than 700 public services, including law enforcement, animal control, flu shots, transportation planning, foster care, and more. While some County services – such as law enforcement, road maintenance and repair, and land-use planning – are only provided to the unincorporated areas, many are an extension of the State and are also provided to people in the incorporated cities. news.content: The measles virus under a microscope. The virus has infected 1,004 people in Pennsylvania. It's now the largest outbreak in decades. BSIP / Universal Images Group via Getty Oct. 5, 2026, 9:37 PM UTC By Erika Edwards Pennsylvania’s measles outbreak is now the largest in the U.S. in three decades. On Monday, the state surpassed South Carolina’s outbreak earlier this year, which topped out at 997. That outbreak was contained within six months. Pennsylvania’s outbreak, which began in late April, shows no sign of slowing. “I would bet that this goes on for at least another three to six months,” said Dr. John Goldman, an infectious disease expert at the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center. “We have seen an increase in vaccinations, but we aren’t seeing enough people get vaccinated to stop the epidemic.” On Monday, the Pennsylvania Department of Health reported 1,004 measles cases, with 198 hospitalizations. Nearly a third of the cases have been in children. Among the pediatric measles cases, 18% have needed hospitalization. Dehydration has become a common problem, particularly among babies and younger children, said Dr. Evan Shirey, a pediatric infectious disease physician at Penn State Health Golisano Children’s Hospital in Hershey. Doctors are also seeing young patients with liver problems. “One of the more common things that the measles virus can do is cause hepatitis or infection of the liver,” Shirey said. “These children will feel very sick, very nauseous, with abdominal pain and vomiting, and they can’t take a bottle or can’t keep food or liquid down.” Other children are developing severe and irreversible neurological damage because of brain inflammation, or encephalitis, Shirey said. “In some of these cases, it’s a child who can’t recognize their own mother, who’s disoriented and confused,” Shirey said. Still others have developed secondary bacterial infections. Five people in the state have died, according to the health department. Those people include a teenager with severe brain inflammation and a 40-year-old woman with a history of asthma, as well as two babies. One of those babies was a newborn who died after his mother went into labor a month early. There are few details about the fifth person who died, other than the person hadn’t been vaccinated and lived in Lancaster County, where the bulk of measles cases are. Lancaster County is home to the nation’s largest Amish population, with approximately 44,000 residents as of 2025 . There is nothing in the religion that is inherently anti-vaccine, but historically, their vaccination rates have been lower than those of the general population, Goldman said. According to an NBC News investigation , 88.5% of kindergartners in 2024 had the measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine. A vaccination rate of at least 95% is the accepted level of herd immunity needed to protect against a measles outbreak. “There’s nothing special about Lancaster. The exact same thing could happen in any county in the country that has a large percentage of unvaccinated people,” Goldman said. “If it hasn’t happened yet, it’s only because measles hasn’t gotten into that county yet.” The outbreak in South Carolina, which ended in April, was previously the largest in approximately 30 years , according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. That outbreak was linked to a community of people who emigrated from Ukraine over the past few decades. State health officials credited a massive surge in vaccinations with bringing the outbreak to a halt. In the northwestern corner of the state, where the outbreak was centered, nearly 15,000 MMR vaccinations were given during the South Carolina outbreak, up 82% compared with the previous year, according to the South Carolina Department of Public Health . As of Monday, the Pennsylvania health department said it’s given just 8,843 MMR doses so far in response to the outbreak. Ohio is also dealing with a growing measles outbreak along the border it shares with Pennsylvania. As of Thursday, Ohio had logged 210 measles cases , with 13 hospitalizations. Most cases are concentrated in the northeastern part of the state, in Geauga, Ashtabula and Wayne counties

news.content_zh: 截至2026年10月5日,宾夕法尼亚州正面临三十年来最大规模的麻疹 暴发,确诊病例1,004例,住院治疗198例。据报道,已有五人死亡,其中包括一名患有严重脑部炎症的青少年和两名婴儿。暴发 于 4 月下旬开始,尽管 疫苗接种 有所增加,但没有显示出放缓的迹象。近三分之一的病例涉及儿童,其中一些人出现了严重的神经损伤和肝脏并发症。暴发 集中在兰开斯特县,该县是全国阿米什人口最多的县,该县历来 疫苗接种 率较低。迄今为止,宾夕法尼亚州卫生部已注射了 8,843 剂 MMR 疫苗,但官员警告说,这不足以遏制疫情。南卡罗来纳州的 暴发 于 2026 年 4 月结束,此前是约 30 年来最大的一次,并通过 疫苗接种 的大幅上涨得到遏制。然而,宾夕法尼亚州目前的局势仍未得到解决,人们担心病毒的传播和对弱势群体的影响。
