All rights reserved More Health: Health News Parenting Wellness Healthy Eating Mental Health Addiction Newsletters October 09, 2026 Chester County high school is closed Friday due to measles case Oxford Area High School has been directed to verify its staff’s immunity documentation. Anyone who is not protected from the virus cannot attend school for 21 days. By Molly McVety PhillyVoice Staff Illness Measles from Ken Ruinard/USA Today Network via Reuters Connect Oxford Area High School is closed Friday due to a confirmed case of measles in its school community. Above, a vial of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine. Read More Oxford Area High School is closed Friday due to a confirmed measles case in the school community. The Chester County Health Department is contacting people who may have been exposed to the virus, David A. Woods, superintendent of Oxford Area School District, said in a letter to families Thursday. The school was closed so officials can verify immunity documentation for all staff members who work in the building. The district has students' vaccination records on file. MORE: Pennsylvania's ban on most e-cigarette products begins soon Anyone who is not vaccinated against measles, or able to prove their vaccination status, will not be allowed to attend school or school functions and must quarantine for 21 days. "We recognize that situations such as this can be unsettling, especially when they involve the health of children," Woods said. "Please know that we are committed to keeping our school community informed, supporting our families and working in partnership with public health officials to help protect the health and safety of everyone in our schools." Enhanced cleaning and disinfection was completed at the school "out of an abundance of caution," Woods said. Measles is a highly contagious virus that spreads through the air when infected people cough, sneeze or talk. People who are not protected from measles can contract it by breathing in air up to two hours after someone with measles has left the area. Measles is contagious between four days before and four days after a rash develops. Health officials have urged people who have never had measles or have not received two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine to get vaccinated. Two doses of the vaccine are 97% effective at preventing the virus, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Oxford Area High School's measles case comes as the state has been grappling with the United States' largest measles outbreak in 35 years. As of Friday morning, the state's measles dashboard shows 1,078 cases and 207 hospitalizations in 39 counties this year. Chester County has reported 86 cases. Philadelphia has not reported any case this year, but health officials have warned of potential exposures at the Philadelphia International Airport and the neonatal intensive care unit of the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia. Last week, the state reported that an unvaccinated Lancaster County resident tested positive for measles and died, marking the state's fifth measles-associated death this year. Pennsylvania defines measles-related deaths as those that occur within 30 days of the onset of symptoms from a lab-confirmed measles case and are not due to unrelated causes. Pennsylvania's outbreak has provoked a clash between Gov. Josh Shapiro and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has posted debunked claims that MMR vaccines contain fetal tissue and accused Shapiro of fabricating deaths. The CDC has only listed two measles deaths nationwide. Shapiro has said Pennsylvania will not accept any federal funding to fight the measles outbreak until the CDC acknowledges its other measles-related deaths. Emergency Posts Officials Aim to Stop Disease Spread as Second Measles Case Reported Public Risk Remains Low – October 8, 2026 Contributor Discover more Community Announcements Service Letters to Editor Submission Local Business Directory OSWEGO COUNTY – The Oswego County Health Department announced another confirmed case of measles in an unvaccinated adult resident. This second individual resides with the first confirmed case and is now recovering and no longer contagious to others. No additional patient information will be released to protect their privacy. “Our County Health Department is doing a great job monitoring this situation closely,” said Oswego County Legislator Paul House, District 8, chairman of the Legislature’s Health Committee. “They have been providing ongoing guidance about measles symptoms and prevention strategies to the public, and especially to anyone who may have been exposed to the virus, to help reduce any further spread of the disease.” Dr. Christina Liepke, Oswego County Medical Director, said the risk to the public remains low right now because of how these two cases are connected. “Still, the measles virus is a highly contagious respiratory disease that is easily spread by coughing and sneezing,” she said. “I want to remind everyone to be aware of its symptoms, which include a rash with a high fever and cough. Also, please call your health care provider before going into their office to avoid spreading it to other patients and medical staff.” Oswego County Public Health Director Vera Dunsmoor also stressed the importance of vaccination in preventing the spread of disease. “Vaccines not only help protect children and adults from preventable diseases but also help build ‘herd immunity’ to safeguard communities from potential outbreaks,” she said. “Please check your vaccination status and make sure your kids are up to date with their vaccinations as well.” For optimal protection, the federal Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine, with the first dose given to children aged 12 to 15 months, and the second dose given between 4 to 6 years of age. “Once again, I urge residents to get vaccinated,” she stressed. “It’s the best way to protect yourselves and your children. Just two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine is 97% effective against disease transmission – for a lifetime! The Oswego County Health Department offers weekly immunization clinics every Tuesday at the Nick Sterio Public Health Clinic, 70 Bunner St., Oswego. Adults and children can receive various vaccinations by appointment only from 9 to 11 a.m. and 1 to 3 p.m. Most insurances are accepted and no one will be turned away. To make a vaccination appointment, call the health department’s Preventive Division at 315-349-3547. The measles virus is a highly contagious respiratory disease that is easily spread by coughing and sneezing. Initial symptoms include a high fever, cough, red eyes and runny nose. One to four days later, a rash develops on the face and spreads to the rest of the body, hands and feet. A person with measles is considered contagious from four days before the rash appears to four days afterward. While the incubation period for measles is typically 7-14 days, symptoms can appear up to 21 days after exposure. Anyone not protected from it is at risk of serious health complications, especially those under 5 years of age. Measles during pregnancy can increase the risk of early labor, miscarriage and low-birth-weight infants. To make a vaccination appointment, report a potential exposure, or learn more about the measles virus and vaccine, call your primary care provider or the health department’s Preventive Division at 315-349-3547. Due to the limited risk to the public at this time, the Oswego County Health Department will not issue a news release for new confirmed measles cases in the immediate future. If and when it is determined there is a risk for potential exposure, the public will be notified immediately. For up-to-date reports on confirmed measles cases, click on New York State Department of Health’s (NYSDOH’s) measles dashboard. It is updated weekly, on Tuesday afternoons, and shows cases reported through Saturday of the previous week. For more general information about the measles virus, click on NYSDOH. The Legislature’s Health Committee oversees the Health Department. In addition to Legislator House, committee members include Vice Chairman Roy E. Reehil, District 5; Gena Bartlett, District 24; Dorothy Caldwell, District 17; Richard Kline, District 12; Michael Solowy, District 23; and Lee B. Walker, Jr., District 15. Photograph: efired/Getty Images View image in fullscreen The US is enduring its worst year for measles since 1991. Photograph: efired/Getty Images Pennsylvania faces largest measles outbreak in decades as case count rises to 1,000 Neighboring states are also reporting hundreds of cases, with over 3,800 recorded across the country Pennsylvania has surpassed 1,000 measles cases this year, state health officials calculate, making it the largest state outbreak in more than three decades. The benchmark comes as neighboring New York declared a state of emergency about measles rates there. Pennsylvania’s health department said on Monday 1,004 cases of measles had been confirmed. Five Pennsylvania residents have died after contracting the disease, with 198 hospitalizations. Lancaster county, with sizable Amish and Mennonite populations, remains the hardest hit, with 391 cases, according to official figures. Cases numbers have risen over the past three months, with the highest number of infections in the 24-49 age range. Pennsylvania health officials brace for expected spread of measles outbreak Read more The numbers, however, are not included in a CDC count due to an ongoing dispute between Pennsylvania’s governor, Josh Shapiro, and the US health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr, over how to classify measles-related mortality. Shapiro has called Kennedy “incompetent”, and Kennedy has publicly questioned whether the state’s recorded fatalities were directly caused by measles. The CDC – which Kennedy oversees – currently lists two measles deaths in the US this year. Shapiro has expanded access to the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine in affected communities. “I want every Pennsylvanian to know this: measles does not care about your county, your faith, or your social circle,” he said in August. “I urge everyone to take this seriously and to discuss any concerns with their trusted health care provider.” In New York state, Governor Kathy Hochul declared a state of emergency on Monday as well, citing 108 cases in the state as of 3 October. Ohio, which also shares a border with Pennsylvania, has also reported advancing numbers of cases, with more than 200 this year. Like in Pennsylvania, Ohio has a significant Amish population. The US is enduring its worst year for measles since 1991. As of 1 October, the CDC reported 3,887 confirmed cases this year, along with the highest number of measles-associated deaths in decades. In addition to Pennsylvania, outbreaks have been reported in several states, including Texas and Utah, as well as South Carolina, which had the largest outbreak with 997 cases reported. Health officials in Pennsylvania have said the state’s current outbreak started in April, west of Philadelphia and attributed the outbreak to low vaccination rates. According to the Associated Press, the most recent outbreak to surpass 1,000 cases occurred in New York City in the early 1990s. That outbreak infected more than 4,500 people. During the 1989 and 1991 resurgences, 55,000 infections and 123 deaths ⁠were recorded, according to Reuters. The domestic US spread of measles was eliminated in 2000 by high vaccination rates, but those rates have fallen in recent years to below the 95% coverage needed to prevent outbreaks. In November, international health officials will meet to determine if the US and Mexico have lost their measles-free status. Photograph: efired/Getty Images Pennsylvania faces largest measles outbreak in decades as case count rises to 1,000 Neighboring states are also reporting hundreds of cases, with over 3,800 recorded across the country Pennsylvania has surpassed 1,000 measles cases this year, state health officials calculate, making it the largest state outbreak in more than three decades. The benchmark comes as neighboring New York declared a state of emergency about measles rates there. Pennsylvania’s health department said on Monday 1,004 cases of measles had been confirmed. Five Pennsylvania residents have died after contracting the disease, with 198 hospitalizations. Lancaster county, with sizable Amish and Mennonite populations, remains the hardest hit, with 391 cases, according to official figures. Cases numbers have risen over the past three months, with the highest number of infections in the 24-49 age range. Pennsylvania health officials brace for expected spread of measles outbreak Read more The numbers, however, are not included in a CDC count due to an ongoing dispute between Pennsylvania’s governor, Josh Shapiro, and the US health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr, over how to classify measles-related mortality. Shapiro has called Kennedy “incompetent”, and Kennedy has publicly questioned whether the state’s recorded fatalities were directly caused by measles. The CDC – which Kennedy oversees – currently lists two measles deaths in the US this year. Shapiro has expanded access to the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine in affected communities. “I want every Pennsylvanian to know this: measles does not care about your county, your faith, or your social circle,” he said in August. “I urge everyone to take this seriously and to discuss any concerns with their trusted health care provider.” In New York state, Governor Kathy Hochul declared a state of emergency on Monday as well, citing 108 cases in the state as of 3 October. Ohio, which also shares a border with Pennsylvania, has also reported advancing numbers of cases, with more than 200 this year. Like in Pennsylvania, Ohio has a significant Amish population. The US is enduring its worst year for measles since 1991. As of 1 October, the CDC reported 3,887 confirmed cases this year, along with the highest number of measles-associated deaths in decades. In addition to Pennsylvania, outbreaks have been reported in several states, including Texas and Utah, as well as South Carolina, which had the largest outbreak with 997 cases reported. Health officials in Pennsylvania have said the state’s current outbreak started in April, west of Philadelphia and attributed the outbreak to low vaccination rates. According to the Associated Press, the most recent outbreak to surpass 1,000 cases occurred in New York City in the early 1990s. That outbreak infected more than 4,500 people. During the 1989 and 1991 resurgences, 55,000 infections and 123 deaths ⁠were recorded, according to Reuters. The domestic US spread of measles was eliminated in 2000 by high vaccination rates, but those rates have fallen in recent years to below the 95% coverage needed to prevent outbreaks. In November, international health officials will meet to determine if the US and Mexico have lost their measles-free status. news.content_title: Pennsylvania Measles Outbreak Tops 1,000 Cases, Becoming the Largest in the U.S. in 3 Decades
news.content: NEED TO KNOW Pennsylvania's Department of Health said in an update on Monday, Oct. 5 that it recorded 1,004 total cases of measles Nearly 200 people have been hospitalized and five deaths have been reported since the outbreak began in April An infectious disease expert said he expects cases to continue for at least another three to six months Pennsylvania has recorded 1,000 measles cases, making it the largest outbreak in the U.S. in three decades. Pennsylvania's Department of Health shared in an update on Monday, Oct. 5 that it logged 1,004 total cases of measles in 2026, surpassing the number of South Carolina's measles outbreak earlier this year, according to Associated Press , NBC News and ABC News . The current outbreak started in April, and since then, there have been 992 measles cases recorded. Last week alone, 106 cases were reported, according to the health department's data. So far, 198 people have been hospitalized and five people have died. Stock photo of a blood sample with measles virus. Credit: Getty According to the health department, fewer than 1% of people diagnosed with measles were fully vaccinated. Health experts said low vaccination rates contributing to the outbreaks, per the AP. Dr. John Goldman, an infectious disease expert at the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center, told NBC News that he expects the measles outbreak in Pennsylvania to continue on for several more months. "I would bet that this goes on for at least another three to six months," he told the outlet. "We have seen an increase in vaccinations, but we aren't seeing enough people get vaccinated to stop the epidemic." The Pennsylvania Department of Health also reported that 32% of those diagnosed with measles were under 18, and 18% of those pediatric patients required hospitalization. Dr. Evan Shirey, a pediatric infectious disease physician at Penn State Health Golisano Children's Hospital, told NBC News that children are particularly vulnerable to measles and its complications. "One of the more common things that the measles virus can do is cause hepatitis or infection of the liver," she told the outlet. "These children will feel very sick, very nauseous, with abdominal pain and vomiting, and they can't take a bottle or can't keep food or liquid down." She said measles can also cause brain inflammation in children, potentially resulting in irreversible neurological damage or secondary bacterial infections. Stock photo of a doctor with a patient after a vaccination. Credit: iStockphoto/Getty Pennsylvania isn't the only state that has battled a measles outbreak this year. South Carolina's outbreak from October 2025 to April 2026 totaled 997 cases. The Centers for Disease Control (CDC) said 3,887 total measles cases have been reported in the U.S. this year as of Oct. 1. The agency also noted that there have been 42 new outbreaks reported this year. Never miss a story — sign up for PEOPLE's free daily newsletter to stay up-to-date on the best of what PEOPLE has to offer, from celebrity news to compelling human interest stories. CDC guidance calls for two doses of the MMR vaccine during childhood to be vaccinated against measles. The first is recommended at 12 to 15 months, followed by another dose between the ages of 4 to 6. The agency said the two doses are 97% effective against measles. After Pennsylvania announced its fifth death due to measles, the CDC told ABC News in a statement that it "has mounted an aggressive response to measles outbreaks across the country." "Texas, South Carolina, Virginia, Kansas, New Mexico, and Wisconsin requested CDC Epi-Aids and worked alongside federal teams to help bring their outbreaks rapidly and successfully under control," the agency said, adding, that the "CDC has not received a formal Epi-Aid request from Pennsylvania" and "if requested, CDC stands ready to deploy epidemiologists to support the state's identified needs." news.content_original: NEED TO KNOW Pennsylvania's Department of Health said in an update on Monday, Oct. 5 that it recorded 1,004 total cases of measles Nearly 200 people have been hospitalized and five deaths have been reported since the outbreak began in April An infectious disease expert said he expects cases to continue for at least another three to six months Pennsylvania has recorded 1,000 measles cases, making it the largest outbreak in the U.S. in three decades. Pennsylvania's Department of Health shared in an update on Monday, Oct. 5 that it logged 1,004 total cases of measles in 2026, surpassing the number of South Carolina's measles outbreak earlier this year, according to Associated Press , NBC News and ABC News . The current outbreak started in April, and since then, there have been 992 measles cases recorded. Last week alone, 106 cases were reported, according to the health department's data. So far, 198 people have been hospitalized and five people have died. Stock photo of a blood sample with measles virus. Credit: Getty According to the health department, fewer than 1% of people diagnosed with measles were fully vaccinated. Health experts said low vaccination rates contributing to the outbreaks, per the AP. Dr. John Goldman, an infectious disease expert at the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center, told NBC News that he expects the measles outbreak in Pennsylvania to continue on for several more months. "I would bet that this goes on for at least another three to six months," he told the outlet. "We have seen an increase in vaccinations, but we aren't seeing enough people get vaccinated to stop the epidemic." The Pennsylvania Department of Health also reported that 32% of those diagnosed with measles were under 18, and 18% of those pediatric patients required hospitalization. Dr. Evan Shirey, a pediatric infectious disease physician at Penn State Health Golisano Children's Hospital, told NBC News that children are particularly vulnerable to measles and its complications. "One of the more common things that the measles virus can do is cause hepatitis or infection of the liver," she told the outlet. "These children will feel very sick, very nauseous, with abdominal pain and vomiting, and they can't take a bottle or can't keep food or liquid down." She said measles can also cause brain inflammation in children, potentially resulting in irreversible neurological damage or secondary bacterial infections. Stock photo of a doctor with a patient after a vaccination. Credit: iStockphoto/Getty Pennsylvania isn't the only state that has battled a measles outbreak this year. South Carolina's outbreak from October 2025 to April 2026 totaled 997 cases. The Centers for Disease Control (CDC) said 3,887 total measles cases have been reported in the U.S. this year as of Oct. 1. The agency also noted that there have been 42 new outbreaks reported this year. Never miss a story — sign up for PEOPLE's free daily newsletter to stay up-to-date on the best of what PEOPLE has to offer, from celebrity news to compelling human interest stories. CDC guidance calls for two doses of the MMR vaccine during childhood to be vaccinated against measles. The first is recommended at 12 to 15 months, followed by another dose between the ages of 4 to 6. The agency said the two doses are 97% effective against measles. After Pennsylvania announced its fifth death due to measles, the CDC told ABC News in a statement that it "has mounted an aggressive response to measles outbreaks across the country." "Texas, South Carolina, Virginia, Kansas, New Mexico, and Wisconsin requested CDC Epi-Aids and worked alongside federal teams to help bring their outbreaks rapidly and successfully under control," the agency said, adding, that the "CDC has not received a formal Epi-Aid request from Pennsylvania" and "if requested, CDC stands ready to deploy epidemiologists to support the state's identified needs." Newsroom Technical Support Health Now Officials say 2 Allegheny County measles cases are related Eden Christian Academy in the North Hills says it is affected By James Engel 3 Min Read • Oct. 9, 2026 | 47 seconds ago Go Ad-Free today A lab test for measles comes back positive. (Adobe Stock) The Allegheny County Health Department said Friday a second county resident who has tested positive for measles was likely exposed while at school. The department said the infection is related to a separate confirmed case announced Monday — the first involving a county resident — despite the fact that officials previously said there were “no school-related exposures.” “They do not live in the same household, which suggests there was likely a previously unknown exposure at the school,” the department said in a statement. Ronnie Das, a spokesman for the department, declined to say at which school the exposure took place. But Eden Christian Academy, which operates three campuses in the North Hills — elementary schools in Ross and Pine and an “upper school” in Ohio Township — said in a statement it was “recently notified by local public health authorities of measles within our school community.” The school said its policy and privacy regulations barred it from disclosing information about the person who was infected. But, the statement said, “We are working directly and in full cooperation with the Allegheny County Health Department and implementing their protocol to mitigate further spread.” The academy enrolls more than 800 students, according to its website. Measles vaccination rates among Eden Christian Academy’s student body are far below the roughly 95% required for herd immunity against the disease. At Eden’s elementary schools, only about 83% of students were immunized, according to county data from last school year. That figure was closer to 90% at its upper school, though only 80% of students there had all required vaccinations. Between all its campuses, more than 550 students were not vaccinated against measles last year. Only one student, however, filed for a medical exemption to vaccination; the rest were religious or moral objectors. Officials described both infected individuals in the county as unvaccinated minors. The county previously said that anyone who visited the Target at Pine Creek Shopping Center in McCandless (9805 McKnight Road) between 3:45 and 5:45 p.m. Thursday, Oct. 1, may have been exposed. “This connection significantly expands our investigation,” Dr. Jillian Irwin, the county health department medical director, said in a statement. “Determining how these individuals were infected and the details of all additional exposures is key to successfully stopping further spread.” The department said it will call or text those who may have been exposed. Confirmed cases of measles — 1,136 across the state as of Friday, according to Pennsylvania Health Department data — had already been recorded in neighboring Westmoreland and Armstrong counties, although before this week, no infections were noted in Pennsylvania’s second largest population center. The outbreak has yet to result in any confirmed cases in Philadelphia. The state health department has so far reported five measles-related deaths since late August. Only one student, however, filed for a medical exemption to vaccination; the rest were religious or moral objectors. Officials described both infected individuals in the county as unvaccinated minors. Others question what they see as a lengthy list of childhood shots. By Hope Kirwan October 9, 2026 Updated October 9, 2026 at 1:13 pm Download Read Transcript Pedestrians walk through downtown Viroqua, Wis., on Tuesday, Oct. 6, 2026. Angela Major/WPR Tattoo Zuzu sits on Viroqua’s busy Main Street, with an eclectic mix of art and thrifted treasures filling the front of the shop. The name is in honor of owner Audra Grosz’s 5-year-old daughter, a nickname Grosz’s mother loved from “It’s a Wonderful Life.” Her daughter was a big part of why Grosz and her husband moved from Madison to Viroqua four and a half years ago. She said they were looking for the slower pace of life that comes with living in a city of 4,500 people, and she now appreciates how her neighbors help each other and support local businesses. Understanding Wisconsin, Together. WPR’s “Wisconsin Today” newsletter keeps you connected to the state you love without feeling overwhelmed. No paywall. No agenda. No corporate filter. X/Twitter This field is for validation purposes and should be left unchanged. Email The tight-knit community is also located in one of the southwestern Wisconsin counties experiencing an outbreak of measles since early August. There have been 240 cases in the outbreak so far across Grant, Iowa, Lafayette and Vernon counties. Wisconsin now has the fourth-highest number of cases of the highly contagious and potentially deadly disease in the country, according to the latest data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Vernon County, where Viroqua is located, has by far the lowest rate of vaccinations against measles in the state. Only 42 percent of 2-year-olds had the shot last year, according to data from the Wisconsin Department of Health Services. By comparison, just under 80 percent of all Wisconsin 2-year-olds were vaccinated last year. But that’s still well below the 95 percent that health experts say is needed to keep the virus from spreading. Health What Pennsylvania’s measles outbreak could mean for pregnancy care across America It's raising new questions about immunity testing before pregnancy, early vaccinations for babies and the many complications that could rise from infection. New cases of congenital measles and increasing exposure risks are putting a spotlight on the vulnerabilities of pregnancy and postpartum care in America in an era of lowering vaccination rates. (Getty Images) Barbara Rodriguez Health Reporter Published October 6, 2026, 5:00 a.m. CT 2026-10-06 05:00 5:00 October 6, 2026 am America/Chicago Republish this story Share Bluesky Facebook Email A deadly measles outbreak in Pennsylvania, which has infected more than 975 people this year and been linked to five deaths, has also infected at least 50 pregnant women in the state. Doctors in outbreak areas are making changes to how they care for pregnant patients and their babies, offering a glimpse of what may be in store across the nation as cases spread. Among the deaths were two infants in Lancaster County, an area about 60 miles west of Philadelphia and the epicenter of the Pennsylvania outbreak. A newborn had congenital measles, which was passed in utero through an unvaccinated mother who was infected. It is not clear whether the other infant, who was reportedly 6 weeks old at the time of death and had a genetic birth disorder, was exposed in utero or after birth. Some Pennsylvania-based doctors have experienced an uptick in anxious questions from patients about the implications of measles on just about all aspects of pregnancy care: What do more cases mean for a current pregnancy? Are additional precautions needed for someone planning to get pregnant soon? How concerned should parents with a newborn be about public outings? The 19th thanks our sponsors. Become one. It all depends, doctors in Pennsylvania and nationally told The 19th, on preventative care measures taken prior to pregnancy and a person’s proximity to an outbreak. What is certain is that new cases of congenital measles and increasing exposure risks are putting a spotlight on the vulnerabilities of pregnancy and postpartum care in America in an era of lowering vaccination rates. “Air doesn’t know that there’s a border between Pennsylvania and Ohio, or that there’s a border between New Jersey and New York,” said Dr. Sharee Livingston, an OBGYN in Lancaster County. “We are dealing with a respiratory illness, and even if we weren’t dealing with a respiratory illness, none of us live in a vacuum.” An evolving outbreak (Getty Images) Livingston never came across a single case of measles during her medical training in the mid-2000s, and neither did many of her peers. But in the past six months, Livingston estimates that she has treated at least a dozen patients infected with the highly contagious disease. Livingston did not share more information about the patients, including whether they were all women or if any were pregnant. The Pennsylvania Department of Health (DOH) told The 19th that, as of Friday, a total of 977 measles cases had been reported in 2026, and 53 of those were among pregnant women. As of early October state health officials have reported nearly 40 percent of Pennsylvania’s cases were coming from Lancaster County. The five measles-associated deaths — the infants, a 40-year-old woman, an 18-year-old and a 20-year-old with leukemia — were the first in the state in 35 years. “Measles wasn’t a conversation we were having before, but it is now,” said Dr. Kisha Davis, president-elect of the American Academy of Family Physicians. DOH told The 19th it could not confirm any estimate of the number of congenital measles cases in the state or provide more details about the infected pregnant women, citing state privacy laws. The department said there is no nationally standardized definition for congenital measles and that it is working with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to develop a system for tracking and reporting cases. They have been tracking cases during pregnancy and in “very young children” and said that since Oct. 2, more than 100 measles cases in the state have been in children under the age of 4. NBC News reported that at least six newborns in the state have been infected with measles during the outbreak, citing a Pennsylvania doctor. There have been more than 3,800 confirmed measles cases in the United States this year, the highest number in decades. Roughly 95 percent of the infections are among unvaccinated people or individuals whose vaccination status is unknown. It is unclear how many of those people were pregnant or postpartum at the time of infection. But Dr. Kevin Ault, an OBGYN who recently started working at Penn State Health in Hershey — about 30 miles northwest of Lancaster County — noted that more than a quarter of cases were in adults of childbearing age. “At any given time, about 1 percent of Americans are pregnant. So there’s an intersection there of unvaccinated adults and pregnant people that are going to be in this scenario,” said Ault, who is a fellow with the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) and serves in the organization’s expert group on infectious diseases and immunization. Doctors do not recommend that pregnant patients get the measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine because it carries a live virus, making immunization prior to pregnancy critical. Vaccinated pregnant people pass antibodies to their infants and have an immune system that is better positioned to keep a future fetus and baby safe from measles or to reduce complications in the rare event of a breakthrough infection. Livingston has been trying to reassure vaccinated patients who may still worry about infections, reminding them of these robust protections. But, she noted, “if the pregnant person believes that they’ve had an exposure and they’re unvaccinated, that’s where it becomes a problem. Because then there’s a risk to both the fetus and the mother.” A ‘disconcerting’ reality (Getty Images) An infection in an unvaccinated person during pregnancy has a host of complications including pregnancy loss, premature delivery and low birth weight. New guidelines on congenital measles released last month by the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) warn of a 25 to 30 percent rate of infection if measles is passed through the birth parent within days of a birth. The guidelines had been in the works for some time but carried more urgency after the infant fatalities in Pennsylvania, said Dr. Pia Pannaraj, a member of the AAP’s Committee on Infectious Diseases and a professor of pediatrics at the University of California, San Diego. “Many doctors that are practicing right now might never have seen measles in their lifetime, so they know it from the textbooks, but that’s not the same as having a patient,” she said. “So we’re having to educate providers: ‘How do you recognize measles? This is what the rash looks like.’” The AAP guidelines break down different scenarios for monitoring congenital and newborn measles infections. In some cases, babies without overt symptoms of measles birthed by an infected parent can be given a post-exposure antibody known as immune globulin — but it may not help if infection has already occurred. Treatment in general for infected babies is limited and includes monitoring possible complications, like a fever or pneumonia. “There’s only basically what we call supportive care,” Pannaraj said. “So we treat the symptoms as they arrive as best we can, but there’s no way to basically kill the measles virus, and there’s no way to prevent the complications that will occur.” Infected babies can be at higher risk for encephalitis, a type of brain swelling, as well as a rare but fatal brain inflammation that can appear later in life. “Mom takes the hit of getting the disease, but the infants are at the highest risk for measles complications of anybody that could get measles,” Pannaraj added, noting that babies’ immune systems are incredibly underdeveloped. Dr. Holly Cummings, an OBGYN in Philadelphia and the chair of Pennsylvania’s section of ACOG, said she’s increasingly ordering bloodwork to check the measles immunity of patients who are thinking about getting pregnant. This hasn’t always been Cummings’ approach. She already assesses her patients’ immunity for other viruses but relied on the general understanding that most people have received the MMR series, which is 97 percent effective at preventing measles. Several doctors told The 19th that they’ve worked under an assumption that children growing up in the 1990s and onward went through public schools that mandated the MMR vaccine. Those mandates are still in place, but exemption laws have been expanded since then. ACOG, which has guidelines on measles that it developed more than a decade ago, recommends that doctors assess a patient’s immunity with either proof of vaccination or through bloodwork. For patients born in the ‘90s, electronic medical records of their childhood vaccinations may also be more readily available to doctors. A measles immunity check before pregnancy may become a necessity in the future, but it will depend on circumstances like community spread and declining vaccination rates, Davis said. “The vast majority of folks are still vaccinated — the fact that we are having to have that conversation again feels a little disconcerting,” she said. These clinical considerations will carry more weight as more adults choose not to vaccinate their families, and as their children reach childbearing age. Vaccination rates for routine vaccines continue to decline among kindergartners, according to new CDC data. In Pennsylvania, more than half of counties have an MMR vaccination rate below 95 percent, the threshold for herd immunity. That includes Philadelphia County and some groups of children in Lancaster County. While some of the most impacted areas in the state are far from Philadelphia, Cummings doesn’t want to make assumptions about her patients’ vaccine status. In September, public health officials reported a measles exposure at several locations within the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia complex, including a NICU lounge. “In the context of this current measles outbreak — and particularly for me right now given that there’s such a high number of cases in Pennsylvania — it does feel important for me to bring it up and ensure that my patients are protected,” she said. Changing vaccine landscape (Joe Raedle/Getty Images) There are implications for future care beyond the frequency of immunity testing. Doctors may reexamine how they advise parents about early MMR vaccination for their babies. Infants as young as six months old can be approved for an early MMR shot if they will be in an area with potential measles exposure. This option, Pannaraj said, used to be reserved for infants traveling internationally to high-risk exposure areas. But doctors are increasingly recommending an early shot if a child is living in or traveling domestically to an outbreak region. An early shot doesn’t negate the need for two shots later, which have been timed for maximum effectiveness. “Is there going to be a time where we need to think about earlier vaccination?” she said. “Now, I hope that’s not the case, because currently the outbreaks are still limited within the United States. We’re all working hard to make sure it stays that way and to try to get rid of the outbreak.” Emphasizing the importance of vaccination has been complicated in recent years. The politicization of pandemic-era mitigation policies gave rise to a new wave of online misinformation about the safety and efficacy of vaccines, including the MMR vaccine. Disinformation over the disputed link between the MMR vaccine and autism flourished in the late ‘90s, but vaccine disinformation has a more powerful megaphone now through the federal government. Both President Donald Trump and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. have spread false information about routine childhood vaccines. In August, Trump claimed without evidence that the MMR shot can be “quite lethal.” And while Kennedy’s department has occasionally promoted the MMR vaccine, he falsely said last year that the shot causes annual deaths. In 2021, Kennedy gave a speech in Lancaster County where he downplayed the threat of measles. His record shapes public perception: New polling shows 40 percent of adults are unsure whether or not Kennedy recommends the MMR vaccine, and another 29 percent think he does not recommend it. Kennedy oversees the CDC, which has not recognized all five deaths reported in Pennsylvania. The department says on its measles dashboard that it is working to standardize a definition for measles deaths. “These are not new efforts. What is new today is the fact that there’s been a corporatization of the anti-vaccine movement,” Chelsea Clinton, vice chair of the Clinton Foundation and assistant professor at Columbia University’s Mailman School of Public Health, told The 19th. “There are deep profit motives frequently fueling many of the loudest voices. I think some have deeply painful personal experiences and extrapolated out of those without scientific evidence or data and yet really believe they’re trying to save other families.” Still, public health officials in Pennsylvania are seeing a response to the outbreak. In August, health providers reported administering more than 46,000 doses of the MMR vaccine — a massive jump from the roughly 25,000 doses they recorded monthly during the first half of the year. Doctors say a person who is thinking about getting pregnant should get the MMR vaccine or check their immunity through bloodwork prior to conception. Someone who is pregnant and not vaccinated should consult with health providers about any special precautions to take to avoid an infection. “We should be talking to women and to anyone whose partner may be thinking about being pregnant so that being caught up on your vaccines is just part of what someone is thinking about while also maybe trying to stop smoking, and drink more water, and eat healthier and all the other things that people often say they’re trying to optimize for their health before getting pregnant,” Clinton said. Livingston credits state and federal public health officials for being responsive to the outbreak in her county, but she sees opportunities for more equitable care that helps people walk into pregnancy the healthiest version of themselves — which in turn can help to mitigate future adverse outcomes. For now, Livingston is leaning on evidence-based best practices. She believes recent lessons from the pandemic around immunization will ultimately help her community move forward. “I don’t mean to sound really flowery or overly positive, but I am hopeful,” she said. “I believe that most people want to be healthy during their pregnancies. They care tremendously about their unborn child, and so I think when people understand that that’s our angle, it makes it a little bit easier to have the conversation and maybe adopt best practices.” Additional reporting by Isabela Espadas Barros Leal. Health What Pennsylvania’s measles outbreak could mean for pregnancy care across America It's raising new questions about immunity testing before pregnancy, early vaccinations for babies and the many complications that could rise from infection. New cases of congenital measles and increasing exposure risks are putting a spotlight on the vulnerabilities of pregnancy and postpartum care in America in an era of lowering vaccination rates. (Getty Images) Barbara Rodriguez Health Reporter Published October 6, 2026, 5:00 a.m. CT 2026-10-06 05:00 5:00 October 6, 2026 am America/Chicago Republish this story Share Bluesky Facebook Email A deadly measles outbreak in Pennsylvania, which has infected more than 975 people this year and been linked to five deaths, has also infected at least 50 pregnant women in the state. Doctors in outbreak areas are making changes to how they care for pregnant patients and their babies, offering a glimpse of what may be in store across the nation as cases spread. Among the deaths were two infants in Lancaster County, an area about 60 miles west of Philadelphia and the epicenter of the Pennsylvania outbreak. A newborn had congenital measles, which was passed in utero through an unvaccinated mother who was infected. It is not clear whether the other infant, who was reportedly 6 weeks old at the time of death and had a genetic birth disorder, was exposed in utero or after birth. Some Pennsylvania-based doctors have experienced an uptick in anxious questions from patients about the implications of measles on just about all aspects of pregnancy care: What do more cases mean for a current pregnancy? Are additional precautions needed for someone planning to get pregnant soon? How concerned should parents with a newborn be about public outings? The 19th thanks our sponsors. Become one. It all depends, doctors in Pennsylvania and nationally told The 19th, on preventative care measures taken prior to pregnancy and a person’s proximity to an outbreak. What is certain is that new cases of congenital measles and increasing exposure risks are putting a spotlight on the vulnerabilities of pregnancy and postpartum care in America in an era of lowering vaccination rates. “Air doesn’t know that there’s a border between Pennsylvania and Ohio, or that there’s a border between New Jersey and New York,” said Dr. Sharee Livingston, an OBGYN in Lancaster County. “We are dealing with a respiratory illness, and even if we weren’t dealing with a respiratory illness, none of us live in a vacuum.” An evolving outbreak (Getty Images) Livingston never came across a single case of measles during her medical training in the mid-2000s, and neither did many of her peers. But in the past six months, Livingston estimates that she has treated at least a dozen patients infected with the highly contagious disease. Livingston did not share more information about the patients, including whether they were all women or if any were pregnant. The Pennsylvania Department of Health (DOH) told The 19th that, as of Friday, a total of 977 measles cases had been reported in 2026, and 53 of those were among pregnant women. As of early October state health officials have reported nearly 40 percent of Pennsylvania’s cases were coming from Lancaster County. The five measles-associated deaths — the infants, a 40-year-old woman, an 18-year-old and a 20-year-old with leukemia — were the first in the state in 35 years. “Measles wasn’t a conversation we were having before, but it is now,” said Dr. Kisha Davis, president-elect of the American Academy of Family Physicians. DOH told The 19th it could not confirm any estimate of the number of congenital measles cases in the state or provide more details about the infected pregnant women, citing state privacy laws. The department said there is no nationally standardized definition for congenital measles and that it is working with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to develop a system for tracking and reporting cases. They have been tracking cases during pregnancy and in “very young children” and said that since Oct. 2, more than 100 measles cases in the state have been in children under the age of 4. NBC News reported that at least six newborns in the state have been infected with measles during the outbreak, citing a Pennsylvania doctor. There have been more than 3,800 confirmed measles cases in the United States this year, the highest number in decades. Roughly 95 percent of the infections are among unvaccinated people or individuals whose vaccination status is unknown. It is unclear how many of those people were pregnant or postpartum at the time of infection. But Dr. Kevin Ault, an OBGYN who recently started working at Penn State Health in Hershey — about 30 miles northwest of Lancaster County — noted that more than a quarter of cases were in adults of childbearing age. “At any given time, about 1 percent of Americans are pregnant. So there’s an intersection there of unvaccinated adults and pregnant people that are going to be in this scenario,” said Ault, who is a fellow with the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) and serves in the organization’s expert group on infectious diseases and immunization. Doctors do not recommend that pregnant patients get the measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine because it carries a live virus, making immunization prior to pregnancy critical. Vaccinated pregnant people pass antibodies to their infants and have an immune system that is better positioned to keep a future fetus and baby safe from measles or to reduce complications in the rare event of a breakthrough infection. Livingston has been trying to reassure vaccinated patients who may still worry about infections, reminding them of these robust protections. But, she noted, “if the pregnant person believes that they’ve had an exposure and they’re unvaccinated, that’s where it becomes a problem. Because then there’s a risk to both the fetus and the mother.” A ‘disconcerting’ reality (Getty Images) An infection in an unvaccinated person during pregnancy has a host of complications including pregnancy loss, premature delivery and low birth weight. New guidelines on congenital measles released last month by the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) warn of a 25 to 30 percent rate of infection if measles is passed through the birth parent within days of a birth. The guidelines had been in the works for some time but carried more urgency after the infant fatalities in Pennsylvania, said Dr. Pia Pannaraj, a member of the AAP’s Committee on Infectious Diseases and a professor of pediatrics at the University of California, San Diego. “Many doctors that are practicing right now might never have seen measles in their lifetime, so they know it from the textbooks, but that’s not the same as having a patient,” she said. “So we’re having to educate providers: ‘How do you recognize measles? This is what the rash looks like.’” The AAP guidelines break down different scenarios for monitoring congenital and newborn measles infections. In some cases, babies without overt symptoms of measles birthed by an infected parent can be given a post-exposure antibody known as immune globulin — but it may not help if infection has already occurred. Treatment in general for infected babies is limited and includes monitoring possible complications, like a fever or pneumonia. “There’s only basically what we call supportive care,” Pannaraj said. “So we treat the symptoms as they arrive as best we can, but there’s no way to basically kill the measles virus, and there’s no way to prevent the complications that will occur.” Infected babies can be at higher risk for encephalitis, a type of brain swelling, as well as a rare but fatal brain inflammation that can appear later in life. “Mom takes the hit of getting the disease, but the infants are at the highest risk for measles complications of anybody that could get measles,” Pannaraj added, noting that babies’ immune systems are incredibly underdeveloped. Dr. Holly Cummings, an OBGYN in Philadelphia and the chair of Pennsylvania’s section of ACOG, said she’s increasingly ordering bloodwork to check the measles immunity of patients who are thinking about getting pregnant. This hasn’t always been Cummings’ approach. She already assesses her patients’ immunity for other viruses but relied on the general understanding that most people have received the MMR series, which is 97 percent effective at preventing measles. Several doctors told The 19th that they’ve worked under an assumption that children growing up in the 1990s and onward went through public schools that mandated the MMR vaccine. Those mandates are still in place, but exemption laws have been expanded since then. ACOG, which has guidelines on measles that it developed more than a decade ago, recommends that doctors assess a patient’s immunity with either proof of vaccination or through bloodwork. For patients born in the ‘90s, electronic medical records of their childhood vaccinations may also be more readily available to doctors. A measles immunity check before pregnancy may become a necessity in the future, but it will depend on circumstances like community spread and declining vaccination rates, Davis said. “The vast majority of folks are still vaccinated — the fact that we are having to have that conversation again feels a little disconcerting,” she said. These clinical considerations will carry more weight as more adults choose not to vaccinate their families, and as their children reach childbearing age. Vaccination rates for routine vaccines continue to decline among kindergartners, according to new CDC data. In Pennsylvania, more than half of counties have an MMR vaccination rate below 95 percent, the threshold for herd immunity. That includes Philadelphia County and some groups of children in Lancaster County. While some of the most impacted areas in the state are far from Philadelphia, Cummings doesn’t want to make assumptions about her patients’ vaccine status. In September, public health officials reported a measles exposure at several locations within the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia complex, including a NICU lounge. “In the context of this current measles outbreak — and particularly for me right now given that there’s such a high number of cases in Pennsylvania — it does feel important for me to bring it up and ensure that my patients are protected,” she said. Changing vaccine landscape (Joe Raedle/Getty Images) There are implications for future care beyond the frequency of immunity testing. Doctors may reexamine how they advise parents about early MMR vaccination for their babies. Infants as young as six months old can be approved for an early MMR shot if they will be in an area with potential measles exposure. This option, Pannaraj said, used to be reserved for infants traveling internationally to high-risk exposure areas. But doctors are increasingly recommending an early shot if a child is living in or traveling domestically to an outbreak region. An early shot doesn’t negate the need for two shots later, which have been timed for maximum effectiveness. “Is there going to be a time where we need to think about earlier vaccination?” she said. “Now, I hope that’s not the case, because currently the outbreaks are still limited within the United States. We’re all working hard to make sure it stays that way and to try to get rid of the outbreak.” Emphasizing the importance of vaccination has been complicated in recent years. The politicization of pandemic-era mitigation policies gave rise to a new wave of online misinformation about the safety and efficacy of vaccines, including the MMR vaccine. Disinformation over the disputed link between the MMR vaccine and autism flourished in the late ‘90s, but vaccine disinformation has a more powerful megaphone now through the federal government. Both President Donald Trump and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. have spread false information about routine childhood vaccines. In August, Trump claimed without evidence that the MMR shot can be “quite lethal.” And while Kennedy’s department has occasionally promoted the MMR vaccine, he falsely said last year that the shot causes annual deaths. In 2021, Kennedy gave a speech in Lancaster County where he downplayed the threat of measles. His record shapes public perception: New polling shows 40 percent of adults are unsure whether or not Kennedy recommends the MMR vaccine, and another 29 percent think he does not recommend it. Kennedy oversees the CDC, which has not recognized all five deaths reported in Pennsylvania. The department says on its measles dashboard that it is working to standardize a definition for measles deaths. “These are not new efforts. What is new today is the fact that there’s been a corporatization of the anti-vaccine movement,” Chelsea Clinton, vice chair of the Clinton Foundation and assistant professor at Columbia University’s Mailman School of Public Health, told The 19th. “There are deep profit motives frequently fueling many of the loudest voices. I think some have deeply painful personal experiences and extrapolated out of those without scientific evidence or data and yet really believe they’re trying to save other families.” Still, public health officials in Pennsylvania are seeing a response to the outbreak. In August, health providers reported administering more than 46,000 doses of the MMR vaccine — a massive jump from the roughly 25,000 doses they recorded monthly during the first half of the year. Doctors say a person who is thinking about getting pregnant should get the MMR vaccine or check their immunity through bloodwork prior to conception. Someone who is pregnant and not vaccinated should consult with health providers about any special precautions to take to avoid an infection. “We should be talking to women and to anyone whose partner may be thinking about being pregnant so that being caught up on your vaccines is just part of what someone is thinking about while also maybe trying to stop smoking, and drink more water, and eat healthier and all the other things that people often say they’re trying to optimize for their health before getting pregnant,” Clinton said. Livingston credits state and federal public health officials for being responsive to the outbreak in her county, but she sees opportunities for more equitable care that helps people walk into pregnancy the healthiest version of themselves — which in turn can help to mitigate future adverse outcomes. For now, Livingston is leaning on evidence-based best practices. She believes recent lessons from the pandemic around immunization will ultimately help her community move forward. “I don’t mean to sound really flowery or overly positive, but I am hopeful,” she said. “I believe that most people want to be healthy during their pregnancies. They care tremendously about their unborn child, and so I think when people understand that that’s our angle, it makes it a little bit easier to have the conversation and maybe adopt best practices.” Additional reporting by Isabela Espadas Barros Leal. analysis.brief_en: A measles outbreak in Pennsylvania has infected over 975 people and at least 50 pregnant women, with five deaths linked to the outbreak, including two infants. The outbreak, centered in Lancaster County, has raised concerns about the risks of congenital measles and the impact on pregnancy care in the U.S. as vaccination rates decline. Doctors are emphasizing the importance of pre-pregnancy vaccination to protect both mothers and infants. The Pennsylvania Department of Health is tracking cases but cannot confirm the number of congenital measles cases due to privacy laws. Preventative measures and awareness are being prioritized to mitigate risks.

Photograph: Shannon Stapleton/Reuters New York governor declares state of emergency after spike in measles cases The deadly outbreak in Pennsylvania is its largest in more than three decades, and confirmed cases in New York are up The New York governor, Kathy Hochul, declared a state of emergency on Monday in response to a dramatic spike in measles cases in the state. Hochul’s administration said the emergency declaration was in response to a “growing number of measles cases across rural areas of New York and neighboring states”, including Pennsylvania, which has been grappling with a deadly outbreak that is its largest in more than three decades. The declaration expands the pool of people who can administer vaccines against measles and allows more individuals to order testing. It comes as there have been 108 confirmed cases of measles in New York so far for the year, up from just one reported case in 2023. In Pennsylvania, which neighbors New York, five people have died after contracting the disease, and there have been 198 hospitalizations. The state surpassed 1,000 measles cases on Monday while Ohio has also seen an increase. New York, Pennsylvania and Ohio have sizable Amish populations, which tend to be undervaccinated. And undervaccination has been a driving factor in measles spreading after its domestic US spread had been eliminated in 2000 by high vaccination rates. “After reviewing the latest data on measles cases in New York state, I am declaring a State Disaster Emergency to strengthen our ongoing efforts to confront this disease,” Hochul said. “No one should get seriously ill or die from a vaccine-preventable disease. That is why I have taken steps to increase the number of health professionals who can vaccinate and test. These emergency measures will protect New Yorkers and support our community partners as they work tirelessly to address the spread of this disease.” The US is experiencing its worst year for measles since 1991, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, with nearly 3,900 cases reported. Of New York’s 108 measles cases, 101 have been reported outside of New York City, the state said. Since 15 July, 92 cases have been reported in underimmunized rural communities. It is a stark increase from previous years. Beside the one reported case in 2023, there were only 15 in 2024 – and in 2025, there were a total of 48 measles cases. The Trump administration health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr, has been criticized for his response to the measles outbreak. Before his appointment as health secretary, he was best known as an anti-vaccine activist. Kennedy headlined an anti-vaccine conference in Washington DC in mid-September, as measles cases surged. He told the crowd there that they had a “strong and steadfast friend at the White House”. Meanwhile, the Pennsylvania governor, Josh Shapiro, has called Kennedy “incompetent”, and the two men have clashed over how to classify measles-related deaths. “The concerning rise in measles cases is due to a decrease in childhood vaccines driven by misinformation and is causing a public health emergency,” said state senator Gustavo Rivera, who chairs the senate’s health committee. At least 95% of a community must be vaccinated against measles to prevent outbreaks. news.content_title: Measles cases reach 4,080 for the year — the highest in decades
news.content: A sign at a University of Utah health clinic warns visitors about the spread of measles. The state has had 535 reported cases this year, among the largest counts in the country. (Photo by McKenzie Romero/Utah News Dispatch) Measles cases for the calendar year surpassed 4,000 for the first time in decades, with as many as five deaths in Pennsylvania, as the federal government steps in with financial help for states but also fans vaccination fears and skepticism. A weekly report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention showed 4,080 cases this year as of Oct. 8, up 192 cases in a week. Pennsylvania, which has reported five confirmed deaths from measles, alone had 142 new cases for the week — for a total of 1,105 for the year. The CDC has recognized just two of the state's reported deaths. Measles cases have reached a 35-year high Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, a Democrat, has protested the CDC's death count; his state's five deaths would be more than the three deaths reported in 2025 for the entire nation. Other states with large numbers of cases, more than 200, did not see their case numbers change for the week: South Carolina (670 for the year), Utah (535) and Wisconsin (207). States with more cases included New York, which declared a measles emergency, with 19 new cases for a total of 103 this year; and Iowa, up 17 cases to 39. Kentucky reported separately on Friday that cases there had reached 104, up 10 from last week. Pennsylvania, which has become ground zero for this year's outbreaks, reported this week that a new awareness and pop-up vaccine clinics are leading to more measles vaccinations. All but five states have had at least one measles case this year. The last time the United States had this many cases was in 1991, reaching 9,643 cases as the nation still struggled to roll out vaccinations for the disease, amid budget cuts that hit programs in big cities. Pennsylvania's health department this week announced "a surge of interest" in vaccinations as more residents become aware of the outbreak — more than 56,000 doses were given out in September, more than twice the usual monthly volume. The state has added pop-up clinics in the most affected areas. All but four of the measles cases were among unvaccinated people. The Lewistown Sentinel reported that an 18-year-old woman there died in September from brain swelling as a result of the measles virus after two of her brothers survived the disease. While the federal government has offered states more funding to combat measles, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy moved forward this week on plans to emphasize vaccine injury, announcing a new clinic and work to strengthen a database that tracks problems after a vaccination. "We must listen to patients and families who report vaccine injuries — not dismiss or gaslight them," Kennedy said in a statement. analysis.time: The measles outbreak reached 4,080 cases as of October 8, 2026, with a weekly increase of 192 cases. Pennsylvania reported five new cases for the week, bringing its total to 1,105 for the year. The last time the U.S. had this many cases was in 1991.
analysis.location_and_population: The outbreak spans multiple U.S. states, with Pennsylvania being a major hotspot. Other states with significant cases include South Carolina, Utah, and Wisconsin. All but five states have had at least one measles case this year, and all but four cases were among unvaccinated individuals.
analysis.event: Measles cases for the calendar year surpassed 4,000 for the first time in decades, with five confirmed deaths in Pennsylvania. The CDC reported 4,080 cases as of October 8, 2026, and the state of Pennsylvania has become ground zero for this year's outbreaks.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The outbreak has led to a surge in vaccination interest, with over 56,000 doses given out in September. Pennsylvania's health department reported 142 new cases for the week, and the CDC has recognized only two of the state's reported deaths. The outbreak has raised concerns about vaccine safety and public health measures.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The federal government has provided financial support to states, while the CDC has emphasized the need for vaccine injury tracking. Pennsylvania has launched pop-up vaccine clinics and reported increased awareness. The situation remains under investigation, with some states declaring emergencies and others experiencing rising case numbers.

analysis.brief_en: The measles outbreak in the United States has reached a 35-year high, with 4,080 cases reported as of October 8, 2026, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Pennsylvania has been the epicenter of this surge, reporting 1,105 cases for the year and five confirmed deaths, though the CDC has only recognized two of these. The state has seen a significant increase in new cases, with 142 reported in a single week, and has responded by launching pop-up vaccine clinics to boost immunization rates. Other states like South Carolina, Utah, and Wisconsin also reported high numbers, with over 200 cases each. The outbreak has sparked debates about vaccine safety, with Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy emphasizing the need to address vaccine injuries. Despite federal financial support, the situation remains under investigation, and the last time the U.S. had this many cases was in 1991. The rise in cases highlights the importance of vaccination efforts and the challenges in controlling the spread of the measles virus.

Despite federal financial support, the situation remains under investigation, and the last time the U.S. had this many cases was in 1991. The rise in cases highlights the importance of vaccination efforts and the challenges in controlling the spread of the measles virus.

While the article highlights the public health concern, it does not provide specific case counts, death counts, or exposure numbers. The situation is described as under investigation, with no clear details on the response measures taken by authorities. The outbreak has raised awareness about vaccine hesitancy in the region, emphasizing the need for accurate information and community engagement. The article does not mention any official actions or interventions, leaving the response status uncertain. This event reflects broader challenges in maintaining vaccination rates and managing public health crises in rural areas.

news.content: Find us on Google 📌 America's birthday 🎂 Start the day smarter ☀️ Get the USA TODAY app U.S. Politics Sports Entertainment Life Money Travel Opinion Crossword ONLY AT USA TODAY: Newsletters For Subscribers Real Estate From the Archives USA TODAY PLAY Crossword Marvel Comics eNewspaper Magazines Investigations Video Podcasts Humankind Advertise Your Business WITNESS (True Crime) Just Curious Best-selling Booklist Top Workplaces Nomination Legals Press Releases Cars Boats Grocery Shopping OUR PORTFOLIO: Real Estate 10BEST USA TODAY Store Shopping Money Essentials Blueprint WITNESS (True Crime) Southern Kitchen Home Internet Services PITTSBURGH Measles Add Topic Allegheny County school site of second confirmed measles case this week Finch Walker USA TODAY NETWORK Updated Oct. 9, 2026, 10:31 a.m. ET Hear this story Two residents in Allegheny County, Pennsylvania, have tested positive for measles. One case is linked to a private Christian school, while another involved potential exposure at a Target in Ross Township. Health officials advise those who may have been exposed to contact their healthcare provider before visiting a facility. This article was updated to include information from Allegheny County Health Department. In less than a week, two Allegheny County residents have tested positive for measles. On Oct. 5, the county health department said an unvaccinated minor had been sickened by the virus causing an outbreak that's left five people dead in Pennsylvania. Then, on Oct. 8, the agency confirmed that a second person had contracted the virus. Both attend the same school, so it's likely a previous exposure went undetected at the school, the health department said. "This connection significantly expands our investigation," said Dr. Jillian Irwin, Allegheny County Health Department's medical director. "Determining how these individuals were infected and the details of all additional exposures is key to successfully stopping further spread." Here's what to know. Who has measles in Allegheny County? A second Allegheny County resident tested positive for measles, the county health department said on Oct. 8. The individual is not in the same family as the first measles case, but both people attend the same school, which means there was likely a previously unknown exposure at the school, the department said in an Oct. 9 release. The health department did not provide any information about the second individual's age, vaccination status or what specific school they attend, though Pittsburgh's Public Source reported that the individual was a child at a private Christian school in the North Hills. Earlier in the week, an unvaccinated minor tested positive for measles, according to an Oct. 5 release from Allegheny County Health Department. They did not provide any additional information about the individual, citing privacy concerns. The number of measles cases in Allegheny County will be updated daily as needed online. Was I exposed to measles in Allegheny County? A spokesperson for Allegheny County Health Department told Pittsburgh's Public Source that the department was working with school officials at Eden Christian Academy to contain the spread, with spokesperson Ronnie Das saying the health department has "been providing specific guidance to the school nurse and administration of an impacted school on how to organize lists of immune staff and students and ensuring school staff understands who needs to quarantine and for how long." The department will call or text people who were exposed to the two measles cases while the two children were contagious, according to the Oct. 9 release. Eden Christian Academy has elementary school campuses in Ross and Pine, as well as a school for older children in Ohio Township. A spokesperson for the school didn't say which campus was impacted. While there were no school-related exposures involving the first measles case, other locals could have come into contact with the virus, according to the health department. Shoppers at the Ross Township Target, located at 9805 McKnight Road, may have been exposed to measles on Thursday, Oct. 1 between 3:45 p.m. and 5:45 p.m. What should I do if I was exposed to measles? If you believe you may have been exposed to measles, you should talk to your healthcare provider about what to do, the county health department said. Do not go to a healthcare facility without calling ahead. Those who are unvaccinated are most at risk of catching measles. Anyone who is partially vaccinated, meaning they received one dose of the MMR vaccine rather than the recommended two, may still be susceptible to the disease. Two doses of the vaccine are about 97% effective in preventing infection, according to the Centers for Disease Control. Allegheny County is recommending that healthcare providers administer the MMR vaccine on an accelerated schedule to children ages six months and older due to the outbreak. If you were vaccinated in Pennsylvania, you can check your vaccination status on the state department of health's website. If you have not been vaccinated, you should schedule your shots with your healthcare provider or the immunization clinic in Downton Pittsburgh, the county health department said. If you're uncertain if you've been vaccinated, there's no risk in getting an additional dose of the MMR vaccine. What are the symptoms of measles? How does measles spread? Measles spreads when a person infected with the virus breathes, coughs or sneezes. It spreads through the air and on surfaces, and it can remain in the air and on surfaces for up to two hours after the person has left an area. The illness starts with fever, cough, runny nose and red, watery eyes, and is then followed by a rash that begins on the head or face and spreads downward. Symptoms can show up seven to 21 days after exposure, and a person is contagious four days before and four days after the rash begins. How many measles cases are there in Pennsylvania? As of Oct. 9 morning, there were 1,078 confirmed cases of measles throughout Pennsylvania, thought Pennsylvania Department of Health was expected to update that number later in the afternoon. Across the state, there had been five measles-associated deaths, and 207 people had been hospitalized with measles in 2026. More than 99% of all cases occurred in people who were not fully vaccinated. Finch Walker is the Pittsburgh Connect Reporter for the USA TODAY Network. Contact Walker at FWalker@usatodayco.com. Officials are investigating the outbreak and advising exposed individuals to contact healthcare providers before visiting facilities. As of October 9, 2026, Pennsylvania has 1,078 confirmed measles cases, with five deaths and 207 hospitalizations in 2026. Over 99% of cases involved unvaccinated individuals, emphasizing the risk for those not fully immunized. The health department is working with the school to manage the spread and will update the case count daily. Details about the second case, including age and vaccination status, remain undisclosed due to privacy concerns.
news.content_zh: 在宾夕法尼亚州阿勒格尼县,一周内报告了两例 麻疹 确诊病例,两人就读于同一所私立基督教学校。卫生部门将一例病例与学校联系起来,另一例病例与罗斯镇一家塔吉特商店的潜在接触史有关。官员们正在调查 暴发,并建议接触者在前往设施之前联系医疗保健提供者。截至 2026 年 10 月 9 日,宾夕法尼亚州已确诊 1,078 例 麻疹 病例,到 2026 年将有 5 例死亡,207 例住院治疗。超过 99% 的病例涉及未接种疫苗的个体,这强调了未完全免疫的人面临的风险。卫生部门正在与学校合作控制疫情传播,并将每天更新病例数。由于隐私问题,有关第二个病例的详细信息(包括年龄和 疫苗接种 状态)仍未公开。

Lancaster County Coroner urges vaccination after third measles-associated death WGAL US LIVE Current Time 0:00 / Total Duration 0:55 Sorry, this video is not available, please check back later. Advertisement Updated: 5:20 PM EDT Oct 5, 2026 Editorial Standards i Annie Jennemann Data Journalist Pennsylvania measles cases reach more than 1,000. Track outbreaks in your state Updated: 5:20 PM EDT Oct 5, 2026 Editorial Standards i Annie Jennemann Data Journalist The Pennsylvania Department of Health reported more than 1,000 measles cases confirmed so far in 2026 Monday. The 1,004 cases have been reported in 39 out of Pennsylvania's 67 counties. More than a third of the measles cases were in Lancaster County with 391 cases, according to the latest data . The county with the second-largest number of cases was Mifflin with 118 cases. Advertisement The Pennsylvania Department of Health has reported 198 hospitalizations and five deaths associated with measles as of Monday. Just four of the confirmed 1,004 cases were people who were vaccinated. The two deaths are the first reported in 2026. Three deaths were reported in 2025, according to data from the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Measles cases across the U.S. have surged in 2026.
