Photograph: Raquel Natalicchio/Houston Chronicle via Getty Images View image in fullscreen The measles outbreak has hit the state’s Amish community, which has low vaccination rates, particularly hard. Photograph: Raquel Natalicchio/Houston Chronicle via Getty Images Pennsylvania health officials brace for expected spread of measles outbreak Most counties don’t have their own health agencies, and some specific population groups have low vaccination rates Pennsylvania is bracing for a wave of measles cases, with some public health officials concerned that it’s “only a matter of time” until the disease spreads beyond the outbreak’s center. Last week the state reported its fifth measles-associated death amid 943 confirmed cases across 39 counties. The outbreak comes amid concerns that public health in the US has been hit by increasing vaccine skepticism, especially due to the power and influence of the controversial health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr. Contributing to the challenge is that Pennsylvania is one of the few US states where its counties mostly lack their own health department, with only seven of its 67 counties having their own. Pennsylvania reports fifth measles-related death of the year amid outbreak Read more Lancaster county, which doesn’t have its own health department, has seen the highest number of cases, at 381, believed to be mostly among the Amish or similar religious groups who have historically low rates of measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine uptake. Health officials, doctors and other members of the community in the county are now attempting to establish its own health department to better tackle the outbreak. Jeanne Franklin, the director of Chester county’s health department, said that her county, which has the third highest number of cases, at 83, is preparing for an influx of cases from neighboring Lancaster. “We have a very long border with Lancaster county, and these types of disease don’t care about borders,” Franklin said. “It’s going to keep going and find a person who isn’t vaccinated. We’re operating with the assumption that the disease may jump and spread to non-Plain [Amish] community members. Our goal is to prevent that, but we assume that it may happen.” She added that although many Amish people have not been vaccinated, it’s not because they are anti-vaxxers, but rather because “they were either unaware of it or they don’t seek out healthcare as frequently as other residents”. She added: “But they’re willing to have the conversation and make a decision on what’s happening today. They’re not making decisions based on the myths out there, but because their neighbors are impacted.” Amid active surveillance of measles cases, contact tracing and setting up community vaccination centers, the county is also working to dispel misinformation some of its residents have regarding the safety of the vaccine. “We have people in key positions saying it isn’t an outbreak, it isn’t a problem. We have people who approach our nurses and say that they were told the vaccine will make them sterile, or that there’s a microchip within it,” Franklin said. But for Franklin, the fact that Chester county is one of the few counties to have its own health department is a clear advantage in the race to stop the spread of the disease. “By having our own health department [it] means that we already have the infrastructure in place, and we prepare for these things all year round,” Franklin said. “With the number of counties [the state has] to provide support to, they can’t possibly know all the key partners in a geographical area.” She added: “The state has a finite set of employees, while I can pull my employees away from their normal jobs and say we need help with this. We live here, we know it, and we’re working with the communities and the organizations who know us. I think every county needs a health department, but we’re just not set up that way in Pennsylvania while other states are.” Dr Richard Lorraine, the medical director of Montgomery county’s office of public health, said that it was a “matter of time” before the third most populous county in Pennsylvania would begin to see measles cases. “We recognize that essentially it’s all around us, and so a big focus for the county is immunization,” Lorraine said. “It’s the best preventative measure and where the county is focusing its efforts on.” skip past newsletter promotion after newsletter promotion Working closely with community organizers, Lorraine said the county was making sure that every resident was able to be vaccinated regardless of their insurance status. “Because we are a public health agency, our mandate is to provide for members of our population for the most part who are underinsured, and there’s a very high percentage who aren’t insured,” Lorraine said. “And through our partnership with pharmacies we’re able to open these clinics for everyone. So whether you have insurance or if you don’t, we can work it out so that someone is able to administer a vaccine.” Lora Werner, the director of the Delaware county health department, said that her agency was facing several challenges in protecting residents from the virus. Among them was the collapse of Crozer Health, Delaware county’s largest healthcare system, due to bankruptcy last year. “They were a huge provider of pediatric care,” Werner said. “And although we do have a high vaccination rate across Delaware county, there are pockets where they aren’t as good.” For Werner, the newly established local health department has been a gamechanger for promoting public health initiatives in the county. “We are the newest health department on the block, and we’re so passionate about the fact that we’re now here and can serve our residents,” Werner said. “We’re deeply integrated into the social networks.” She added: “Creating a new department was very challenging, and we’re a very odd state in this regard,” Werner said. “If you want to have one you need to have a referendum to establish one. But it’s not required, so we have a mishmash of the counties that have taken that step and those that have not.” The Guardian has approached the Pennsylvania health department for comment. Photograph: Raquel Natalicchio/Houston Chronicle via Getty Images Pennsylvania health officials brace for expected spread of measles outbreak Most counties don’t have their own health agencies, and some specific population groups have low vaccination rates Pennsylvania is bracing for a wave of measles cases, with some public health officials concerned that it’s “only a matter of time” until the disease spreads beyond the outbreak’s center. Last week the state reported its fifth measles-associated death amid 943 confirmed cases across 39 counties. The outbreak comes amid concerns that public health in the US has been hit by increasing vaccine skepticism, especially due to the power and influence of the controversial health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr. Contributing to the challenge is that Pennsylvania is one of the few US states where its counties mostly lack their own health department, with only seven of its 67 counties having their own. Pennsylvania reports fifth measles-related death of the year amid outbreak Read more Lancaster county, which doesn’t have its own health department, has seen the highest number of cases, at 381, believed to be mostly among the Amish or similar religious groups who have historically low rates of measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine uptake. Health officials, doctors and other members of the community in the county are now attempting to establish its own health department to better tackle the outbreak. Jeanne Franklin, the director of Chester county’s health department, said that her county, which has the third highest number of cases, at 83, is preparing for an influx of cases from neighboring Lancaster. “We have a very long border with Lancaster county, and these types of disease don’t care about borders,” Franklin said. “It’s going to keep going and find a person who isn’t vaccinated. We’re operating with the assumption that the disease may jump and spread to non-Plain [Amish] community members. Our goal is to prevent that, but we assume that it may happen.” She added that although many Amish people have not been vaccinated, it’s not because they are anti-vaxxers, but rather because “they were either unaware of it or they don’t seek out healthcare as frequently as other residents”. She added: “But they’re willing to have the conversation and make a decision on what’s happening today. They’re not making decisions based on the myths out there, but because their neighbors are impacted.” Amid active surveillance of measles cases, contact tracing and setting up community vaccination centers, the county is also working to dispel misinformation some of its residents have regarding the safety of the vaccine. “We have people in key positions saying it isn’t an outbreak, it isn’t a problem. We have people who approach our nurses and say that they were told the vaccine will make them sterile, or that there’s a microchip within it,” Franklin said. But for Franklin, the fact that Chester county is one of the few counties to have its own health department is a clear advantage in the race to stop the spread of the disease. “By having our own health department [it] means that we already have the infrastructure in place, and we prepare for these things all year round,” Franklin said. “With the number of counties [the state has] to provide support to, they can’t possibly know all the key partners in a geographical area.” She added: “The state has a finite set of employees, while I can pull my employees away from their normal jobs and say we need help with this. We live here, we know it, and we’re working with the communities and the organizations who know us. I think every county needs a health department, but we’re just not set up that way in Pennsylvania while other states are.” Dr Richard Lorraine, the medical director of Montgomery county’s office of public health, said that it was a “matter of time” before the third most populous county in Pennsylvania would begin to see measles cases. “We recognize that essentially it’s all around us, and so a big focus for the county is immunization,” Lorraine said. “It’s the best preventative measure and where the county is focusing its efforts on.” skip past newsletter promotion after newsletter promotion Working closely with community organizers, Lorraine said the county was making sure that every resident was able to be vaccinated regardless of their insurance status. “Because we are a public health agency, our mandate is to provide for members of our population for the most part who are underinsured, and there’s a very high percentage who aren’t insured,” Lorraine said. “And through our partnership with pharmacies we’re able to open these clinics for everyone. So whether you have insurance or if you don’t, we can work it out so that someone is able to administer a vaccine.” Lora Werner, the director of the Delaware county health department, said that her agency was facing several challenges in protecting residents from the virus. Among them was the collapse of Crozer Health, Delaware county’s largest healthcare system, due to bankruptcy last year. “They were a huge provider of pediatric care,” Werner said. “And although we do have a high vaccination rate across Delaware county, there are pockets where they aren’t as good.” For Werner, the newly established local health department has been a gamechanger for promoting public health initiatives in the county. “We are the newest health department on the block, and we’re so passionate about the fact that we’re now here and can serve our residents,” Werner said. “We’re deeply integrated into the social networks.” She added: “Creating a new department was very challenging, and we’re a very odd state in this regard,” Werner said. “If you want to have one you need to have a referendum to establish one. But it’s not required, so we have a mishmash of the counties that have taken that step and those that have not.” The Guardian has approached the Pennsylvania health department for comment. news.content_title: Pa. health officials face multiple fronts as measles outbreak overlaps with respiratory virus season
news.content: Vials of measles, mumps and rubella vaccine are displayed on a counter at a Walgreens Pharmacy in Mill Valley, California, in a 2015 file photo. (Photo illustration by Justin Sullivan/Getty Images) This story was originally published by WESA . It is not available for republishing. Pennsylvania's measles outbreak crossed a historic threshold this week: at 1,078 cases in 41 counties, the state has recorded the nation's largest measles outbreak in the last three decades. Five people have died with infections and nearly 200 people have been hospitalized. As the outbreak overlaps with the start of the respiratory virus season, state health officials are facing several fronts. And despite a recent rift with the Trump administration , it appears that federal help is still on the table. "It's all hands on deck," Pennsylvania Health Secretary Dr. Debra Bogen said Monday. "We have a very robust response from our own Department of Health as well as many of our partners across the state." Local officials confirmed the first case among Allegheny County residents Monday , though people were exposed in August at Children's Hospital of Pittsburgh when infected patients from out of town visited the emergency room. Health providers across Pennsylvania have administered nearly double the number of measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccines in a typical month since the outbreak began. Pennsylvania medical providers typically administer around 25,000 doses of the MMR vaccine per month. In August, that number jumped to 49,000 doses. In September, providers administered 53,000 doses of the vaccine. UPMC Presbyterian Hospital in the Oakland neighborhood of Pittsburgh on October 13, 2025. (Photo by Jessica Kourkounis for the Pennsylvania Capital-Star) The MMR vaccine is extremely effective in preventing measles infections, according to the American Academy of Pediatrics. One dose is about 93% effective against infections. The recommended second dose brings that immunity up to 97%, and it's lifelong. Bogen stressed the importance of the MMR vaccine at an event at the Hilltop Pharmacy in Pittsburgh's Allentown neighborhood Monday. "The MMR vaccine has proven to be effective for decades, and we didn't have cases for decades because of the effectiveness of the vaccine," Bogen said. Still, measles infections continue to climb in Pennsylvania. More than half of the state's 67 counties have tallied cases. Nearly 30 new infections were reported just over the weekend. It's not yet clear if the state's effort to ramp up vaccinations have improved waning immunity in Pennsylvania classrooms. One in three kindergarteners in Allegheny County attend class at a school with immunization rates below the recommended threshold. Bogen said the state is coordinating its measles response with federal health agencies such as the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. But the outbreak has placed Pennsylvania at odds with U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr . Under his leadership, the CDC website reflects just two of the five measles-associated deaths in Pennsylvania. In a letter to the CDC last month, Bogen requested support from the federal government, but on the condition that the CDC acknowledge the additional deaths. "The CDC's choice not to publicly recognize the deaths undermines our response," Bogen wrote . "If CDC is unable to transparently and accurately communicate information about those measles-associated deaths, the Department will respectfully rescind our request," for aid, she wrote. It's all hands on deck. We have a very robust response from our own Department of Health as well as many of our partners across the state. – Pennsylvania Health Secretary Dr. Debra Bogen On Monday, Bogen doubled down on her comments, contending that "not recognizing the deaths minimizes... the loss of life that we've had to vaccine-preventable illness." "I just want people to understand how serious this infection can be," she said. Bogen said the state is determining the need for additional support from the federal government to manage the measles outbreak. She downplayed the impact of such help, noting that it would add one or two people to the department's staff of 300 already responding to the outbreak. news.content: Find us on Google 📌 America's birthday 🎂 Start the day smarter ☀️ Get the USA TODAY app U.S. Politics Sports Entertainment Life Money Travel Opinion Crossword ONLY AT USA TODAY: Newsletters For Subscribers Real Estate From the Archives USA TODAY PLAY Crossword Marvel Comics eNewspaper Magazines Investigations Video Podcasts Humankind Advertise Your Business WITNESS (True Crime) Just Curious Best-selling Booklist Top Workplaces Nomination Legals Press Releases Cars Boats Grocery Shopping OUR PORTFOLIO: Real Estate 10BEST USA TODAY Store Shopping Money Essentials Blueprint WITNESS (True Crime) Southern Kitchen Home Internet Services NEWS Measles Add Topic Ohio measles cases increase 400% from last year in latest ODH update Chad Murphy James Powel Mary Walrath-Holdridge USA TODAY NETWORK Oct. 8, 2026, 2:44 p.m. ET Hear this story Ohio's 2026 measles outbreak has grown to 228 cases across 21 counties, with a significant increase in recent weeks. Ohio's total number of 2026 measles cases is already more than 400% greater than all of 2025. Nationwide, measles cases have reached a 35-year high, surpassing 4,000 infections for the year. Health officials state the vast majority of cases are among unvaccinated individuals and urge vaccination as the best protection. Measles has spread to another Ohio county and another with a near double-digit increase as Ohio's third measles outbreak of 2026 continues. The state had 22 new cases in the past week, a 120% increase from the 10 new cases reported the week before, the Ohio Department of Health reports. ODH is reporting 228 cases in 21 counties so far this year, according to its summary of infectious diseases dashboard, updated Oct. 8. That number is 406% greater than the 45 cases reported in all of 2025. news.content: FILE – This undated image made available by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention on Feb. 4, 2015, shows an electron microscope image of a measles virus particle. (Cynthia Goldsmith/Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, via AP, File) By Seth C. Kalichman | Professor of Psychological Sciences at UConn PUBLISHED: October 7, 2026 at 5:27 AM EDT Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... In the midst of the worst U.S. measles outbreak in decades, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has abruptly changed how it counts deaths from measles. Pennsylvania health officials have identified four measles-associated deaths in 2026 . The CDC currently counts zero. The discrepancy is not because Pennsylvania and the CDC disagree about whether people died. It is about what counts as a measles death. It is about the CDC , under the direction of Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., denying that measles is as big a problem as it is. The CDC now counts measles deaths using data from the National Center for Health Statistics, a system designed primarily for tracking mortality trends rather than identifying individual deaths. Previously, measles deaths were counted using reports from state and local health officials. The change at the CDC has left deaths officially recognized by state authorities out of the federal tally. The CDC changed its approach to counting measles deaths after Secretary Kennedy refuted the deaths reported by Pennsylvania health officials. The changes made at the CDC minimized their reported death rate. Changing the definition of measles deaths occurred as the evidence for an expanding measles epidemic became inconvenient for Secretary Kennedy. The changed definition essentially moved the goalposts. Moving the goalposts is one of the more familiar tactics of denialism. Whether denying climate change, HIV causes AIDS, the severity of COVID-19, or the effectiveness of vaccines, denialists repeatedly change what counts as evidence when the evidence contradicts their beliefs. Denialism is not new to public policy. We have seen policymakers refute scientific evidence on climate change, vaccine safety, and HIV/AIDS. That brings us to back to Secretary Kennedy. What distinguishes Mr. Kennedy is the breadth of scientific facts he has challenged over the years, from refuting the safety and effectiveness of vaccines to supporting claims that HIV does not cause AIDS. Many of the alarms sounded about his record during his Senate confirmation hearings are now being realized. Last year, Mr. Kennedy dismissed all 17 members of the CDC’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices and replaced them with a smaller panel of mostly vaccine skeptics and denialists. The new committee subsequently changed federal vaccine policy. Routine hepatitis B vaccination at birth is no longer recommended for infants whose mothers test negative for hepatitis B. COVID-19 vaccination recommendations shifted toward individual decision-making. Despite no evidence that thimerosal is harmful, it is now federal policy to recommend thimerosal-free influenza vaccines. The CDC also reorganized the childhood immunization schedule, reducing the number of vaccines universally recommended for children. These were not the only changes. Mr. Kennedy also terminated promising mRNA vaccine research. He has repeatedly emphasized vitamin A in discussions of measles prevention and treatment. While vitamin A has a role in treating severe measles, it does not prevent measles. Discussing vitamins in the context of vaccination creates yet more confusion. And during all of this chaos, measles continues to spread. Johns Hopkins University’s U.S. measles tracker reported 2,289 cases in 2025. The number in 2026 has already surpassed 3,300, making this the worst year for measles in the United States in decades. And regardless of what the CDC is counting, people are dying of measles. CT vaccine opponents shout down legislators and health officials at Capitol event On September 17, Mr. Kennedy addressed the convention of the Children’s Health Defense, the anti-vaccination-focused organization that he founded and formerly chaired. Secretary Kennedy told the audience “Let me be clear. You have a strong and steadfast friend at the White House.” He also said, “In our country we care about rare illnesses and deaths. We care about every child who dies from measles. They get headlines. I’d ask you to care about children who are dying or suffering or being injured by vaccine injuries.” Pennsylvania state health authorities report four measles-associated deaths, so far, this year. The CDC says there are none. It is reasonable for the CDC to refine how medical records are examined and how laboratory procedures are conducted. But it is wrong for the CDC to make inconvenient truths disappear by changing how and what events are counted. Public health serves us best when we can trust the CDC is counting what happened, not deciding to count what Secretary Kennedy prefers to have happened. Seth C. Kalichman is a professor of Psychological Sciences at UConn , Storrs and a public health researcher. His work focuses on infectious diseases. news.content: Human Interest Measles Outbreak, Vaccine Information, and Public Health with Dr. Lori Handy from CHOP Dr. Lori Handy, The Associate Director of the Vaccine Education Center and a practicing Physician in infectious diseases at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia, was on the Public Affairs Show to... Markus Goldman Updated Oct 7, 2026 3:39 PM EDT Dr. Lori Handy, The Associate Director of the Vaccine Education Center and a practicing Physician in infectious diseases at Children's Hospital of Philadelphia , was on the Public Affairs Show to discuss the importance and safety of vaccines. Dr. Handy dispels the terrible misinformation and lies about vaccines by discussing the science of a vaccine. We also talk about how it reacts with the human body both positively and negatively. Dr. Handy discusses how much vaccines have been studied, and how they have been studied. Dr. Handy also describes what it's like to get sick from measles, pertussis, chicken pox and a few other diseases that can be prevented by vaccines. You can get more information about vaccines at The Children's Hospital of Philadelphia's Vaccine Education Center, here . Measles Information : Dr. Paul Offit outlines three common causes of hospitalization and death from measles: pneumonia, dehydration and encephalitis. He then details three lesser-known severe outcomes of measles. The first is immune amnesia, a condition that depletes memory B and T cells. This increases a person’s susceptibility to other infections to which they were previously immune. The second is acute demyelinating encephalomyelitis (ADEM), a rare but often severe autoimmune disorder. As Dr. Offit describes, one of the four deaths in Pennsylvania in 2026 was because of ADEM. It occurred in an 18-year-old boy. The third condition he describes is subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE), a delayed, uniformly fatal chronic brain infection. SSPE occurs when the virus continues to replicate in the person’s brain after they appear to have recovered. Years after the initial measles infection, the person begins to lose personality features and motor skills until they succumb to the infection. With the resurgence of measles, Dr. Offit reiterates the importance of staying up to date on MMR vaccination. Weaken the virus: Viruses are weakened, so they reproduce very poorly once inside the body. Vaccines for measles, mumps, rubella , rotavirus , polio (oral version; not used in the U.S.), chickenpox (varicella) , and influenza (intranasal version) are made this way. These are all vaccines that protect against viruses. Viruses cannot reproduce on their own. They need cells from other organisms to make more virus particles. Viruses reproduce thousands of times during a natural infection, meaning an infection that occurs after exposure to the virus in the community. Live, weakened vaccine viruses usually reproduce fewer than 20 times. This is enough to cause immunity, but not enough to cause disease. The immune response generates "memory B cells" that protect against infection in the future. Find out more about these and other cells of the immune system. Thank you for listening. The advantage of live, weakened vaccines is that one or two doses usually lead to lifelong immunity. The limitation of this approach is that these kinds of vaccines usually cannot be given to people with weakened immune systems (like people with cancer or AIDS). Find out more about what happens when the immune system doesn’t work properly. Markus Goldman Children's Hospital of Philadelphia Measles Vaccines Markus Goldman Author Markus Goldman is a part time member of the WMMR air staff. He is on every Sunday Night from 7-Midnight. Markus is also the WMMR Public Affairs Director. The Beasley Public Affairs Show airs at 6:30AM every Sunday Morning on WMMR. Markus has been at WMMR for almost 22 years. news.title: Amid worst measles outbreak in decades, one clinic leans on years of hard-won trust to keep vulnerable people safe - CNN
news.rss_summary_html: Amid worst measles outbreak in decades, one clinic leans on years of hard-won trust to keep vulnerable people safe  CNN

news.content_title: Amid worst measles outbreak in decades, one clinic leans on years of hard-won trust to keep vulnerable people safe
news.content: Belleville, Pennsylvania — Main Street is bustling on a Wednesday afternoon in late September. Cars mix with horse-and-buggy carriages on the road, many coming and going from the weekly Sale Day — a market spread over 10 acres with livestock, fruits and vegetables, flowers and other goods available to purchase. Lively conversations in English and Pennsylvania Dutch fill the barn where a produce auction stretches until lunchtime; bids for a pint of bright red cherry tomatoes run from 90 cents to $1.30. As dozens of people mix and mingle through the afternoon — Amish and other Plain people, so named for their simple way of dressing, as well as “English,” as they refer to folks outside of their community — there are no direct indications that a measles outbreak is raging in the area. Only one woman has a mask on, which she says she’s been wearing any time she’s left home since the start of the Covid-19 pandemic. One vendor is closed for “unexpected family obligations,” and one regular auction attendee is mourned after her recent sudden death after having “flu-like symptoms.” Tourists are visiting from Brooklyn. But less than a mile away at the Central Pennsylvania Clinic, measles is front and center. Ad Feedback A turn off of Main Street quickly opens up to an idyllic rural valley, filled with lush farms set to a backdrop of rolling green mountains. An unlined road leads across a babbling river to reveal a striking gray building up on a hill, a massive barn raised in the traditional style that uses only wood pegs — no nails — to hold the structure together. The front door is locked, with a photo and description of measles hanging in the window, along with a notice asking visitors to “ring doorbell for service.” Dr. Katherine Mascia swings the door open with a big smile and a quick question: “Any measles symptoms today?” Beneath the genuine smile is true heartbreak. A massive measles outbreak in the area — as of Wednesday, the largest and deadliest the United States has had in decades — is bringing significant pain and suffering to the families she cares for. “In the five years that I’ve worked here, I don’t think we’ve had so many patients admitted to the hospital all within the span of a few weeks,” Mascia said. “We might usually have maybe one patient who’s admitted for their complex care needs, but to have so many all at the same time, it’s really unprecedented.” The Central Pennsylvania Clinic is centered around caring for children and adults with genetic disorders that are especially common among the Amish and broader Plain community, a group that also tends to have lower vaccination rates than average. Michelle Gustafson for CNN Defying politics More than 1,000 measles cases have been reported by the Pennsylvania Department of Health since the outbreak started in April, surpassing recent record-breaking outbreaks – in Texas and South Carolina last year – to become the worst in the US since the early 1990s. The clinic’s home of Mifflin County is one of the hardest-hit, near the epicenter in nearby Lancaster County. The patients who the Central Pennsylvania Clinic serves are especially vulnerable to the severe effects of a measles infection. The nonprofit is centered around caring for children and adults with genetic disorders that are especially common among the Amish and broader Plain community, a group that also tends to have lower vaccination rates than average. The Plain people are known for their ​caution toward government and other nonreligious authority. But as measles tears through many of their hometowns in central Pennsylvania, the national conversation has become paradoxically politically charged. Leaders from the federal government and the Pennsylvania government have clashed over the response , with much of the debate centered around the five deaths that have come during this outbreak. Disputes over the definition of what counts as a measles death and how news of the deaths is shared with the public have disrupted public health response plans. The strength of the trust between the clinic and its community has faced some of its greatest tests over the past few months. Michelle Gustafson for CNN Meanwhile, the Central Pennsylvania Clinic’s staff is focused on how to best keep everyone safe and healthy. They’re leaning on the clinic’s well-forged foundation of trust. It has taken persistence and patience — sometimes years — for the clinic to build those relationships, and the strength of that trust has faced some of its greatest tests over the past few months. When Pennsylvania reported a measles-associated death in an 18-year-old in Mifflin County, Mascia said, the clinic started to get tons of calls — from patients they knew and other members of the broader community — who just wanted to know what happened. They weren’t paying attention to what government officials were arguing about on social media, she said. They wanted a clear understanding of how the young person died. “I’m quite honored that they’re calling us and asking those questions. It helps me feel like they really trust us,” Mascia said. “But it puts pressure on us, too.” She said she reached out to the county coroner directly to get a formal statement on the cause of death, and she references that statement when patients have questions. “We want to keep that line of communication open with the community, and it’s so important to provide accurate information and be consistent with the messaging,” she said. Morning light is seen over corn fields and farmland in Belleville, Pennsylvania on Friday, October 2, 2026. Mifflin County, where Belleville is situated, is near the epicenter of the largest measles outbreak in the United States. Michelle Gustafson for CNN Although the clinic is well-equipped in many ways, it's not built to treat measles patients. Michelle Gustafson for CNN The clinic has uniquely carved out space for opportunities to build a rapport with the community. Michelle Gustafson for CNN Consistent communication and a resilient response Central Pennsylvania Clinic leaders have been thinking about and planning for a measles outbreak in the community since the start of the West Texas outbreak in January 2025, Mascia said. Their patients are vulnerable, and their offices, while incredibly well-equipped in many ways, are not built to treat measles patients. “We don’t have advanced ventilation systems, and we don’t have negative-pressure rooms, so if a person who is infected with measles comes in, our entire building is compromised for two hours,” Mascia said. Pennsylvania requires a throat swab, a blood sample and a urine sample to confirm a measles case — arduous tasks for both ill patients, who often had to take a taxing horse and buggy ride to the clinic, and for clinic staff who have to work within the constraints of their facility. The rear entrance to the clinic building, which also hosts a federally qualified health center, has become a makeshift triage center for people with suspected measles cases. The back parking lot is large enough for cars and buggies to spread out, and clinic staffers meet families at the door, where they can lead the patient into a small storage barn to collect urine samples. It was important to have a logistical plan to keep operations safe, Mascia said, but she pointedly explains that the most critical way to protect their patients is to raise vaccination rates. The measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine is extremely effective. One dose is 93% effective against measles, and the recommended second dose bumps that protection up to 97% — and the immunity is lifelong. Extensive research has also demonstrated the vaccine’s safety . Childhood vaccination rates have been falling nationwide, with a record share of parents opting to exempt their new kindergartners from the required shots last school year. Vaccination rates tend to be lower among Plain people, but it’s not because of an inherent opposition, experts say. There are certain shared values within the community, but there are also varied individual beliefs and opinions about vaccines, as there would in any broad group of people, Mascia said. Consistency in the clinic’s messaging around vaccination has been the key to raising coverage rates. If the patients sense any type of coercion from doctors or if they feel forced into a decision about something like a vaccination, they’ll completely disengage from all health care – an outcome that would be particularly troublesome for the vulnerable patients they care for. “We share that it’s our strong recommendation that everyone be fully vaccinated,” Mascia said. “And if they’re not interested, we repeat our recommendation and say ‘we’re here to help if and when you change your mind.’” In the Amish and broader Plain community, the experience of a neighbor and advice from a family member carry significantly more weight than findings from a study published in the most prestigious medical journal or recommendations from the leading clinical society, said Dr. Helge Hartung, who joined the Central Pennsylvania Clinic last year. The Central Pennsylvania Clinic has uniquely carved out space for opportunities to build that kind of rapport – but it takes time. Two hours are blocked off for new patient visits, and every visit after that is scheduled for an hour. The main exam room ​is extra large, with space to fit the whole family — the average of which includes seven children — for conversations that affect every member. There’s time and space to answer questions, Mascia said, and her well-informed patients come with many of them. “What I’m seeing are families trying to weigh all the information that they are getting from us, from the community, from other sources,” she said. “They are families truly trying to make the best decision for their child.” A few years ago, the federal government stopped providing MMR shots to the clinic through Vaccines for Children, a federally funded program that provides routine immunizations at no cost to children who might not otherwise be able to afford them. The government told Mascia that it was withdrawing because of the lack of demand for the shots, she said. But cost is a key consideration for many of her patients when making health care decisions, and she worried about the families who did want to get vaccinated but couldn’t afford it after this change. The state government has since stepped up to help keep the clinic’s small in-house pharmacy sufficiently stocked with MMR vaccines, and the timing has been critical. Mascia says she hasn’t pushed the issue of vaccination much more than usual since the measles outbreak started — just the standard consistent messaging — but the requests from families have noticeably increased. A handmade quilt adorns the clinic's vestibule. Michelle Gustafson for CNN Dr. Helge Hartung leads the clinic's home care program. Michelle Gustafson for CNN Confronting challenges The Pennsylvania Department of Health has hosted nearly 200 pop-up vaccination clinics where workers have given thousands of MMR doses since the start of the measles outbreak this spring. Government-sponsored programs like this would typically deter most Plain people, but the Central Pennsylvania Clinic has built up enough trust in the community that simply hosting vaccination events in the clinic building has been enough to drive significant turnout. More than two dozen people were vaccinated at a pop-up clinic it hosted in mid-August, and 73 more were vaccinated at a second one in mid-September. Interest in the September pop-up spiked significantly after the death in Mifflin County was reported. “That shows me that this community does care about preventing those serious consequences,” Mascia said. “They want to do what they can, and they know that our strongest tool is through vaccinations.” Vaccinating a hundred people within the Belleville community “is considered very successful,” the state health department said. “One of the most important strategies for building trust is recognizing that a successful response must include the people who Pennsylvanians turn to in their daily lives for guidance, like primary care doctors, pharmacists, faith leaders, and community leaders,” the state health department said in an email to CNN. “The Central Pennsylvania Clinic has been an integral part of the Belleville community for more than a decade, caring for the medical needs of these Pennsylvanians and creating lasting relationships. Their partnership in hosting these vaccination clinics provides a layer of trust that DOH can build upon to help residents understand the unmatched protection available through the MMR vaccine.” The Central Pennsylvania Clinic also aims to meet patients where they are — both philosophically and physically. Doctors and nurses regularly make house visits to see patients whose health conditions or financial situations make it difficult to travel to the offices. But patients have increasingly requested home visits because fear of infection during the measles outbreak has made them afraid to leave their homes. Horse-and-buggy carriages share space with cars in Belleville. Michelle Gustafson for CNN Clinic staff is happy to travel to patients’ homes to administer MMR vaccines when requested, too. Sometimes the visits are coordinated to be at a certain hour or to a certain part of the property, to avoid raising eyebrows among neighbors. Hartung, who leads the clinic’s home care program, knows a family who skipped going to church for more than month to avoid possible measles exposures to their vulnerable infant. As soon as the baby turned 6 months, they requested a home visit for an early vaccination. “The first thing the mother said was, ‘Now we can go to church again,’” Hartung said. “If they’re missing church, it goes to show you how significant the fear and concern is.” But the measles outbreak has added even more layers of complication to the home visit operation. Instead of mapping the most efficient route between homes, Hartung is now planning his home visit schedule based on the patients’ vulnerability to an infection. It adds dozens of miles and significantly more time between appointments. “In a normal time, we might do it by distance, a straightforward route. Now we’re really looking at the most vulnerable sequence, just in case there is a measles encounter that we didn’t anticipate,” he said. “We, of course, are all vaccinated, but we always worry that we might actually become a vector, so we plan that out the best we can.” Hartung says he knows that he’s gained a patient’s trust when they start calling him by his last name. When formal titles are dropped, it’s a sign that he has found his way in. “When they’re very formal, it could go either way,” he said. “It’s great to hear, ‘Hartung, what do you think?’” In recent weeks, Dr. Katherine Mascia says, there’s been a marked increase in patients cancelling appointments or simply not showing up to the clinic. Michelle Gustafson for CNN The rear entrance to the clinic building has become a makeshift triage center for people with suspected measles cases. Michelle Gustafson for CNN Wide-reaching worries Mascia recently needed to send a young patient to the emergency department, where the family learned that the closest newborn intensive care unit was full and had to be diverted to another hospital system. There have been only a few other times that patients have been diverted to a different hospital system due to a lack of available beds, Mascia said, but the typically rare event has been happening much more frequently during this measles outbreak. And in recent weeks, Mascia says, there’s been a marked increase in patients cancelling appointments or simply not showing up to the clinic. “Sometimes it’s a sudden, eerie kind of stillness,” she said. “Whenever there’s a missed appointment, I’m always concerned that something really severe happened. Right now, you just have to assume the patient has measles.” The clinic almost always has the time and space to reschedule or fit in a new appointment, but missed appointments aren’t always rescheduled, and gaps in care can lead to serious consequences for her patients. “It’s very important to keep on top of these conditions to make sure patients have the best possible outcomes,” Mascia said. Young children can rapidly outgrow dosages for important medications or miss the chance to manage a condition with physical therapy before needing surgery. Measles has also kept the broader community away from fundraising events that are critical to keeping the nonprofit up and running. Plain families put handmade quilts, baked goods, farm equipment and livestock up for sale and gift their earnings back to the clinic. Michelle Gustafson for CNN The vast majority of the Central Pennsylvania Clinic’s operating budget comes from direct community donations, many of which happen at large auctions that take place a few times throughout the year. Plain families will put handmade quilts, baked goods, farm equipment and sometimes livestock up for sale and gift their earnings back to the clinic. Clinic executive director Louise Yoder said that a few of the most recent auctions were a bit less successful – and measles was one of the main reasons why. “People are sick and not wanting to go to events like this,” she said. Part of the clinic’s goal in providing culturally competent care to the community is an understanding that finances can be restrictive for many patients. The team works with local hospitals to negotiate special rates for their patients who are Amish or members of the broader Plain community, a group whose philosophical beliefs keep them from enrolling in formal health insurance plans. But the measles outbreak is raising the stakes. “With the sheer number of hospital stays and ICU admissions that we’re seeing because of measles, I do wonder about the financial toll on this community,” Mascia said. “It concerns me.”…

A massive measles outbreak in the area — as of Wednesday, the largest and deadliest the United States has had in decades — is bringing significant pain and suffering to the families she cares for. “In the five years that I’ve worked here, I don’t think we’ve had so many patients admitted to the hospital all within the span of a few weeks,” Mascia said. “We might usually have maybe one patient who’s admitted for their complex care needs, but to have so many all at the same time, it’s really unprecedented.” The Central Pennsylvania Clinic is centered around caring for children and adults with genetic disorders that are especially common among the Amish and broader Plain community, a group that also tends to have lower vaccination rates than average. Michelle Gustafson for CNN Defying politics More than 1,000 measles cases have been reported by the Pennsylvania Department of Health since the outbreak started in April, surpassing recent record-breaking outbreaks – in Texas and South Carolina last year – to become the worst in the US since the early 1990s. The clinic’s home of Mifflin County is one of the hardest-hit, near the epicenter in nearby Lancaster County. The patients who the Central Pennsylvania Clinic serves are especially vulnerable to the severe effects of a measles infection. The nonprofit is centered around caring for children and adults with genetic disorders that are especially common among the Amish and broader Plain community, a group that also tends to have lower vaccination rates than average. The Plain people are known for their ​caution toward government and other nonreligious authority. But as measles tears through many of their hometowns in central Pennsylvania, the national conversation has become paradoxically politically charged. Leaders from the federal government and the Pennsylvania government have clashed over the response , with much of the debate centered around the five deaths that have come during this outbreak. Disputes over the definition of what counts as a measles death and how news of the deaths is shared with the public have disrupted public health response plans. The strength of the trust between the clinic and its community has faced some of its greatest tests over the past few months. Michelle Gustafson for CNN Meanwhile, the Central Pennsylvania Clinic’s staff is focused on how to best keep everyone safe and healthy. They’re leaning on the clinic’s well-forged foundation of trust. It has taken persistence and patience — sometimes years — for the clinic to build those relationships, and the strength of that trust has faced some of its greatest tests over the past few months. When Pennsylvania reported a measles-associated death in an 18-year-old in Mifflin County, Mascia said, the clinic started to get tons of calls — from patients they knew and other members of the broader community — who just wanted to know what happened. They weren’t paying attention to what government officials were arguing about on social media, she said. They wanted a clear understanding of how the young person died. “I’m quite honored that they’re calling us and asking those questions. It helps me feel like they really trust us,” Mascia said. “But it puts pressure on us, too.” She said she reached out to the county coroner directly to get a formal statement on the cause of death, and she references that statement when patients have questions. “We want to keep that line of communication open with the community, and it’s so important to provide accurate information and be consistent with the messaging,” she said. Morning light is seen over corn fields and farmland in Belleville, Pennsylvania on Friday, October 2, 2026. Mifflin County, where Belleville is situated, is near the epicenter of the largest measles outbreak in the United States. Michelle Gustafson for CNN Although the clinic is well-equipped in many ways, it's not built to treat measles patients. Michelle Gustafson for CNN The clinic has uniquely carved out space for opportunities to build a rapport with the community. Michelle Gustafson for CNN Consistent communication and a resilient response Central Pennsylvania Clinic leaders have been thinking about and planning for a measles outbreak in the community since the start of the West Texas outbreak in January 2025, Mascia said. Their patients are vulnerable, and their offices, while incredibly well-equipped in many ways, are not built to treat measles patients. “We don’t have advanced ventilation systems, and we don’t have negative-pressure rooms, so if a person who is infected with measles comes in, our entire building is compromised for two hours,” Mascia said. Pennsylvania requires a throat swab, a blood sample and a urine sample to confirm a measles case — arduous tasks for both ill patients, who often had to take a taxing horse and buggy ride to the clinic, and for clinic staff who have to work within the constraints of their facility. The rear entrance to the clinic building, which also hosts a federally qualified health center, has become a makeshift triage center for people with suspected measles cases. The back parking lot is large enough for cars and buggies to spread out, and clinic staffers meet families at the door, where they can lead the patient into a small storage barn to collect urine samples. It was important to have a logistical plan to keep operations safe, Mascia said, but she pointedly explains that the most critical way to protect their patients is to raise vaccination rates. The measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine is extremely effective. One dose is 93% effective against measles, and the recommended second dose bumps that protection up to 97% — and the immunity is lifelong. Extensive research has also demonstrated the vaccine’s safety . Childhood vaccination rates have been falling nationwide, with a record share of parents opting to exempt their new kindergartners from the required shots last school year. Vaccination rates tend to be lower among Plain people, but it’s not because of an inherent opposition, experts say. There are certain shared values within the community, but there are also varied individual beliefs and opinions about vaccines, as there would in any broad group of people, Mascia said. Consistency in the clinic’s messaging around vaccination has been the key to raising coverage rates. If the patients sense any type of coercion from doctors or if they feel forced into a decision about something like a vaccination, they’ll completely disengage from all health care – an outcome that would be particularly troublesome for the vulnerable patients they care for. “We share that it’s our strong recommendation that everyone be fully vaccinated,” Mascia said. “And if they’re not interested, we repeat our recommendation and say ‘we’re here to help if and when you change your mind.’” In the Amish and broader Plain community, the experience of a neighbor and advice from a family member carry significantly more weight than findings from a study published in the most prestigious medical journal or recommendations from the leading clinical society, said Dr. Helge Hartung, who joined the Central Pennsylvania Clinic last year. The Central Pennsylvania Clinic has uniquely carved out space for opportunities to build that kind of rapport – but it takes time. Two hours are blocked off for new patient visits, and every visit after that is scheduled for an hour. The main exam room ​is extra large, with space to fit the whole family — the average of which includes seven children — for conversations that affect every member. There’s time and space to answer questions, Mascia said, and her well-informed patients come with many of them. “What I’m seeing are families trying to weigh all the information that they are getting from us, from the community, from other sources,” she said. “They are families truly trying to make the best decision for their child.” A few years ago, the federal government stopped providing MMR shots to the clinic through Vaccines for Children, a federally funded program that provides routine immunizations at no cost to children who might not otherwise be able to afford them. The government told Mascia that it was withdrawing because of the lack of demand for the shots, she said. But cost is a key consideration for many of her patients when making health care decisions, and she worried about the families who did want to get vaccinated but couldn’t afford it after this change. The state government has since stepped up to help keep the clinic’s small in-house pharmacy sufficiently stocked with MMR vaccines, and the timing has been critical. Mascia says she hasn’t pushed the issue of vaccination much more than usual since the measles outbreak started — just the standard consistent messaging — but the requests from families have noticeably increased. A handmade quilt adorns the clinic's vestibule. Michelle Gustafson for CNN Dr. Helge Hartung leads the clinic's home care program. Michelle Gustafson for CNN Confronting challenges The Pennsylvania Department of Health has hosted nearly 200 pop-up vaccination clinics where workers have given thousands of MMR doses since the start of the measles outbreak this spring. Government-sponsored programs like this would typically deter most Plain people, but the Central Pennsylvania Clinic has built up enough trust in the community that simply hosting vaccination events in the clinic building has been enough to drive significant turnout. More than two dozen people were vaccinated at a pop-up clinic it hosted in mid-August, and 73 more were vaccinated at a second one in mid-September. Interest in the September pop-up spiked significantly after the death in Mifflin County was reported. “That shows me that this community does care about preventing those serious consequences,” Mascia said. “They want to do what they can, and they know that our strongest tool is through vaccinations.” Vaccinating a hundred people within the Belleville community “is considered very successful,” the state health department said. “One of the most important strategies for building trust is recognizing that a successful response must include the people who Pennsylvanians turn to in their daily lives for guidance, like primary care doctors, pharmacists, faith leaders, and community leaders,” the state health department said in an email to CNN. “The Central Pennsylvania Clinic has been an integral part of the Belleville community for more than a decade, caring for the medical needs of these Pennsylvanians and creating lasting relationships. Their partnership in hosting these vaccination clinics provides a layer of trust that DOH can build upon to help residents understand the unmatched protection available through the MMR vaccine.” The Central Pennsylvania Clinic also aims to meet patients where they are — both philosophically and physically. Doctors and nurses regularly make house visits to see patients whose health conditions or financial situations make it difficult to travel to the offices. But patients have increasingly requested home visits because fear of infection during the measles outbreak has made them afraid to leave their homes. Horse-and-buggy carriages share space with cars in Belleville. Michelle Gustafson for CNN Clinic staff is happy to travel to patients’ homes to administer MMR vaccines when requested, too. Sometimes the visits are coordinated to be at a certain hour or to a certain part of the property, to avoid raising eyebrows among neighbors. Hartung, who leads the clinic’s home care program, knows a family who skipped going to church for more than month to avoid possible measles exposures to their vulnerable infant. As soon as the baby turned 6 months, they requested a home visit for an early vaccination. “The first thing the mother said was, ‘Now we can go to church again,’” Hartung said. “If they’re missing church, it goes to show you how significant the fear and concern is.” But the measles outbreak has added even more layers of complication to the home visit operation. Instead of mapping the most efficient route between homes, Hartung is now planning his home visit schedule based on the patients’ vulnerability to an infection. It adds dozens of miles and significantly more time between appointments. “In a normal time, we might do it by distance, a straightforward route. Now we’re really looking at the most vulnerable sequence, just in case there is a measles encounter that we didn’t anticipate,” he said. “We, of course, are all vaccinated, but we always worry that we might actually become a vector, so we plan that out the best we can.” Hartung says he knows that he’s gained a patient’s trust when they start calling him by his last name. When formal titles are dropped, it’s a sign that he has found his way in. “When they’re very formal, it could go either way,” he said. “It’s great to hear, ‘Hartung, what do you think?’” In recent weeks, Dr. Katherine Mascia says, there’s been a marked increase in patients cancelling appointments or simply not showing up to the clinic. Michelle Gustafson for CNN The rear entrance to the clinic building has become a makeshift triage center for people with suspected measles cases. Michelle Gustafson for CNN Wide-reaching worries Mascia recently needed to send a young patient to the emergency department, where the family learned that the closest newborn intensive care unit was full and had to be diverted to another hospital system. There have been only a few other times that patients have been diverted to a different hospital system due to a lack of available beds, Mascia said, but the typically rare event has been happening much more frequently during this measles outbreak. And in recent weeks, Mascia says, there’s been a marked increase in patients cancelling appointments or simply not showing up to the clinic. “Sometimes it’s a sudden, eerie kind of stillness,” she said. “Whenever there’s a missed appointment, I’m always concerned that something really severe happened. Right now, you just have to assume the patient has measles.” The clinic almost always has the time and space to reschedule or fit in a new appointment, but missed appointments aren’t always rescheduled, and gaps in care can lead to serious consequences for her patients. “It’s very important to keep on top of these conditions to make sure patients have the best possible outcomes,” Mascia said. Young children can rapidly outgrow dosages for important medications or miss the chance to manage a condition with physical therapy before needing surgery. Measles has also kept the broader community away from fundraising events that are critical to keeping the nonprofit up and running. Plain families put handmade quilts, baked goods, farm equipment and livestock up for sale and gift their earnings back to the clinic. Michelle Gustafson for CNN The vast majority of the Central Pennsylvania Clinic’s operating budget comes from direct community donations, many of which happen at large auctions that take place a few times throughout the year. Plain families will put handmade quilts, baked goods, farm equipment and sometimes livestock up for sale and gift their earnings back to the clinic. Clinic executive director Louise Yoder said that a few of the most recent auctions were a bit less successful – and measles was one of the main reasons why. “People are sick and not wanting to go to events like this,” she said. Part of the clinic’s goal in providing culturally competent care to the community is an understanding that finances can be restrictive for many patients. The team works with local hospitals to negotiate special rates for their patients who are Amish or members of the broader Plain community, a group whose philosophical beliefs keep them from enrolling in formal health insurance plans. But the measles outbreak is raising the stakes. “With the sheer number of hospital stays and ICU admissions that we’re seeing because of measles, I do wonder about the financial toll on this community,” Mascia said. “It concerns me.”...

news.wechat_summary_zh: 时间：暴发 自 2026 年 4 月以来一直在进行，文章于 2026 年 10 月 7 日发表。事件日期没有明确说明，但 暴发 被描述...；地点与对象：暴发 以宾夕法尼亚州米夫林县为中心，特别是贝尔维尔，该镇以阿米什人和平原社区而闻名。这些社区的 麻疹 比率较低，并且由于其遗传性疾病而特别容易受到 麻疹 的影响。；事件：麻疹 麻疹 暴发 正在宾夕法尼亚州中部发生，自 2026 年 4 月以来报告了 1，000 多例病例。麻疹 被描述为美国几十年来最严重的一次，它导致大量入院和死亡，特别是在弱势群体中。；影响与风险：截至 2026 年 10 月 2 日，宾夕法尼亚州已报告超过 1，000 起 麻疹 病例，超过了德克萨斯州和南卡罗来纳州最近的 麻疹 病例。暴发 已导致五人死亡，死因成为公众争论的话题。该诊所为弱势群体服务，...；应对与不确定性：宾夕法尼亚州中部诊所正在积极响应 暴发，与社区保持沟通、提供准确信息并实施分诊措施。然而，该诊所没有能力治疗麻疹患者，而麻疹引发了有关麻疹相关死亡的定义以及如何与公众共享信息的争议。

news.title_zh: 追踪 麻疹 和世界上的 疫苗-可预防疾病 - Think Global Health
news.source_body_en: This article from Think Global Health, published on October 6, 2026, focuses on tracking measles and other vaccine-preventable diseases globally. It highlights the challenges faced in disease monitoring and response, particularly in conflict-affected regions such as Ukraine, Gaza, Sudan, and Myanmar. The piece also discusses the broader implications of global health financing and the need for stronger leadership in health diplomacy. While the article does not report specific outbreaks or confirmed cases of measles, it emphasizes the importance of addressing gaps in cofinancing commitments and the collective failure of global health security when outbreaks go undetected for extended periods. The analysis includes references to the U.S. and other countries' health policies and their impact on disease control efforts.
news.content_zh: Think Global Health 的这篇文章于 2026 年 10 月 6 日发表,重点跟踪全球范围内的 麻疹 和其他 疫苗 可预防疾病。它强调了疾病监测和应对所面临的挑战,特别是在乌克兰、加沙、苏丹和缅甸等受冲突影响的地区。这篇文章还讨论了全球卫生融资的更广泛影响以及加强卫生外交领导力的必要性。虽然文章没有报告具体的 暴发 或 麻疹 确诊病例,但它强调了解决联合融资承诺差距的重要性,以及当 暴发 长期未被发现时全球卫生安全集体失败的重要性。该分析参考了美国和其他国家的卫生政策及其对疾病控制工作的影响。

outbreak passes 1,000 cases in worst year for US since 1991 By Nick Viviani FOX Local Health Published October 5, 2026 11:05 PM EDT Share Copy Link Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Reddit Published October 5, 2026 11:05 PM EDT article Paramyxovirus measles virus, and virions of the polyomavirus, simian virus SV40, revealed in the photomicrograph film, 1981. Image courtesy Centers for Disease Control (CDC) / Dr Erskine Palmer. (Photo by Smith Collection/Gado/Getty Images) The Brief Health officials in Pennsylvania have recorded 1,004 measles cases since an outbreak began in April. Five people have died in connection with the outbreak and nearly 200 hospitalizations have been reported. Nearly 3,900 measles cases have been reported across the United States, the most since 1991. A measles outbreak in Pennsylvania has become the largest one experienced by a state in more than three decades as the number of reported cases crosses into four-digit territory. Local perspective: Pennsylvania health officials have recorded 1,004 cases since April, when the outbreak began west of Philadelphia. They also indicated that nearly 200 hospitalizations have occurred and five deaths have been reported. By the numbers: That number of cases pushes Pennsylvania’s total past other states where large outbreaks have occurred this year, including Texas and South Carolina, where an outbreak resulted in 997 cases. Those major outbreaks have helped drive the overall number of cases in the United States to nearly 3,900, which is the highest total since 1991. The last time a single state recorded an outbreak as large as what is happening in Pennsylvania was in the early 1990s, when 4,500 cases were reported in New York City over the course of multiple years. RELATED: Recall issued for over 122,000 cases of Gatorade sold in 37 states due to undeclared food colorings Big picture view: Health officials are blaming the outbreaks on low vaccination rates. Vaccinations were credited with helping the U.S. eliminate the domestic spread of measles in 2000. Since then, however, the vaccination rate has fallen below the 95% coverage considered necessary to keep outbreaks from happening. Now, international health officials plan to meet next month to decide whether the U.S. and Mexico should still be considered measles-free. Dig deeper: Measles is caused by a highly contagious virus. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention states that up to 9 out of 10 people who are susceptible and exposed to the virus will get it. The virus can spread when people who have it breathe, cough, or sneeze, or it can be transferred on contaminated surfaces. The Source: Information for this article was taken from the Associated Press. This story was reported from Orlando. October 6, 2026 in Health, News Reading Time: 3 mins read New York Declares Statewide Measles Emergency as Cases Hit 108 New York Governor Kathy Hochul declared a statewide measles emergency on Monday, signing an executive order as the state’s case count climbed to 108 for the year. Executive Order 65 puts a State Disaster Emergency in place for all of New York through November 4. A disaster emergency gives the governor power to temporarily change or suspend certain state rules so officials can move faster than the usual red tape allows. Here, that means getting more vaccines into arms and more tests done. “After reviewing the latest data on measles cases in New York State, I am declaring a State Disaster Emergency to strengthen our ongoing efforts to confront this disease,” Hochul said in a statement. As of October 3, New York had confirmed 108 measles cases in 2026. Seven are in New York City, and the other 101 are spread across the rest of the state. Most of the spread is recent. Of the 108 cases, 92 have been reported since July 15, largely in rural communities across 18 counties where vaccination rates are low. Lewis County alone has recorded 11 cases. The biggest change under the measles emergency is who can give the vaccine. Paramedics, advanced EMS providers, pharmacists and midwives can now administer the MMR shot, which protects against measles, mumps and rubella. That expanded group can vaccinate children as young as 2. Nurses can also now order measles tests, which before required a doctor. Local health departments have already given more than 1,000 MMR doses in rural areas since the outbreak picked up. The state calls the vaccine the most effective protection against the disease. Hochul’s measles emergency also comes with a crisis brewing next door. Pennsylvania had 977 cases and five deaths as of October 2, many in rural counties that border New York. This week, Pennsylvania passed 1,000 cases, making it the largest measles outbreak in the country in three decades. The last outbreak that size happened in New York City in the early 1990s and stretched over several years. New York’s order is the first declaration of its kind since measles cases began rising across the country in 2025. Measles spreads easily through the air and can lead to pneumonia, brain swelling and death. One rare complication, called subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, is brain inflammation that can show up years after someone recovers from measles and cause permanent brain damage. Outbreaks take hold when vaccination rates in a community fall below about 95 percent, the level needed to keep measles from moving person to person. The surge is happening while the nation’s top health official is Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a longtime anti vaccine activist who chaired the group Children’s Health Defense for years before Trump named him Secretary of Health and Human Services. Since taking over in 2025, Kennedy fired all 17 members of the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices, the expert panel that guides national vaccine policy, and replaced them with vaccine skeptics. He also moved to shrink the childhood vaccine schedule, changes a judge has since halted. Kennedy has claimed the measles vaccine causes deaths “every year.” The Infectious Diseases Society of America says no deaths have been shown to be linked to the MMR vaccine in healthy people. At a congressional hearing this year, Kennedy insisted, “I have never been anti-vaccine,” while also claiming vaccines are not properly tested for safety. He has argued the national outbreak began in January 2025, before he took office. More recently, Kennedy has changed his tune, telling parents on CNN they should get their children vaccinated for measles and calling the shot effective. The stakes reach beyond New York. The United States declared measles eliminated in 2000, meaning the disease was no longer spreading continuously inside the country. In November, officials with the Pan American Health Organization, the regional arm of the World Health Organization, will meet to decide whether the US and Mexico keep that measles free status. news.wechat_summary_zh: 时间：纽约州州长 Kathy Hochul 于 2026 年 10 月 6 日宣布 麻疹 进入紧急状态，该州全年病例数攀升至 108...；地点与对象：截至 2026 年 10 月 3 日，纽约州已有 108 例确诊的 麻疹 病例。其中 7 例发生在纽约市，101 例分布在该州其他地区，特别是 麻疹 发病率较低的 18...；事件：由于病例数量不断增加，纽约州于 2026 年 10 月 6 日宣布全州进入紧急状态 麻疹。州长签署了一项行政命令，允许药剂师、护理人员、助产士和护士分别管理 MMR 疫苗 和进行 麻疹 测试。；影响与风险：截至2026年10月3日，纽约州已确诊108例麻疹病例，自7月15日以来报告了92例。该州正在经历严重的麻疹，麻疹病毒可导致肺炎、脑肿胀和死亡等严重并发症。亚急性硬化性全脑炎 是一种罕见的并发症，可在感染数年...；应对与不确定性：该州已实施灾难紧急状态，以加快 疫苗 的分发和测试。自 暴发 开始以来，地方卫生部门已在农村地区注射了 1，000 多剂 MMR 疫苗。州长有权暂时更改或暂停州规则，以更有效地解决 暴发 问题。

Support WBUR Home Local Coverage Health Measles is surging in the U.S., and doctors warn Massachusetts could be at risk Play03:29 Close× Copy the code below to embed the WBUR audio player on your site <iframe width="100%" height="124" scrolling="no" frameborder="no" src="https://player.wbur.org/news/2026/10/06/mass-boston-measles-county-vaccination-rates"></iframe> Copy embed code Priyanka Dayal McCluskey October 06, 2026 Share A vial of the combination measles, mumps and rubella vaccine. (Mary Conlon/AP) Editor's Note: This story was featured in WBUR's weekly health newsletter, CommonHealth. If you like what you read and want it in your inbox, sign up here. As measles surges in the United States at the highest level in decades, doctors and public health officials are warning Massachusetts could be vulnerable to an outbreak. While 96.5% of the state's kindergarteners had received measles vaccines as of last school year, state data shows some counties dipped below the 95% threshold considered essential for herd immunity, making their students more vulnerable to infections. So far this year, two cases of measles have been recorded in Massachusetts. But Dr. David Lyczkowski, president of the Massachusetts chapter of the American Academy of Pediatrics, said he’s watching the outbreak a couple states away in Pennsylvania, and he’s concerned. “It is a roll of the dice,” he said. “I'm worried that it's just a matter of time before we see an outbreak.” Registered nurse Danielle Capuano prepares a vaccine at Hyde Park Pediatrics. (Jesse Costa/WBUR) Vaccination rates vary widely across communities and schools. Many schools are at 100% — meaning every kindergarten student is up to date on vaccines. But in some others, 1 out of 5 has not received their measles shots, according to data from the state Department of Public Health reviewed by WBUR. The numbers include the 2025-2026 school year; data for the current school year is not yet available. Support WBUR In Franklin County in Western Massachusetts, 89.7% of kindergarteners had received their measles shots. On Martha’s Vineyard, the vaccination rate for measles was 91.2%. And in the more populous Suffolk County, which includes Boston, the rate was 94.2% — an improvement compared with prior years, but still below the 95% threshold needed to guard against the spread of the virus. “The number of classrooms that are out there that could be the site of the next measles outbreak — it's really alarming,” Lyczkowski said. Across the country, measles has appeared in almost every state and is spreading more rapidly than it did last year. By the beginning of October, there were 3,887 confirmed cases in the United States this year, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — the vast majority in people who are unvaccinated. The biggest outbreak in decades is now unfolding in Pennsylvania, where state officials have tracked over 1,000 cases and five deaths associated with the disease. “With soaring measles activity in the U.S. and abroad, it is likely that measles will be introduced into Massachusetts,” said Ann Scales, a spokesperson for the state Department of Public Health. “We are fortunate to have an overall very high rate of measles vaccination in Massachusetts but acknowledge that there are undervaccinated pockets where an outbreak of limited size could occur.” She said if there are suspected cases of measles in Massachusetts, state officials work with healthcare providers to identify and isolate infected people as quickly as possible. Meanwhile, pediatricians say, vaccine hesitancy is on the rise, fueled at least in part by statements from President Trump and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. questioning the safety of routine childhood vaccines, despite decades of evidence that they are safe and effective, and save lives. In August, Trump signed an executive order promoting fewer vaccines for children, and advocating to break up the measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, vaccine into three separate shots — which currently don’t exist in the U.S. Support WBUR These kinds of statements often come up during patient visits at Dr. Jonathan Schwab’s office in Northampton. “ It definitely has an effect on people either making their decisions — or certainly questioning the recommendations that I suggest,” said Schwab, a pediatrician for over 35 years. “When you hear people who are in a high position in our country say things that are incorrect, even if you know that they're incorrect, it starts to make you worried,” he said. “I think that's just human nature.” (Map courtesy Massachusetts Department of Public Health) Vaccines are not always easy to access — families who live in rural areas face greater challenges getting medical care than people who live in more populated areas. And studies suggest families in rural areas are more likely to question the importance of vaccines. Statewide, the number of parents choosing not to vaccinate their children for religious reasons has been ticking upward since the COVID-19 pandemic. In Massachusetts, 1,169 kindergarten students had religious exemptions last year, representing 1.6% of children statewide. That’s up from fewer than 700 children in 2020. In Franklin County, more than 5% of kindergarten students had religious exemptions, and nearly 8% were out of compliance — meaning they had no exemption and hadn’t submitted records to show proof of vaccination. Nationally, too, more families are seeking exemptions, and vaccination rates are falling. The CDC reports 92.4% of U.S. kindergarteners had received measles vaccines in the last school year. Pediatricians recommend two doses of the MMR vaccine for full protection, with the first shot given at age 1 and the second between ages 4 and 6. Dr. Elisabeth DiPietro at Hyde Park Pediatrics. She encourages families to get the measles vaccine. (Jesse Costa/WBUR) Dr. Elisabeth DiPietro urges her patients to get all their vaccines when they’re due, especially — right now — the MMR vaccine. Support WBUR When a person with measles passes through a room, infectious particles can remain in the air for hours. Nine out of 10 unvaccinated people who come in contact with the virus will catch it. “It is very contagious,” DiPietro said. The virus causes fever and rash, and can lead to serious long-term health problems, particularly for young children who are not immunized. In some cases, measles can lead to blindness, brain damage or death. DiPietro, a pediatrician in Hyde Park, said she was among a group of college students who got sick with measles during an outbreak in 1987, even though she had received one dose of vaccine. She said that experience showed her just how quickly the virus can spread. As for whether measles could show up in Massachusetts again, DiPietro says: “It’s not if — it’s when.” “It'll be lucky or unlucky whether or not the virus happens to travel through Western Mass. or Dukes County,” she said, noting the lower vaccination rates in those areas. DiPietro said over the past two years, she’s noticed a big increase in hesitancy among her patients. She said more families are asking questions and raising concerns about vaccines. “Families really struggle when they're getting conflicting advice and information from the CDC, from the health secretary, and from the president, that's really in conflict with their primary care pediatrician that they've known and trusted for years,” she said. “There’s just so much confusion and chaos.” This segment aired on October 6, 2026.
