The clinic offered free MMR vaccinations as the South Carolina Department of Health reported 876 cases of measles earlier in the week, most centered in Spartanburg County. (Sean Rayford/Getty Images/TNS) (Sean Rayford/Getty Images North America/ / Tribune News Service) Add Spokesman-Review on Google By Tim Henderson Stateline.org Measles cases for the calendar year surpassed 4,000 for the first time in decades, with as many as five deaths in Pennsylvania, as the federal government steps in with financial help for states but also fans vaccination fears and skepticism. A weekly report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention showed 4,080 cases this year as of Thursday, up 192 cases in a week. Pennsylvania, which has reported five confirmed deaths from measles, alone had 142 new cases for the week – for a total of 1,105 for the year. The CDC has recognized just two of the state’s reported deaths. Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, a Democrat, has protested the CDC’s death count; his state’s five deaths would be more than the three deaths reported in 2025 for the entire nation. Other states with large numbers of cases, more than 200, did not see their case numbers change for the week: South Carolina (670 for the year), Utah (535) and Wisconsin (207). States with more cases included New York, which declared a measles emergency, with 19 new cases for a total of 103 this year; and Iowa, up 17 cases to 39. Kentucky reported separately on Friday that cases there had reached 104, up 10 from last week. Pennsylvania, which has become ground zero for this year’s outbreaks, reported this week that a new awareness and pop-up vaccine clinics are leading to more measles vaccinations. All but five states have had at least one measles case this year. The last time the United States had this many cases was in 1991, reaching 9,643 cases as the nation still struggled to roll out vaccinations for the disease, amid budget cuts that hit programs in big cities. Pennsylvania’s health department this week announced “a surge of interest” in vaccinations as more residents become aware of the outbreak – more than 56,000 doses were given out in September, more than twice the usual monthly volume. The state has added pop-up clinics in the most affected areas. All but four of the measles cases were among unvaccinated people. The Lewistown Sentinel reported that an 18-year-old woman there died in September from brain swelling as a result of the measles virus after two of her brothers survived the disease. While the federal government has offered states more funding to combat measles, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy moved forward this week on plans to emphasize vaccine injury, announcing a new clinic and work to strengthen a database that tracks problems after a vaccination. “We must listen to patients and families who report vaccine injuries – not dismiss or gaslight them,” Kennedy said in a statement. ✕

Health officials say the infected person is recovering at home while investigators trace potential exposures in the community. Public Health has identified several locations where people may have been exposed to the highly contagious virus: Family Industrial Medical Center in San Luis Obispo October 5 from 8:30 a.m. to 10:30 a.m. October 6 from 12:30 p.m. to 3 p.m. Arroyo Grande Community Hospital Emergency Room October 7 from 6:30 a.m. to 1 p.m. 1/1 Skip Ad Continue watchingafter the adVisit Advertiser websiteGO TO PAGE Anyone who was at those locations during the listed times is urged to monitor for symptoms for up to 21 days after exposure. Measles symptoms typically appear seven to 21 days after exposure and can include a high fever, cough, runny nose, red or watery eyes, and a rash that usually starts on the face before spreading to the rest of the body. "Measles is extremely contagious, but it is also preventable with vaccination," said Interim County Health Officer Dr. Rick Rosen. He encouraged residents to ensure they are up to date on their measles vaccinations and to contact a healthcare provider if symptoms develop. Health officials say the measles virus spreads through the air when an infected person coughs, sneezes, or even breathes, and can remain in the air for up to an hour after that person leaves an area. According to health officials the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine remains the best protection against infection. Two doses provide about 97% protection against measles. Issued on: 05/10/2026 - 23:23Modified: 06/10/2026 - 03:39 1 min Reading time Share By: FRANCE 24 A file image of a sign warning against measles symptoms stands outside a South Carolina Department of Public Health Mobile Health Unit in Spartanburg, South Carolina, on February 6, 2026. © Jayla Whitfield-Anderson, Reuters New York Governor Kathy Hochul declared a statewide disaster emergency on Monday over a measles outbreak, the first such declaration by a US state since cases began ‌surging in 2025. "No one should get seriously ill or die from a vaccine-preventable disease," Hochul said in a statement. New York has reported 108 measles cases this year through October 3, including 92 since July 15 in under-immunised rural communities across 18 ‌counties, well above typical annual levels, according to the executive order. Local health departments have administered more than 1,000 MMR doses in rural areas since July 15. Neighbouring Pennsylvania is battling a fast-spreading outbreak, ‌with 977 cases and five deaths as of October 2, mostly in rural counties that border New York, the order said. Pennsylvania health officials said on Monday the state's total had passed 1,000 cases, making it the largest state outbreak in more than three decades. The US is having its worst year for measles since 1991, with nearly 3,900 cases reported, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The order allows registered nurses to order tests for suspected measles and pharmacists to vaccinate children as young as two. It also requires all MMR vaccinations to be reported to state or New York City immunisation registries within 72 hours, while waiving adults' consent for such reporting. Vaccination itself still requires the consent of the patient or a legal guardian. The emergency took effect on Monday and runs through November 4. supplementary_news.content: Skip to content Download Our AppsNewsletterAdvertise With UsContact UsAbout Us 47° Watertown, NY Watch Live Send It To 7 News Weather Sports Community Contests We the People North Country Professionals Aging Untold Home Watch Live Election Results Presidential Election Map New York Interactive Results News Health Interviews Obituaries Your Turn Craig's To-Do List Military Matters Blast from the Past National Meet The Team Weather Delays, Closings and Cancellations Sports Athlete of the Week Community North Country All Stars North Country Focus 7NEWS Community Calendar Chris Manning's TV Dinners Mr. Food Pick-a-Pet Contests North Country Professionals Community Health Center of the North Country Taylor Brothers Team Clayton Dental Office/Black River Dental THRIVE Wellness & Recovery TV Schedule About Us Meet The Team Contact Us Job Openings NextGen TV Circle Country Local News Live InvestigateTV Watching Your Wallet PowerNation Digital Marketing Gray AI Policy Hochul declares emergency over measles outbreak Measles outbreak(MGN | MGN Image (Credit)) By 7 News Staff Published: Oct. 5, 2026 at 8:19 PM UTC Share Add Us On GoogleAdd as a preferred source on Google ALBANY, New York (WWNY) - Gov. Kathy Hochul has declared a state disaster emergency over the growing number of measles cases across rural areas of New York. She said this enables the state to respond more swiftly to the outbreak and allows healthcare professionals to take additional steps to get more New Yorkers vaccinated and tested, if needed. “No one should get seriously ill or die from a vaccine-preventable disease,” said Hochul. “That is why I have taken steps to increase the number of health professionals who can vaccinate and test. These emergency measures will protect New Yorkers and support our community partners as they work tirelessly to address the spread of this disease.” Case numbers As of Oct. 3, there have been seven confirmed cases in New York City and 101 in the rest of the state, for 108 total cases this year, amid a global and domestic increase in measles cases. Lewis County has had 11 people test positive for measles. None of them had been vaccinated. Vaccine The state says the MMR vaccine is highly effective and is the best protection against measles. Most people born before 1957 are considered immune because they were likely exposed to the virus. Those who received the vaccine between 1963 and 1967 may have received a vaccine that wasn’t as effective and should talk to their health care provider about getting revaccinated. Since July 15, local health departments have administered more than 1,000 doses of the MMR vaccine across rural areas of New York state. Measles symptoms and complications Measles is a highly contagious respiratory disease that causes rash and fever. In some cases, measles can reduce the immune system’s ability to fight other infections like pneumonia. The disease is caused by a virus spread by coughing or sneezing into the air. People can catch the disease by breathing in the virus or, less commonly, by touching a contaminated surface, then touching the eyes, nose or mouth. Serious complications of measles include hospitalization, pneumonia, miscarriage, preterm birth, brain swelling, immune amnesia and death. Long-term complications can include subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, a type of brain inflammation resulting from an earlier measles infection that can lead to permanent brain damage years after the initial infection. Measles Dashboard The state has launched a Measles Dashboard that allows the public to track local health risks and raise awareness about measles. Copyright 2026 WWNY. All rights reserved. The Pike County General Health District made the announcement Thursday, stating conduct contact tracing is underway so that officials may provide guidance for anyone who may have been exposed to the virus. Measles is highly contagious and may lead to serious health complications, especially in young children. Symptoms typically develop a week or two after contact and include the following: High fever Rash Cough Runny nose Red, watery eyes Powered By 10 Boone County seeks PSC review as water main breaks persist after replacements Share Next Stay The best form of protection against the virus is the MMR vaccine. Nearly 4,000 cases have been reported nationwide this year in dozens of states, including West Virginia and Kentucky, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. CDC numbers show fewer cases were confirmed in all of last year. Measles was declared eliminated from the U.S. in 2000, but since early 2025, cases have been increasing. supplementary_news.content: 24/7 LiveNew York CityNew JerseyLong IslandNorthern SuburbsConnecticut 64° HEALTH & FITNESS Hochul declares state disaster emergency over ongoing measles outbreak Monday, October 5, 2026 6:51PM Stream New York's #1 news - AccuWeather - original content 24/7 NEW YORK (WABC) -- Governor Kathy Hochul has issued an executive order on Monday declaring a State Disaster Emergency in response to the growing number of measles cases across rural areas of New York and neighboring states. As of October 3, there have been seven confirmed cases in New York City and 101 in New York State outside of of the city, for 108 total cases this year, amid a global and domestic increase in measles cases. Since July 15, there have been 92 cases reported among under-immunized, rural communities in 18 counties. Since then, local health departments have administered over 1,000 doses of the MMR vaccine across rural areas of New York State. The executive order signed on Monday expands the network of vaccine administrators to add paramedics, advanced EMS, midwives and pharmacists. "After reviewing the latest data on measles cases in New York State, I am declaring a State Disaster Emergency to strengthen our ongoing efforts to confront this disease," Governor Hochul said. "No one should get seriously ill or die from a vaccine-preventable disease. That is why I have taken steps to increase the number of health professionals who can vaccinate and test. These emergency measures will protect New Yorkers and support our community partners as they work tirelessly to address the spread of this disease." The governor received her flu shot on Monday and is urging all New Yorkers to do the same. New York Governor Kathy Hochul speaks during a news conference, Friday, Oct. 2, 2026, in New York. supplementary_news.content: Wellness Measles cases surpass 1,000 in Pennsylvania amid the state's largest outbreak in decades 1:08 Measles cases surpass 1,000 in Pennsylvania Measles cases surpass 1,000 in Pennsylvania By Mary Kekatos October 05, 2026, 6:48 PM Measles cases in Pennsylvania have surpassed 1,000 so far this year as the state continues to battle its largest outbreak in decades. Monday's update from the Pennsylvania Department of Health (DOH) brings the total number of 2026 measles cases in the state to 1,004 across 39 counties. At least 198 people have been hospitalized, and five measles-associated deaths have been reported, DOH data shows. Related Articles An infant is one of the 2 measles-associated deaths in Pennsylvania Two of the deaths were among unvaccinated adults: an 18-year-old and a 40-year-old. The other two deaths were among infants who were too young to have received the measles, mumps, rubella (MMR) vaccine. The fifth death occurred in an unvaccinated resident of Lancaster County, in southeastern Pennsylvania, but it is unclear how old the individual is. Lancaster County is the epicenter of the state's outbreak, with 391 cases confirmed so far. Fewer than 1% of the state's cases are among those who are fully vaccinated with the MMR vaccine, according to DOH. Measles virus particle, illustration. Kateryna Kon/science Photo Library/Getty Images Last week, following confirmation of the fifth death by the Pennsylvania health department, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) told ABC News in a statement it was "deeply saddened to hear of another death" in the state. "Under Secretary [Robert F.] Kennedy's leadership, CDC has mounted an aggressive response to measles outbreaks across the country. Texas, South Carolina, Virginia, Kansas, New Mexico, and Wisconsin requested CDC Epi-Aids and worked alongside federal teams to help bring their outbreaks rapidly and successfully under control," the statement read. "CDC has not received a formal Epi-Aid request from Pennsylvania. If requested, CDC stands ready to deploy epidemiologists to support the state's identified needs," the statement continued. A CDC Epi-Aid is a rapid, short-term field investigation from the federal health agency of an "urgent public health problem." The Epi-Aid provides resources such as, but not limited to, increasing the workforce available for rapid response and building epidemiologic capacity, according to the CDC . Meanwhile, measles cases in the U.S. have surpassed 3,800 so far in 2026, with cases confirmed in 45 states and Washington, D.C., according to the latest data from the CDC. It's the highest number of illnesses since 1991. Related Articles How hospitals, clinics in Pennsylvania are responding to the measles outbreak The CDC currently recommends that people receive two doses of the MMR vaccine, the first at ages 12 to 15 months and the second between 4 and 6 years old. One dose is 93% effective in preventing measles infection and two doses are 97% effective, the CDC says. Infants aged 6 to 11 months living in or traveling to high-risk outbreak areas may receive an early third dose of the MMR vaccine. However, CDC data shows vaccination rates have been lagging in recent years. During the 2025 to 2026 school year, 92.4% of kindergartners received the MMR vaccine, according to data. This is lower than the 95.2% seen in the 2019 to 2020 school year, prior to the COVID-19 pandemic. In Pennsylvania, more than 8,800 doses of the MMR vaccine have been administered by DOH staff. Of those doses, about 3,500 were administered in August and more than 2,500 were administered in September. ABC News' Youri Benadjaoud contributed to this report. CTV’s Kimberley Fowler reports. Ottawa Public Health (OPH) is alerting residents to several possible measles exposure locations in connection with two confirmed infections in the city. In a news release on Thursday, OPH said the two residents were exposed to measles outside Ontario. Health workers are reaching out directly to people who might have been exposed but are issuing a public notice in order to reach individuals who may have been exposed but could not be contacted directly or whose contact information was incomplete or unavailable. “At this time, the risk to the general population remains low,” OPH says. Ottawa Public Health says individuals who visited the following locations in Ottawa, on the dates and times below, may have been exposed to the measles virus: Tim Hortons at 3224 Hawthorne Rd. When: Thursday, Oct. 1 between 5:30 and 8 p.m. (Monitor until Thursday, Oct. 22) Your Independent Grocer at 1910 St. Laurent Blvd. When: Friday, Oct. 2 between 3:15 and 5:45 p.m. (Monitor until Friday, Oct. 23) Rexall Drugstore at 1910 St. Laurent Blvd. When: Friday, Oct. 2 between 3:45 and 6 p.m. (Monitor until Friday, Oct. 23) Metro Supermarket at 2261 Walkley Rd. When: Friday, Oct. 2 between 4 and 6:15 p.m. (Monitor until Friday, Oct. 23) Subway at 3190 Hawthorne Rd. When: Friday, Oct. 2 between 5:30 and 8 p.m. (Monitor until Friday, Oct. 23) McDonalds at 1796 St. Laurent Blvd. When: Friday, Oct. 2 between 5:30 and 8 p.m. (Monitor until Friday, Oct. 23) Ruby’s Restaurant at 10 York St. When: Friday, Oct. 2 between 6:30 and 9:30 p.m. (Monitor until Friday, Oct. 23) Tim Hortons at 2800 Lancaster Rd. When: Saturday, Oct. 3 between 5:30 and 8 p.m. (Monitor until Saturday, Oct. 24) Individuals who attended the above locations during the specified times may have been exposed to the measles virus and are asked to monitor for symptoms for 21 days from the date of exposure, even if vaccinated, and to check vaccination records to confirm a previous vaccination. “The measles vaccine is typically noted as ‘MMR’, ‘MMRV’ or ‘M’ on records. Most children in Ontario receive two doses of measles vaccine by age seven based on the current routine vaccine schedule: one at 12 months of age and another between four to six years of age,” OPH says. “People born before 1970 likely had measles in the past and are generally considered immune (protected).” If you develop symptoms, call your health care provider and notify them of your recent measles exposure. If you do not have a health care provider, please visit Health811 or call 8-1-1 to connect with a registered nurse for free, secure and confidential health advice. Symptoms of measles Measles is a highly contagious viral respiratory infection caused by the measles virus. Symptoms include high fever, cough, runny nose, white spots in the mouth, and red watery eyes that may be sensitive to light and can appear up to 21 days after exposure but usually occur within seven to 12 days. A few days after symptoms begin, a red rash usually develops that starts on the face and spreads down the body to the arms and legs. This rash usually lasts four to seven days. Symptoms generally last from one to two weeks. (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention / AP) The first measles case in an Allegheny County resident was reported by the Allegheny County Health Department late Monday afternoon. The county said that anyone who visited the Target at Pine Creek Shopping Center in McCandless (9805 McKnight Road) on Thursday, Oct. 1 between 3:45 and 5:45 p.m. may have been exposed to the person with measles The infected person, who is unvaccinated and under 18, is recovering at home. The county said that no school exposures have resulted from this case. The health department said unvaccinated people concerned about being exposed Oct. 1 at the Target should call a healthcare provider right away. The announcement emphasized that people should “not go directly to a healthcare facility without calling ahead.” Two doses of the MMR (measles-mumps-rubella) vaccine are recommended, the county said. People who have had only one dose “may still be susceptible to the virus.” A highly contagious virus, measles spreads “when an infected person breaths, coughs or sneezes. The virus remains in the air and on surfaces for up to two hours, even after the infected person leaves the area.” The Allegheny County Health Department provides free vaccines to people without health insurance. The Immunization Clinic is at 425 First Ave. in Downtown Pittsburgh. Call 412-578-8062 to make an appointment and click here for details. The county noted “there is no risk in getting an additional dose of the MMR vaccine for individuals who are uncertain but may have already received it.”

He would keep the radio on after the game and... See Full Bio Follow: LocalNewskdkaradio The Allegheny County Health Department has confirmed a second case of measles in the county. Officials say the new case is connected to the first case, reported earlier this week. The Health Department says the cases are connected because both patients go to the same school “which suggests there was likely a previously unknown exposure at the school.” The Post-Gazette reports the school is Eden Christian Academy in the North Hills. The first case was reported on Monday and the Health Department reported a possible exposure at the Target on McKnight Road on October 1. “This connection significantly expands our investigation,” said Dr. Jillian Irwin, Allegheny County Health Department Medical Director. “Determining how these individuals were infected and the details of all additional exposures is key to successfully stopping further spread” While no other information has been made available about the most recent exposure, the Health Department say anyone will contact anyone who was potentially exposed to the virus. Anyone who hasn’t been vaccinated against measles is at a significantly higher risk of contracting the virus. “Symptoms to watch for include fever, cough, runny nose, and red, watery eyes, followed by a rash that starts on the head or face and spreads downward,” says the ACHD. “Symptoms can start 7 to 21 days after exposure. An individual with measles can spread the virus to others four days before and four days after the rash begins.” It was reported that two people at a UPMC facility in August tested positive for measles, but it was later clarified that those individuals are not residents of Allegheny County. Monday’s case is the first reported of a person living in Allegheny County. The number of measles cases in Pennsylvania this year has now surpassed 1,000.
